arxiv-2512-00148:
Galaxies like the Milky Way formed inside dark matter halos shaped by both cosmic and local physics. Jonah Rose and a large team introduce the DREAMS Project in 2025, a suite of one thousand and twenty-four simulations. Each run zooms in on a Milky Way-mass halo with cold dark matter.

Every simulation uses its own initial conditions and its own mix of cosmological and astrophysical parameters. Comparing the runs shows which outcomes depend on physics choices and which are robust. The suite gives astronomers a context for the real Milky Way and a way to measure how uncertain their conclusions are. A suite this large turns single-simulation anecdotes into statistics that can be trusted.
arxiv-2512-00448:
The rough Bergomi model captures how market volatility actually behaves, but calibrating it is notoriously hard. Changqing Teng and Guanglian Li propose a computational framework for efficient calibration in 2025, using Wasserstein distance. The model's non-Markovian structure causes both pricing and calibration difficulties.

The authors aim to enhance simulation as well as calibration in one framework. Wasserstein distance measures how far the model's implied distributions sit from market ones, giving calibration a clear target. Faster, reliable calibration makes a realistic volatility model usable on a trading desk, not just in research papers. Wasserstein distance is borrowed from optimal transport, where it measures earth-moving cost. Rough volatility matches market data better than smooth models, which motivates the effort. For a desk that must mark its book each day, the gain is trust. The model can be fit to the tape fast, and the fit can be checked with care.
arxiv-2512-00748:
Ke Liu, Shangde Gao, Yichao Fu, and Shangqi Gao tackle a hard truth in medical imaging in a 2025 paper. When experts outline organs or tumors in a scan, they often disagree. Boundaries can be fuzzy, and each rater brings their own judgment to the task.

Older methods tried to produce one single outline, hiding that spread of opinion. This team models the segmentation task probabilistically, with several raters in mind. Their approach keeps the diversity of expert views instead of averaging it away. It can also adapt to a particular rater's style, which helps doctors get outlines that match how they work.
arxiv-2512-00948:
Benedikt Kantz and six coauthors let people query knowledge graphs in plain words in a 2025 paper. Knowledge graphs store facts as linked entities, but querying them usually takes a special query language, a question-answering system, or a visual editor. Each route demands skills many users lack.

Their approach has users describe a prototype graph in natural language, then edit it visually. Constrained language models turn the words into a draft query graph that follows the graph's ontology. The user then fixes the draft by sight before running it. Joining language with visual editing could open graph data to far more people.
arxiv-2512-01048:
Maya Varma and four coauthors present TRoVe in a 2025 paper on video-language models. These models handle temporal tasks, questions about how a scene changes across frames. Yet recent work suggests they often lean on static cues, like background or a single object's look, instead of real change.

TRoVe discovers error-inducing static feature biases in such models. It hunts for the frozen features that trick a model into wrong answers on temporal questions. Exposing those shortcuts matters for safety and science uses, where change over time is the whole point. A model that ignores motion should not be trusted with surveillance or sports video.
arxiv-2512-01148:
Hamza Tahboub, Weiyan Shi, Gang Hua, and Huaizu Jiang present SocialFusion in a 2025 paper on social AI. Understanding social interactions from visual cues is fundamental for an AI that behaves competently around people. Powerful pretrained vision-language models do well at many tasks, yet they struggle to learn several social perception tasks at once.

Training them jointly often causes negative transfer, where learning one task hurts another. SocialFusion addresses this social degradation in pretrained models. Fixing it matters for uses like reading group photos, classroom scenes, or workplace video. A socially competent model must keep many social skills at once.
arxiv-2512-01248:
Junyuan Zhang and a large team present TRivia in a 2025 paper on table recognition. Table recognition turns a picture of a table into a structured form like HTML or Markdown. It is a core part of document parsing, and it has long relied on supervised learning with labeled examples.

Recent work fine-tunes vision-language models on those labels at scale. TRivia instead fine-tunes such models in a self-supervised way for table recognition. Learning without hand-labeled tables could make document tools cheaper to build for new languages and layouts. Accurate table extraction underpins search, finance, and research tools that read documents.
arxiv-2512-01348:
Sayantan Dey, Alireza Alaei, and Partha Pratim Roy tackle reading handwriting in scarce languages. Tools for neat printed text are strong now. Hand-written text at the scale of a full page is much harder. The task is worse for tongues like Hindi and Urdu with few digital aids.

Scripts in those tongues link letters in ways that foil simple cuts. The team works on page-level reading for such scripts. Their aim is robust optical reading that needs fewer aids. Better tools would open books, forms, and notes in those tongues to search and study.
arxiv-2512-01748:
Stella Etuk and Ashraf Matrawy add sensitivity-aware privacy to language model training. Models can memorize training text, which risks leaking private facts. Differential privacy adds noise to guard that data. Classic methods add the same noise to all parameters.

Uniform noise wastes privacy budget on low-risk parts. Their SA-ADP method scales noise by sensitivity. Sensitive parts get more guard, dull parts get less. That split aims to keep model quality higher at the same privacy level for downstream tasks. Sensitivity scores come from the training data itself, so no hand-made list of private fields is needed before the method can run.
arxiv-2512-01848:
Jinghan Jia, Nathalie Baracaldo, and Sijia Liu make large reasoning models safer with reinforcement learning. Reasoning models write out thought chains. That helps math and logic a lot. It also creates new safety risks inside the chain itself. Unsafe acts can hide in middle steps while final answers look clean.

Training past supervised fine-tuning is their route. Reinforcement signals reward safe reasoning, not just safe endings. The team aims to lift reasoning skill and safety together. Safer chains matter as reasoning models move into health, law, and finance work. Reward design targets the chain, not just the answer, which is where the paper locates the new risk in reasoning models.
arxiv-2512-01948:
Deep research agents are AI systems meant to write analyst-level reports by searching, reading, and synthesizing sources on their own. A 2025 paper from the OPPO AI Agent Team asks how close these systems are to being genuinely useful, rather than merely impressive on question-answering tests.

Most existing agents were validated on benchmarks of short answers, while the harder job of writing a full report went largely unmeasured. The benchmarks that do test reports suffer from fuzzy tasks and subjective scoring, which hides real user needs. The authors' assessment aims to ground the field in what people actually ask research agents to produce.
arxiv-2512-02148:
The flavors of quarks and leptons follow a pattern no one fully understands, and theories that explain it invoke symmetries broken at enormous energies. Anna Chrysostomou and four co-authors show in 2025 that breaking such a flavour symmetry in the early universe could ring gravitational waves loud enough to hear.

They use a flavour gauge group as their working example, with symmetry breaking at scales far beyond any collider's reach. A phase transition at those energies would leave a gravitational-wave signal that future observatories might detect. That turns an untestable high-energy idea into an observational target, one of the few handles on physics at such extremes.
arxiv-2512-02248:
A pulsar's flicker can be unfolded to remove the smearing caused by interstellar gas, a trick called cyclic deconvolution, but only for the right pulsars and telescopes. Jacob Turner evaluates in 2025 the prospects for the technique across a sample of hundreds of pulsars with fast spin periods.

Using the cyclic figure of merit, he rates the chances for many telescope and frequency combinations. He finds the most promising frequency range sits at low frequencies, making observatories like uGMRT, LOFAR, and the MWA the best-suited instruments. A clear prospect map tells observers where cyclic spectroscopy can realistically deliver ultra-sharp views of pulsar emission.
arxiv-2512-02748:
Philip Schaten and co-authors add live streaming to BART, a toolbox for magnetic resonance imaging reconstruction. Interactive real time MRI needs modular parts that pass data along a pipeline without pausing. Rebuilding images while the scan runs lets operators adjust on the fly.

A new protocol streams multidimensional arrays into BART's reconstruction algorithms. Demonstrations use radial FLASH imaging, mixing iterative reconstruction with dynamic coil compression and gradient delay correction. Live, modular reconstruction could shorten scans and improve imaging for moving organs, children, and guided interventions. Live views let a tech move the scan while the child still lies still, which cuts the need for a second pass in most cases.
arxiv-2512-03048:
Austin Spizzirri argues that AI alignment should grow well formed agents rather than stamp values into them. Encoding fixed human value content hits a specification trap, he argues. That trap joins the is ought gap, deep value pluralism, and an extended frame problem into one structural instability.

His syntropic frameworks paper proposes process based, multi agent, developmental mechanisms instead. Agents would become reasons responsive through growth, not through frozen rules. Philosophical groundwork of this kind shapes how labs and lawmakers frame the alignment problem before technical choices harden. Fixed lists of right and wrong age fast in a world that shifts. Growth based frames may age with more grace than rule books cast in stone at one point.
arxiv-2512-03148:
Two models of strongly linked electrons may in fact be one. Yuting Bai and Philip Phillips prove that claim in this 2025 work. One model is the Hatsugai-Kohmoto model with momentum mixing, and the other is the Hubbard model with a twist.

Their proof shows the first model equals the twisted Hubbard model. They then use a known result that a twist does not change bulk physics. So the two models share the same bulk behavior in the charge sector. The result can simplify study of these hard electron systems. Charge behavior is often the part experiments probe first, so the proof has direct value.
arxiv-2512-03348:
Dark matter might slowly decay over cosmic time. Javier Juarez Jimenez and Ana Avilez-López forecast how well future surveys can test that idea in this 2025 work. They focus on two numbers: the share of dark matter that is unstable, and its decay rate.

Their forecasts use redshift-space distortions, patterns in galaxy positions caused by motion. They apply a Fisher matrix method with data expected from Euclid and BOSS. Clear forecasts tell survey teams what precision to aim for. They also show whether decaying dark matter can be told apart from the standard model. Redshift distortions are already measured by surveys, so forecasts rest on proven data types.
arxiv-2512-03548:
Aircraft that take off vertically must tilt into forward flight smoothly. Zexin Lin and co-authors present a learning-based control method in this 2025 work. The tilting rotor shifts the center of gravity and thrust direction during transition.

Current methods control altitude and position separately. That split causes strong vibration and limits adaptability. A learned controller that handles the coupled dynamics could smooth the transition. Safer transitions matter for air taxis and delivery drones now in development. Learning control can adapt to each aircraft, rather than one fixed model for all, which matters as tilting designs vary between makers.
arxiv-2601-06948:
Zhuoran Tan and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers operational runtime behavior mining for Open-Source supply chain security. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Open-source software (OSS) is a critical component of modern software systems.

Yet supply chain security remains challenging in practice due to unavailable or obfuscated source code. Consequently, security teams often rely on runtime observations collected from sandboxed executions to investigate suspicious third-party components. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07048:
Hunter McCoy and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers GPU-Accelerated ANNS. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) is a core problem in machine learning and information retrieval. GPUs offer a promising path to high-performance ANNS through massive parallelism and co-location with downstream applications.

But current GPU indices face three limitations: inability to update without full rebuilds. Lack of efficient quantization for high-dimensional vectors, and poor latency hiding due to data-dependent memory accesses. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07148:
Zhengxiang Wang and Zeyu Dong wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how well AI models think about time. They set out a test called Time Puzzles. Each puzzle asks for a date. To find the date, a model must work step by step from clues. The test checks reasoning that loops back on facts more than once.

Each puzzle mixes two kinds of clues. Some clues pin a fact to a set point in time. The rest link dates by the rules of calendars from more than one culture. A puzzle can have one valid date or more than one. A program builds the puzzles, so the test can stay fresh and hard to game. New sets can be made on demand for checks that go on over time. The test gives teams a clean way to grade time-based thought in a model.
arxiv-2601-07848:
A large Project 8 team studies cyclotron signals inside resonant cavities. Many tests in physics need a grasp of signals from single particles in complex field setups. That grasp is key for cyclotron radiation emission spectroscopy, called CRES. In CRES, charged particles give off such signals, and the tone of the signal tells their energy. Project 8 aims to measure the neutrino mass with this technique. Their 2026 preprint studies the signals in cavities.

A resonant cavity shapes the signal in ways free space does not. A wrong read of those shapes would skew the energy result. Neutrino mass is tiny, so the experiment needs extreme precision. To map the signals with care is core work, not a side detail. The paper serves those who build CRES detectors. It supports a measurement that could settle a basic open question about neutrinos. The full chain must be exact.
arxiv-2601-07948:
Yannick Molinghen and colleagues teach local search to choose its own neighborhoods with reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning has recently been used to improve combinatorial optimization. Its value inside local search metaheuristics is comparatively underexamined. Local search improves solutions by exploring nearby variants, called neighborhoods. Which neighborhood to use, and when, strongly affects results. Their 2026 preprint studies learning methods for that choice.

A learned policy could adapt neighborhood choice to the problem's current state. That beats fixed schedules and hand-tuned rules. The authors come from Belgian universities and a research center focused on applied optimization. Better local search helps routing, scheduling, and planning problems everywhere. The paper serves optimization scholars. It tests reinforcement learning in a workhorse method rather than a showcase problem.
arxiv-2601-08048: Laurin Gray, Katherine Rhode, and Luisa Rebull measure how fast very young stars spin. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses sharp optical spectra from the Hydra tool on the WIYN telescope. The targets are T Tauri stars, which are sun-like stars in their first few million years. The team reports projected spin speeds for 54 stars in IC 5070 and 99 stars in IC 348. Those speeds, plus size estimates, show how young stars shed or keep angular momentum as they form.
arxiv-2601-08148: Seokho Ahn, Sungbok Shin, and Young-Duk Seo enrich user profiles for recommender systems with language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that rich profiles of user preferences are key to better recommendations. Yet there is no consensus on how best to build or use such profiles. The authors revisit recent profiling approaches along four dimensions: knowledge base, preference indicator, impact range, and subject. They then fold semantic profiles into a knowledge graph. The aim is recommendations grounded in structured preference knowledge, not just click history.
arxiv-2601-08348: RotCurves is a Python package for fitting galactic rotation curves at high redshift. The package paper is authored by A. Nestor Shachar, A. Sternberg, S. H. Price, and many collaborators. Rotation curves trace how fast stars and gas orbit at each radius in a galaxy. At high redshift those curves test how early galaxies and their dark matter halos formed. Efficient modelling matters because distant galaxy samples are growing fast. A shared open package lets teams fit curves with the same tools and compare results across surveys.
arxiv-2601-08448:
Kexin Bao and four co-authors split few-shot class-incremental learning into static and dynamic stages. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets systems that must recognize new classes from few examples over time. The core tension is the stability-plasticity dilemma: keep old knowledge while gaining new knowledge.

Their framework, Static-Dynamic Collaboration, assigns the two stages distinct roles to balance that trade-off. Freezing what should stay stable and adapting what should move can cut forgetting. Systems that learn in the field, from scanners to wildlife cameras, face exactly this dilemma. The stage split offers a clean pattern for continual learners with scarce new data.
arxiv-2601-08848:
Zihe Zhang and four co-authors build a chat model to help care for kids in their first three years. Most care bots give the same tips to all. But young kids vary in mood type. One child is shy and slow to warm. The next is bold and quick to fuss. Good care advice should fit the child in front of you.

Their model is called PediaMind-R1. It uses a classic mood frame from child study, tied to a graph of facts on mood types. It then tunes its tips to the mood of the child. A reader in child health tech gets a care bot plan with a clear base. It ties each tip to a known view of how young kids differ.
arxiv-2601-09448:
Ioannis Stylianou and four co-authors let a language model turn words into sound settings. Their 2026 arXiv paper maps natural language prompts to equalizer settings for audio playback. Sound control becomes a conversation: a listener can ask for warmer or brighter sound in plain words.

Standard equalization is static and manual, and it adapts poorly when mood, place, or company changes. The authors tune their system to population-level taste rather than one listener. That choice aims at settings that please most users out of the box. The work points toward audio gear that takes requests the way a good DJ does.
arxiv-2601-09548:
Lucas Michel, Pierre Mathonet, and Naïm Zénaïdi refine a basic tool for carving up real space. Their 2026 arXiv paper, bound for the Journal of Symbolic Computation, studies cylindrical algebraic decompositions. Such a decomposition splits space into cells on which a given semi-algebraic set is a clean union.

A decomposition adapted to a set may use far more cells than needed. The authors pursue minimal and minimum versions, asking for the leanest decompositions possible. Fewer cells mean faster algorithms in robotics, verification, and computer algebra. The paper pushes further on when the smallest decomposition can be found and described.
arxiv-2601-09648:
An unnamed team describes PyMUSAS, a framework for tagging the meanings of words across languages. The 2026 arXiv paper mixes rule-based and neural methods, trained on silver standard data. Its target framework is USAS, the UCREL Semantic Analysis System, which sorts words into semantic fields.

Word sense disambiguation has been tested heavily with WordNet, BabelNet, and the Oxford Dictionary of English. For USAS, no broad open evaluation existed beyond lexical coverage or a single language. PyMUSAS aims to close that gap with a hybrid tagger. Reliable semantic tags support corpus studies of how language is used across cultures.
arxiv-2601-09748:
José Ulloa Araya documents, in Spanish, how to run a full Bitcoin node on Linux. His 2026 arXiv paper covers installation, configuration, and day-to-day use. The work starts from compiling the source code by hand and ends with full synchronization with the network.

The paper walks through the technical phases and the main files Bitcoin Core creates. It also tests, empirically, what key settings do: txindex, prune, dbcache, maxmempool, and maxconnections. A full node verifies the chain without trusting anyone else. A clear Spanish guide widens who can take part in that verification.
arxiv-2601-10248:
Laura Grigori, Daniel Kressner, Nian Shao, and Igor Simunec fix a flaw in fast Krylov tools. Krylov tools build a base for a large space step by step. A random form builds that base fast and with a sound shape. But it warps a key link.

The matrix it yields should match the one from the plain path. In the random path, it oft does not. That gap can slow or spike the solve. The team give a fix that brings the link back. They show it on eigenvalue tasks and on functions of a matrix. The fix keeps the speed and the shape.
arxiv-2601-10448:
Naeem Ramzan and Muhammad Tufail Khan grade the look of ultra HD video sent in layers. New codecs pack video into a base layer and a boost layer. Here the base is VVC, a new top codec. The boost is LCEVC, a light add on layer. A third form uses AI in the codec.

Grades from math scores miss how a clip looks to a viewer. The team use human grades. Viewers rate each form on the same clips. That gives a true rank of the layered forms. The work helps broadcasters pick a form that looks best per bit.
arxiv-2601-10548:
Xizhi Liu, Jie Ma, and Tianming Zhu study a core question in extremal graph theory. Given a small graph F, they ask how many copies of F a large graph can hold as induced subgraphs. The inducibility of F is the best share such copies can reach as the host graph grows. Turán graphs, built from balanced complete parts, are the test case here.

The paper works out the inducibility for this family of graphs. The result adds exact values to a problem where few are known. Such values show which host shapes pack the most copies of a pattern. The work will interest readers in combinatorics who study how local patterns fill large networks.
arxiv-2601-10648:
Joseph Rowan, Buu Phan, and Ashish Khisti study a one-shot coding problem for broadcast messages. One source is encoded a single time and sent to many decoders. Each decoder hears the message through its own noisy channel. The send counts as a success if at least one decoder recovers the source well enough.

The setup uses codebook diversity, meaning the decoders do not all rely on the same codebook. A distortion limit sets how close a recovery must be to count. The problem fits alerts and beacons that must reach someone, anyone, on the first try. The analysis helps engineers judge when one broadcast is enough.
arxiv-2601-10748:
Jun Li and co-authors present AnyECG, an ECG foundation model for broad health profiling. AI methods that read electrocardiograms can spot many heart and non-heart conditions. But most research trains a separate model for each single disease. That split misses how diseases cluster in one patient. It also rarely forecasts future risk.

AnyECG is described as an evolved foundation model, trained to read ECGs as a whole. A single model that profiles many conditions could triage patients faster. It could also flag risks before symptoms grow. The work targets clinics that want one ECG tool with a wide view of health, not a shelf of narrow ones.
arxiv-2601-10948:
Maria G. Sousa, Everton M. C. Abreu, Albert C. R. Mendes, and M. J. Neves study heat and statistics in noncommutative phase spaces. Noncommutative models tweak the rules of position and momentum. They carry a Planck-scale parameter, which makes them semiclassical: close to classical physics, with a whisper of quantum gravity. Such models attract interest as a path toward quantum gravity.

The authors analyze the thermostatistics of Yukawa and Lee-Wick potentials in this setting. They examine negative heat capacities, a strange trait where a system cools as it gains energy. Self-gravitating systems show that trait classically. Seeing how it survives noncommutative tweaks tests the reach of both thermodynamics and Planck-scale models.
arxiv-2601-11548:
Tao Hu tests the Frank-Wolfe method under inexact oracles in this preprint. The 2026 work deals with optimization over convex sets. Frank-Wolfe avoids projections by using a linear minimization oracle. In practice, both gradients and oracles can be inexact.

Hu asks how much error the method can tolerate. For smooth nonconvex functions, a convergence guarantee is given. The rate blends a 1 over root k decay term. An added delta term prices the oracle's inexactness. The study also weighs the oracle's cost against projection. Linear minimization is often far cheaper per step. The results tell users when cheap steps still converge.
arxiv-2601-11848:
Savvas Petridis, Michael Xieyang Liu, Alexander J. Fiannaca, Carrie J. Cai, and Michael Terry study how people brief AI for long jobs. As AI can work for minutes or hours alone, prompts grow into long, full specs. Briefing a human for long work is not the same task.

They set two images side by side: a compass and railway tracks. One hints at a goal with room to roam, and one hints at a fixed path. Their study asks which image fits how users think. The answer can shape tools for long AI work.
arxiv-2601-12048:
Pooneh Afsharijoo, Pedro D. González Pérez, and Hussein Mourtada prove a family of partition identities. Partitions split a whole number into parts. Their identities use partitions in three colours. Rules on the parts come from famed past identities.

Those rules link to the Rogers-Ramanujan and Andrews-Gordon identities, and to recent wider forms of them. The new forms tie partitions to surface singularities of type Ar. Such links often reveal deep ties between counting and geometry. The proofs add a new branch to that story.  The three colour case is the new core of the work.
arxiv-2601-12348:
Haris Khan and Sadia Asif build generative AI agents for content that users can control and that stays protected. Generative tools have changed creative work. Yet users lack fine control over output, and output lacks proof of origin once made.

Their multi-agent frame splits the work among agent roles with set tasks. It adds watermarking in the generation step itself, not as an afterthought. Past multi-agent tools chase quality alone. A built-in mark plus control could aid trust and rights in AI media.  Marks made at birth of a work are hard to strip.
arxiv-2601-12648:
Nafiz Imtiaz Khan, Kylie Cleland, Vladimir Filkov, and Roger Eric Goldman ask whether AI can log training cases for doctors. Radiology trainees must log each procedure case they perform, by hand. Manual logging eats time and invites errors and gaps. The team test whether large language models can automate that documentation.

They evaluate how well models extract case details for the log. They also identify which procedure types are hardest to extract. A final question is how such a tool would fit clinical workflows. If AI logging proves reliable, trainees could spend more time learning. If certain case types fail often, those need human checks. The study weighs feasibility before any replacement of manual work.
arxiv-2601-12748:
Bin Xie and four co authors work on process reward models for reasoning tasks. These models score each step of a reasoning chain, not just the final answer. They have achieved strong results on complex reasoning problems. Their bottleneck is the cost of process level supervision, since human step labels are dear.

A widely used alternative estimates step rewards by Monte Carlo sampling. It defines a step reward as the chance that a policy reaches the right answer from that step. Such estimates are noisy, though, and noise can mislead training. The team pursue noise aware learning for these models. Cleaner step signals could make reasoning training both cheaper and better.
arxiv-2601-13048:
Srividya Ravikumar, Abhinav Anand, Shweta Verma, and Mira Mezini probe how state space models hold long range links in data. Such models score well on long chain tasks. Most past work, though, judged them by score alone and not by how they work inside.

The team runs what they call the first full study of kernel sense in one such model, S4D. They train it on a real task, the hunt for flaws in source code that could aid attacks. They then read the trained kernels to see what spans the model keeps or drops. For builders, the study shifts talk from raw score to clear cause. It shows which long links the model truly uses.
arxiv-2601-13348:
M. Karen Shen, Jessica Huang, and co-authors sort AI chat bot addiction into three kinds. News of heavy chat bot use has raised fears of a new addiction. Yet the state is poorly grasped. Teams lack a clear account of why users get hooked, what marks show, and what forms it takes.

The team names a frame called the AI Genie phenomenon. In it they set three kinds of heavy tie. One is escapist role play. A next is pseudo social company, where the bot fills a friend slot. The last is epistemic rabbit holes, long hunts for facts that never close. A clear sort is a first step to care that fits each kind.
arxiv-2601-13448:
Sofiane Tanji, Samuel Vaiter, and Yassine Laguel make fair machine learning both fair and Pareto sound. Fair tools oft waste skill. A model can be made more fair yet leave a group worse off than it need be, with no gain for a next group. That waste is called Pareto inefficiency.

Old fixes that keep Pareto sound lean to one view of fair. They bend poorly when the fair aim shifts. The team's frame is two level. One level sets the fair aim. The next finds the best model for it in a Pareto sound way. For teams that must show both fair and no waste, the split is the point.
arxiv-2601-13548:
George Wang and Daniel Murfet set up patterning as the twin task of interpretability. Interpretability works back from a trained net to how it acts past its train data. It picks the net's inner parts apart to read its rules.

Patterning runs the next way. Given a wished form of wide act, what train data yields it? Their tool is susceptibilities, marks of how out comes shift when the data spread is nudged a bit. Such marks can point to which data taught which act. For teams that must shape a model's acts by data picks, a twin task with its own tools is a fresh lever.
arxiv-2601-13848:
Corrado Possieri designs stabilizing controllers from input-output data alone in 2026. The setting is continuous-time, linear, time-invariant systems. Classic design needs measures of how inputs and outputs change over time. Those derivatives are hard to measure or estimate well in practice.

Possieri's framework is derivative free, as the title states. Filters process the data to yield a parameterization of the system dynamics. From that form, a stabilizing controller can be built. Such data-driven control suits plants where models are poor but data is rich. The plan needs no state data, which is a plus on real plants. Plant teams can use it when good state reads are hard to get.
arxiv-2601-13948:
Nikita Kuzmin, Songting Liu, Kong Aik Lee, and Eng Siong Chng protect speaker identity in live voice apps in 2026. Streaming speaker anonymization hides who is talking as the audio flows. This real-time case remains underexplored next to offline methods. Neural audio codecs give superior speaker feature disentanglement, keeping words clear while voice traits split off.

Codecs can pair with causal language models for streaming tasks. That pairing can enhance linguistic fidelity and prompt control. Their Stream-Voice-Anon aims to raise the utility of real-time anonymization. Users could then speak in public apps without giving away their voiceprint.
arxiv-2601-14048:
Sahabub Jahedi and co-authors hunt dark matter through a rare kind of interaction in 2026. Lepton flavor violating interactions involving dark matter remain largely unexplored. Flavor violation means a lepton changes type, like a muon becoming an electron. The team studies these interactions in effective field theories.

They analyze astrophysical photons and positrons produced from dark matter annihilation. Telescopes can search for those products as indirect detection signals. A systematic study maps which interactions could leave a visible trace. Null results still teach us where dark matter cannot hide. The scan is broad by design, so gaps in past work stand out. It sets a clear base for the next round of sky hunts.
arxiv-2601-14148:
Meng Li, Tong Xie, Zuodong Zhang, and Runsheng Wang tackle aging and variation in AI chips in 2026. As CMOS technology pushes to the nanoscale, aging effects grow more pronounced. Process variations also increase, posing significant reliability challenges for AI accelerators. Traditional guardband design uses pessimistic timing margins for safety.

Those margins sacrifice significant performance and computational efficiency. They render older approaches inadequate for high-performance AI computing demands. The team pursues cross-layer evaluation and design optimization for reliable accelerators. Chips that age with grace would serve data centers for longer. The full-stack view joins chip wear to code and task plans. That join is where most of the lost speed can be won back.
arxiv-2601-14248:
Tehreem N. Hai, Kristen B. W. McQuinn, and eight co-authors report new data on a small, quiet galaxy in this 2026 paper. The galaxy is Canes Venatici C, a dwarf in the nearby Local Volume. Dwarf galaxies like it are low in mass. This one has stopped forming stars, yet it sits far from big neighbors.

Finds like this are on the rise, and they test a common view. That view says a dwarf's present surroundings are the main cause when it stops forming stars. The team used the Hubble Space Telescope to take fresh data on this case. Their study checks what the new data say about that claim.
arxiv-2601-14348:
Dominik Stammbach and a team from Princeton and Stanford study legal search tools in this 2026 paper. AI tools are often pitched as help for public agencies with heavy workloads. Public defense is a hard case. A constitutional right to counsel meets complex law, huge caseloads, and tight resources there. Defenders work under steep strain.

Yet hard facts on how AI tools serve this work are scarce. The abstract cuts off as the authors set up that gap. Their title names the topic plainly: legal retrieval for public defenders. Readers get a study framed around the real search needs of defense teams, not generic legal tech claims.
arxiv-2601-14448:
Abdullah Enes Doruk presents a perception method for self-driving cars in this 2026 paper. The field is shifting from sparse object detection to dense 3D semantic occupancy prediction. Occupancy maps say which parts of space are filled and by what. Such maps help vehicles face long-tail safety cases, rare scenes that still matter.

Current voxelization methods, which chop space into small cubes, carry flaws. They demand excessive computation. Their fusion of sensor inputs is brittle and static, and it breaks down in dynamic settings. GaussianOcc3D answers with Gaussian-based adaptive multi-modal prediction. Readers get a design meant to keep occupancy maps fast and robust on real roads.
arxiv-2601-15048:
Mingcheng Nie, Ruoxi Chong, and a team of co-authors make the case for a new radio waveform for 6G. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the physical layer, the level where signals are shaped for the air. Work to standardize the sixth generation of wireless has just begun.

Current systems fall short of the goals set for 6G. The authors put forward OTFS as a candidate waveform. OTFS shapes signals in the delay-Doppler domain, a view that suits fast motion. The paper is an invited survey of the path toward making it a standard.
arxiv-2601-15248:
Dennis Scheidt gives a hands-on guide to imaging with a single pixel. His 2026 arXiv tutorial deals with single pixel imaging and compressive sensing. Instead of an array of sensors, the method uses one bucket detector, a simple photodiode, to sample a patterned light field.

That design is cheap and works where sensor arrays do not. It suits odd wavelengths and noisy settings, where it can gather signal well. The tutorial walks through how the method works in practice. It is aimed at readers who want to build or use such a camera.
arxiv-2601-15648:
Manujith K. Michel and Varadharaj R. Srinivasan extend derivations to algebras in a 2026 arXiv paper. A derivation is a map that obeys a product rule, like differentiation does. An iterative derivation comes with a family of higher maps that mimic higher derivatives. The authors start with such a map on a field. They ask when it extends to a central simple algebra over that field.

They prove the extension works under one condition. The field's characteristic must not divide the exponent of the algebra in the Brauer group. The Brauer group classifies such algebras up to a natural equivalence. Conditions of this kind decide when local structure lifts to richer settings. Algebraists use these results when they move tools from fields to the algebras built over them.
arxiv-2601-15748:
Junle Pei and four co-authors build a general theory of quantum entanglement in particle decays in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is the decay of a particle-antiparticle pair. Each particle carries the same spin, denoted S. Each then decays in sequence into a two-body final state. The angles of those decays carry information. Entanglement between the pair can be read from them.

The authors call their framework universal. It aims to cover arbitrary spin, not just one case at a time. A single formalism lets experiments compare results across particles. Collider teams increasingly test quantum effects in decay data. A universal tool helps them speak a common language. The paper is theoretical, aimed at particle physicists.
arxiv-2601-16048:
Wan-Peng Sun and nine coauthors sort fast radio bursts by their light shape. Their 2026 preprint uses the CHIME burst list, its second full list. Bursts are oft split into those that repeat and those seen once. It is not clear if the two groups are truly two kinds. The team lets the data sort bursts with no fixed labels.

They join a map tool with a clump search to group the bursts. The groups rest on the form of each burst in light and tone. Clear groups would hint at more than one birth path for bursts. Weak groups would hint at one wide kind. The work gives a fresh, data led view of this split.
arxiv-2601-16148:
Remy Sabathier and three coauthors build still mesh forms that move in time. Their 2026 preprint sets out ActionMesh, a tool for 3D forms in motion. Past top tools are hard to use in real work. They need long set up, run slow, or give weak forms. A form ready for film or game use must be clean at once.

ActionMesh gives such forms in one forth pass. No long post work is needed to clean the mesh. Fast, clean forms help teams test acts and scenes with speed. The tool aims at real work flows, not just lab demos. It joins time based spread maths with mesh output.
arxiv-2601-16648:
Francesco Guidi, Jingfeng Shan, Mehrdad Saeidi, and their co-authors study how machines learn to act. Their 2026 preprint sets out a design for self-run agents. The design copies two ways that the human brain learns. One way links cues in the world with what tends to follow them.

Most built systems learn only from gains and losses after an act. Human brains also let cues sway a choice before the result is known. The authors join both styles in a single frame for learning from rewards. They argue that this mix can lead to wiser acts. The work speaks to the design of robots, smart cars, and like tools.
arxiv-2601-16848:
Jaume Anguera Peris and Joakim Jaldén plan AI at the edge of phone nets. Edge AI runs tasks near cell towers, not in far clouds. That nearness cuts lag for apps that can't wait. It also suits apps with tight power and size caps. Their 2026 preprint builds chance models for such edge nets.

Those models size how much gear a net zone needs. Many cells share the load in their frame. Right-size plans keep lag low with no waste. Phone firms can use the math to place gear. Such plans grow key as AI moves to the edge.
arxiv-2601-16948:
J. R. Bermejo-Climent and a team of six co-authors hunt a faint mark from the cosmos' birth. That mark is called primordial non-Gaussianity. It would show the first bits did not spread in a pure bell form. The Quaia quasar set gives a vast map for the hunt. Their 2026 preprint adds a fresh gauge to that hunt.

The gauge tracks how mean red shift wobbles across the sky. Those wobbles tie to how galaxies clump with mass. Big-scale clump bias can then bound the birth mark. Fresh gauges add cross-checks for a key cosmic hunt. They also use Quaia's map in a new way.
arxiv-2601-17348:
Srikant Panda, Sourabh Singh Yadav, and Palkesh Malviya audit how vision-language models describe people with disabilities. These models pair images with text for many public tasks. The authors look at person images where disability is present. They find a pattern worth care. Models can start with facts seen in the image. Then they shift to claims the image does not support.

That shift adds guesses about a person's life or limits. Such guesses can harm and mislead at scale. An audit names the flaw so it can be fixed. Better rules would keep descriptions tied to what is seen. The work serves builders of fair image tools.
arxiv-2601-17548:
Narek Maloyan and Dmitry Namiot map prompt injection flaws in agentic coding assistants. Tools like Claude Code, Copilot, and Cursor now write and run code with file and shell access. Skill-based designs widen that reach. The authors run a systematic analysis of the flaws. They sort risks across skills, tools, and protocol layers.

A coding agent tricked by injected text can harm a whole project. It could leak keys, break builds, or ship bad code. A clear map of attack paths helps teams guard each layer. The work serves builders of AI coding tools. It also guides firms that let agents touch live code. Safety must grow with agent power.
arxiv-2601-17848:
Marcos V. de S. Silva, Manuel E. Rodrigues, and C. F. S. Pereira ask if odd black hole mimics can live in a changed theory of gravity. Their 2026 preprint studies black bounces in three dimensions. A black bounce is a shape that acts like a black hole but has no single point of infinite density. The shapes were first found in general relativity. The team works in f(R) gravity, where the rules of gravity are broadened.

They check whether the known bounce shapes still solve the new equations. They also find what kind of matter could hold such shapes up. Each new solution tests how far the idea of a black hole can stretch. Results guide the search for signs that gravity differs from Einstein's version.
arxiv-2601-17948:
Z. Asmaee and K. Azizi compute quantities that reveal the spin structure inside heavy baryons. Their 2026 preprint studies tensor form factors of decuplet hyperons. The particles in view are the Omega-minus, Sigma-star-plus, and Xi-star-minus. Form factors encode how a particle's insides respond to probes. Tensor ones carry news about spin and internal dynamics that simpler factors miss.

The team works within QCD sum rules, a method that ties particle traits to the theory of quarks and gluons. Results for these rare particles are hard to get in the lab. Theory values guide both experiments and lattice studies. The work adds data points for some of the least known members of the baryon family.
arxiv-2601-18048:
Moisés Bravo-Gaete, Jhony A. Herrera-Mendoza, Julio Oliva, and Xiangdong Zhang construct a new family of black holes. Their 2026 preprint gives exact solutions in five dimensions. The holes rotate, carry electric charge, and live in a Lifshitz spacetime, a setting where time and space scale at different rates. The spacetime solves Einstein's equations joined to a dilaton, two Abelian gauge fields, and axionic scalars, with two added Chern-Simons terms.

Exact solutions are rare and valuable in gravity research. They let scholars test ideas about charge, spin, and horizons without numeric fog. A Lifshitz background also links gravity to condensed matter models. The new family widens the map of known black holes.
arxiv-2601-18248:
Mohammad Aghaie and Ryosuke Sato use a toy model to test a bold claim about a famous puzzle. Their 2026 preprint deals with the strong CP problem. A recent claim by Ai, Cruz, Garbrecht, and Tamarit holds that there is no such problem, once limits are taken in a new order. The order in question swaps the volume limit with the sum over topological sectors. Aghaie and Sato examine the claim critically through one-dimensional quantum mechanics of a particle on a ring.

A ring model keeps the theta-vacuum structure but drops the clutter. If the claim fails on the ring, it fails in spirit. Simple models are sharp tools for testing grand claims. The paper is a careful check on a hot idea.
arxiv-2601-18448:
Lloyd Austin Courtenay warns of a leak that can spoil studies which sort bones and shells by shape. Shape work first lines up all forms with a shared fit, so that size and tilt do not skew the chart. Teams then teach a model to sort the lined up forms into groups. The snag is that the shared fit is done on all forms at once, before the split into train and test sets.

That early blend lets facts from the test set seep into the train set. A model can then look sharp in tests for the wrong cause. Courtenay sets out how the leak works and why it counts for shape based claims. The fix is to keep the fit and the split apart, so each test stays fair. Shape fields that now lean on smart models need that care to keep their finds sound.
arxiv-2601-18748:
Aiya Kuchukova, Santosh Vempala, and Daniel Zhang study how fast a dice-walk through packs of hard balls settles to a fair spread. A pack of balls that can't share space is a clean model for stuff that takes room. To draw a fair pack at chance, a walk swaps one ball at a time to a new spot, if the spot is free. How fast that walk forgets its start is the key ask.

The team prove the walk is fast in a wide range of pack depths. Their proof builds new tools that stretch two famed tricks from the world of set counts to the world of space. Those tricks track how one part of a pack leans on the rest. The same tools work for a wide class of point sets with push-apart pairs. Fast walks serve sims in chem and bio.
arxiv-2601-19048:
Han-Hung Lee and three co-authors build a system that creates whole virtual worlds users can steer. World generation feeds games, simulation, and robotics, but three walls block it: control, scale, and speed. Past end to end models had too little data, while object by object methods fixed the resolution and lost detail on big scenes.

Their framework, NuiWorld, aims to clear all three walls at once. Users should be able to shape the world, grow it large, and get it fast. Worlds that obey their makers would serve game design, training sims, and robot practice grounds alike.
arxiv-2601-19348:
Yanhao Sun and five co-authors recheck a quantum key scheme as real devices push it out of its ideal mode. Continuous variable quantum key distribution lets two parties grow a secret key with security backed by physics. A newer two way version resists excess noise better and looks practical.

Real devices, though, are imperfect, and the light field slips from one clean mode into a spread of modes. The team analyzes the scheme in that continuous mode regime. Security claims must survive the move from ideal math to real optics, and this work checks that they do.
arxiv-2601-19448:
Binyan Xu and four co-authors defend neural networks at test time by auditing inputs from outside the model. Backdoor attacks plant hidden triggers that flip a model's answer on cue. Old test time defenses diagnose from inside, repairing the model or hardening inputs, but they stay tangled with the poisoned weights.

Their paradigm uses a vision language model as an external auditor of what comes in. An outside judge is not bound by the victim model's corruption. The shift from internal repair to external audit may hold up better as attacks grow more advanced.
arxiv-2601-19548:
Jan Keim and Angelika Kaplan write about a quiet problem in software projects: knowledge gets scattered. What a system is meant to do may sit in requirements files. Why it was built that way may live in diagrams, code comments, or old documents. As the system changes over years, these pieces drift apart and stop agreeing with each other.

The authors set out a vision for automating the care of this architectural knowledge. Machines would gather the spread-out pieces, link them, and keep them in a structured form. Developers could then find and use the knowledge when they need it. Keeping records in sync should slow architectural erosion, the slow decay of a design. The paper is a roadmap for tools that treat design knowledge as something worth managing on purpose.
arxiv-2601-19648:
P. F. Dias, F. M. Zimmer, N. G. Fytas, and M. Schmidt study a model of magnetism on a honeycomb grid. The Ising model treats each site as a tiny magnet that points up or down. Neighbours influence each other through couplings of different strengths and signs. Here the first and second neighbours favour alignment, while third neighbours favour opposition.

That mix is called frustration, since no arrangement can satisfy every bond at once. Frustrated systems can settle into unusual phases, neither fully ordered nor fully random. The authors investigate which phases win as conditions change on the honeycomb lattice. The honeycomb shape matters in real materials such as graphene-like magnets. Phase diagrams from models like this guide the hunt for new magnetic materials.
arxiv-2601-20148:
Marcus Emmanuel Barnes, Taher A. Ghaleb, and Safwat Hassan present LogSieve, a tool that shrinks build logs from continuous integration systems. Logs are key for finding why a build failed or slowed down. But their growing size makes both human reading and automated analysis slow, costly, and energy-hungry.

Most earlier work on log reduction targets neat system logs, not the noisy text that build pipelines produce. LogSieve is task-aware, so it keeps the lines that matter for the analysis at hand. Smaller, cleaner logs would let language models scan build failures at lower cost and with less noise.
arxiv-2601-20448:
Zhiyu Chen, Minhao Liu, and Yanru Zhang present TimeCatcher, a forecasting framework for time series that refuse to sit still. Lightweight models based on simple networks forecast well by catching stable trends and seasons. But they rest on an assumption of local calm, so they err on long forecasts of wild series, above all when abrupt swings occur.

Such swings are common in domains like web traffic monitoring. TimeCatcher uses a variational framework that is aware of volatility, so it can brace for unstable stretches. Forecasts that admit when the ground is shaky serve planners better than calm lines through stormy data.
arxiv-2601-20548:
Kahraman Kostas and Rabia Yasa Kostas review how machines learn to identify Internet of Things devices, and where that work goes wrong. Their paper looks hard at the identification process, from the choice between unique and class-based methods to feature extraction and evaluation metrics. Data heterogeneity across devices is a recurring problem.

They name specific errors in past studies, such as improper data augmentation and misleading session identifiers. From these they build a guideline for more reproducible, generalizable security models. Device identification underpins network defense, so cleaning up its methods has practical weight. None of the fixes call for new gear. Most call for more care in how a study is set up and run.
arxiv-2601-20848:
Weixin Chen, Li Chen, and Yuhan Zhao build fairness controls that can change after training. Their 2026 paper concerns recommender systems. Most fairness-aware methods fix the fairness demand at training time. They offer little flexibility afterward. In the real world, different stakeholders want different fairness levels. Those demands also shift over time. Retraining for each new demand is prohibitive.

The authors propose a single-train framework for post-training fairness control. One trained model serves many fairness settings. Users can dial the requirement up or down without new training. That design cuts cost and speeds response to new rules. The paper appears in the companion proceedings of the 2026 Web Conference. It targets platforms that must answer to varied fairness demands at once.
arxiv-2601-21348:
Thuy Phuong Vu and co-authors study memorization in diffusion models from a fresh angle. These models can copy training images too closely, which is a problem when new output should match the data's pattern without cloning it. Most fixes change the data or the model itself.

The authors instead look at the denoising process, the step-by-step cleanup that builds each image. Viewing the model as part of a wider pipeline changes where control can be applied. Their angle suggests new ways to dial memorization up or down. That control matters for privacy and for fair use of training data.
arxiv-2601-21548:
Irene Ambrosini and seven co-authors train silicon neurons to play air hockey, a game that punishes slow reactions. The puck moves fast, so choices must land in a split second. Their system uses a compact network of spiking neurons on a mixed analog-digital chip.

Hardware and learning rules were designed together from the start. Training by trial and error reaches solid puck play in very few trials. Few-trial learning matters because real robots wear out and cannot practice forever. The demo shows brain-like chips handling a task where speed, not size, is the whole challenge.
arxiv-2601-21748:
Lin Li and Jiongmin Yong study a control problem where the cost of a decision is itself defined recursively. Their setting is stochastic linear quadratic control, a workhorse model where a system moves with noise and the goal balances performance against effort. Here the cost functional comes through backward stochastic differential equations.

Those equations live in a space where well-posedness, whether a solution exists and is unique, is a subtle issue. The 2026 preprint adopts a framework in which the problem is correctly stated, then works through the control theory on that basis. Results of this kind underpin applications from finance to engineering, where today's cost depends on how future uncertainty will be judged, not just on averages.
arxiv-2601-21948:
Neural decoding tries to rebuild what a person saw from their brain activity, a central problem for brain-computer interfaces. It also promises insight into how the brain represents the visual world. The 2026 preprint behind this entry argues that current methods miss a basic mismatch in granularity.

Human vision and deep vision models work at different levels of detail. Deep models chase semantic invariance, recognizing the same object across many changes, while early human vision keeps fine spatial detail. The authors frame this as deep models with shallow alignment to the brain. Closing that gap could improve both decoding accuracy and our scientific picture of how seeing is organized in the cortex.
arxiv-2601-22148:
Daniel Hawtin and Padraig Ó Catháin study the symmetries of q-graphs, a generalization of graphs built from finite vector spaces. In a q-graph, the vertices are the one-dimensional subspaces of a vector space over a finite field. And the edges are a chosen subset of two-dimensional subspaces.

Symmetries of such objects, the transformations that leave them unchanged, reveal their structure and connect them to finite geometry and coding theory. Their 2026 preprint analyzes those symmetry groups for regular q-graphs, where every vertex behaves alike. q-analogues translate classical combinatorics into a richer finite setting, and their symmetry results feed designs, codes, and network-like structures used across discrete mathematics.
arxiv-2601-22548:
Dani Roytburg, Matthew Bozoukov, and co-authors sanity-check the claim that model judges favor their own work. Past studies found that models, acting as judges, rate their own outputs higher. Their 2026 preprint notes that this self-love is hard to split from plain test confounds.

A skewed test can fake narcissism where none exists. The team sort which biases the vanity claim truly explains. Clean measures matter: judge bias can warp training and leaderboards at scale. The work is a caution and a cleaner yardstick. It asks the field to measure twice.
arxiv-2601-22848:
Camilo Carvajal Reyes and Felipe Tobar build a generator for time series, data that unfold over time. Their method uses flow-based models, which learn to turn noise into realistic series. To keep sampling fast, the work happens in a smaller latent space, a compressed view of the data.

The key addition is a push for symmetry in that latent space, taught by adjusting a pre-trained encoder. Fair synthetic series help test forecasts and train models when real data are scarce. Symmetry keeps the fake series true to how real ones shift and stretch.
arxiv-2601-23248:
Ioannis Anagnostides, Ioannis Panageas, Nikolas Patris, and Tuomas Sandholm prove slow-convergence bounds for a leading online learning algorithm. Follow the Regularized Leader is the premier method for online optimization. Its behavior in potential games, though studied for decades, remained poorly understood.

The authors show it can take exponential, even doubly exponential, time to reach a Nash equilibrium. The result holds for two-player potential games, any permutation-invariant regularizer, and even tiny learning rates. Such bounds redraw expectations for learning in games. Vanishing learning rates do not rescue the algorithm in the proof, which closes a common hope for practitioners.

ashburner-facts-clairvoyance-zoist-1848:
John Ashburner gathered cases of clairvoyance from the journal Zoist in 1848, under the title Facts in Clairvoyance. Subjects in the magnetic trance, witnesses swore, described far-off scenes correctly. Others named hidden objects or read sealed letters without the use of their eyes at all.

Ashburner, a London doctor and keen mesmerist, presents the tales as evidence. Victorian believers treated the file as proof of unseen powers. Skeptics then and now read the same pages very differently indeed. Either way, the book stands as a key primary source for the history of the paranormal in Britain.
barddas-iolo-morganwg-1848:
Iolo Morganwg was a Welsh poet and stone mason who claimed to have found old Bardic texts. This set came out after his death, in the 1862 and 1874 printings of his work. The editor J. Williams ab Ithel put the texts in print. Iolo said the lore came from the druids of old Wales.

In truth, much of the lore was Iolo's own work, shaped in his own mind. The texts set out gods, rites, and rules for bards in a neat scheme. False as old lore, the book still shaped the whole modern druid revival.
bronte-tenant-of-wildfell-hall-1848:
Anne Brontë published The Tenant of Wildfell Hall in 1848, under the name Acton Bell. The novel shocked readers with its tale of a wife fleeing a drunken, brutal husband. It is now read as a bold feminist work far ahead of its Victorian moment.

Helen Graham, a lone widow with a small son, rents Wildfell Hall and paints for bread. Village gossip paints her as fallen, and Gilbert Markham learns her tale from her diary. The diary tells of Arthur Huntingdon's charm, drink, and cruelty, and her flight to save her son. She nurses the dying Huntingdon yet will not return to his house of sin. Brontë insists a wife may save herself, a claim that drew fierce attacks then.
bunsen-egypts-place-universal-history-vo:
Christian Bunsen set Egypt in the frame of all past time in Vol. 1 of Egypt's Place in Universal History, out in English in 1848. Bunsen was a man of state and a deep sage of tongues. Charles Cottrell turned his German text to English. This tome lays the base: sources, scripts, and the first dates for the kings.

His dates were bold and oft too long. Yet he taught English fans to ask when, not just what. The set runs to five fat tomes. This first one is its ground stone.
cia-0000008648:
A communist terrorist group planned to abduct an American official in Cordoba, a CIA report warned in October 1964. The heading gives the target and city but leaves the group's name to the file itself. Threat reports of this kind circulated to protect officials abroad.

Abduction plots forced embassies and consulates to weigh guards, routes, and daily habits. Most warnings never became public, and many plots never came off. Preserved here, the report shows the security side of Cold War work in Latin America. It also shows how much intelligence work dealt in threats stopped, or feared, rather than events completed.

A camp holding both groups shows how captivity worked below the level of Hanoi's famous prisons. Prisoners shared guards, rations, and risk, whatever their uniforms. The pairing joins air losses to a prisoner sighting in one report, as field items often did. A non-American prisoner widens the file beyond US cases, matching the war's real mix of nations. Egypt's 1955 arms deal with the Soviet bloc stunned the West, and in September that year the CIA weighed what would follow from it. The paper judges how Soviet weapons would shift the balance between Egypt and Israel. It also asks how far Moscow's influence in the Arab world might now grow. The estimate marks the moment the Cold War moved openly into the Middle East, with effects that lasted for decades.

The paper surveys Indonesia's outlook with special weight on this dispute. It weighs Sukarno's threats, Dutch resolve, and the risk of open fighting. Within two years the territory passed to Indonesia under a UN-brokered deal, so the study shows the question while its answer was still contested.
