For the moment Lima's left was rallying openly to Havana's example and banner. The short item tracks the work and the groups carrying it out across the country that year.
cia-0000136148: The record dated 3 April 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about a request that Waldorf be interviewed, vetting one more name in the operation's address book. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136248: A cable of 5 May 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with a command message for CADICK on command authority established, the rest breaking off. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136348: Final Operational Situation Report No. 16, dated 30 June 1954, closes the PBSUCCESS sitrep series. By LINC's orders, all troops were told to hold positions, prepare defenses, and be ready to resume attack if the enemy committed treachery. Leaflets announcing cease-fire preparations were dropped on friendly and enemy troops alike, and the report credits the broadcast campaign with helping end hostilities. Contrary to its older catalog date in May, the text is dated 30 June.
cia-0000139048: Information on Gerhart Eisler is requested from the FBI in this March 1944 letter. Eisler arrived in this country from Mexico. There he was connected with a publishing house and group. He is reported to have advised the Communist Party here from 1933 to 1935. He is described as a key man in the Comintern. He wrote articles for the Daily Worker as Hans Berger. He is believed to live in Hollywood, California. Close relations with Soviet officials are reported. Thanks close the letter.
cia-0000139448: Two Arab-American leaders' hostage mission disappointed them. The DCI Hostage Location Task Force reports it for 3-19 December 1986. The two leaders visited Lebanon and Syria recently. They sought release of the American hostages. On 19 December they met with officials in Washington. The National Security Council and State Department attended. The task force attended too. The men conceded their disappointment. They could not verify they ever met the captors' representatives. Their public claims said otherwise.
cia-03002348: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1955/11/06, a CIA publication. Another November briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-03156048: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1959/08/10, a CIA publication. Another August briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
cia-03179148: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1956/03/01, a CIA publication. The March briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-03189348: March 1, 1960 opened with this intelligence bulletin. The daily briefing reached Washington's leadership. A new month of Cold War watching. The library keeps the document safe. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Kept for readers. Kept for readers.
cia-06164248: ARAB PERCEPTIONS OF THE UNITED STATES, a CIA assessment. The Arab view. This file preserves that declassified paper. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
cia-06975748: RE: POLITICAL PLAYBOOK, PRESENTED BY THE U.S. POSTAL SERVICE: BERNIE'S MATH: BO, a CIA document. The playbook file. This file preserves that declassified paper. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cleland-fanny-hill-1748: John Cleland's 1748 Fanny Hill follows a young woman's life in London brothels. It became the most banned book in English. The Tower library holds the full text. It tested every censor. Ink shocked. Bans failed. Prose endured. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
crowe-night-side-of-nature-1848:
Catherine Crowe made ghosts a grave theme in The Night-Side of Nature, her book of 1848. Crowe was a tale smith in Edinburgh. She felt that men of science scorned tales of shades for no good cause. She set out to hoard the best tales: shades at death beds, dreams that rang true, and houses no one could rest in.

Her calm, clear prose won a wide crowd. The book came just as the Fox raps crossed the sea. It primed the land to take the new faith to heart. It is a ground stone of ghost lore.
daedalus-sea-serpent-reports-1848:
A British warship met a sea serpent in the South Atlantic in 1848, and the report would not die. The Daedalus dossier in The Zoologist gathers Captain Peter M'Quhae's report to the Admiralty, Lieutenant Edgar Drummond's journal, and the Times prints of the tale. A like sighting from the ship Daphne stands in the file as well.

The officers told of a long neck, a mane, and a head held clear of the sea at close range. Their rank and calm tone made doubters pause, and the row ran for months in print. No sea serpent report of the age is half so famed. The dossier is the whole quarrel in one file.
diderot-bijoux-indiscrets-1748: Diderot's 1748 Les Bijoux indiscrets tells of a magic ring that makes women's jewels talk. It mocks court morals. The Tower library holds the full text. It whispered scandal. Rings heard. Courts blushed. Wit stung. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
doe-osti-3022475-final-tachnical-report-: DE-SC0023548 got technically finalled, and this DOE final reports the award. The pages detail the findings. The researchers get their closeout. The report was final technical. The data were researcher. The award was closeout. The technical was final. The report was closeout.
dumas-louise-de-la-valliere-1848:
Alexandre Dumas published Louise de la Vallière as part of the Vicomte de Bragelonne cycle in France. English editions carve this titled part from the vast final musketeer novel for separate sale in translation. Its center is the young Louis XIV's first great love and the court it remakes around him.

Louise, a maid of honor, loves the king in secret and with a pure, timid heart. Raoul, her betrothed and Athos's son, is sent away as the king clears his path to her. Madame de Montespan waits in the wings, and court ritual smothers private feeling with splendor. Aramis meanwhile learns a state secret that could shake the throne, the twin in prison. Dumas blends romance and high politics in the twilight of the musketeers' long service.
dumas-man-in-the-iron-mask-1848:
Alexandre Dumas published The Man in the Iron Mask as the close of the musketeer cycle. English editions print this famed part of the Vicomte de Bragelonne as a book by itself. Its plot turns on the legend of a masked prisoner, twin to Louis XIV of France.

Aramis plots to swap the king with his jailed twin and rule France through the double. Porthos dies in a cave blast, and Athos fades as his son Raoul seeks death abroad. D'Artagnan, torn between plot and duty, keeps faith with the crown he has served for decades. The four friends' ends give the gay saga a grave and moving final chord of loss. Few adventure cycles close with such weight on friendship, age, and passing time.
dumas-ten-years-later-1848:
Alexandre Dumas published Ten Years Later as part of the Vicomte de Bragelonne cycle in France. English publishers split the vast final musketeer novel into titled parts for their readers in translation. This part presses on with Louis XIV's young court and the musketeers' last great acts together.

Raoul's hopeless love for Louise, now the king's mistress, drives him toward a soldier's death abroad. Aramis rises as a churchman with secret designs on the throne of France itself in time. Porthos, Athos, and d'Artagnan feel age and the new reign crowd out their old free world. Court balls and secret prisons frame a tale of friendship under a hardening absolute rule. The part builds toward the twin-prince plot that made the cycle's end so famous.
dumas-vicomte-de-bragelonne-1848:
Alexandre Dumas published The Vicomte de Bragelonne in serial form from 1847 to 1850 in France. The huge novel is the third and last of the d'Artagnan romances in his musketeer cycle. English editions often split it into parts, of which this volume is the first great slice.

Thirty-five years on, d'Artagnan serves the young Louis XIV as the crown seeks real power. Raoul, the vicomte and Athos's son, loves Louise de la Vallière, whom the king soon eyes. Court plots, English restoration schemes, and old friendships strain under the rising Sun King's ambition at court. The tone darkens as youth's fellowship gives way to age, rank, and royal will. Readers meet here the seeds of the iron mask tale that ends the saga.
early-travels-palestine-wright-1848:
Pilgrims' tales of the Holy Land crowd Early Travels in Palestine, edited by Thomas Wright in 1848. Arculf in the 600s and Willibald in the 700s lead the company. Bernard, Saewulf, and Sigurd the Crusader add their own reports of the road.

Each traveler describes Jerusalem and Bethlehem as he found them. Shrines, dangers, and wonders crowd their brisk, credulous pages. Wright gathered the texts for Bohn's Library of standard works. The book lets the Middle Ages report from the ground. Its voices are raw and earnest, and it stays a handy door into the age of pilgrimage.
euler-introductio-analysin-1748:
Euler founds analysis as its own field in his Introductio in analysin infinitorum, in Latin from 1748. Functions take their modern form in its opening chapters here. Endless series unfold, and the number e gains the notation and treatment that students still learn from textbooks today across the world.

Many call this the book where modern mathematics truly begins. Euler writes the grammar of a new science with unmatched fertility of mind. Curves, logs, and trig functions all fall into one grand order. The most fertile mind of his age speaks here at full stretch, and the echo of his choices still shapes every page of higher math.
europmc-pmc10048148:
Sallam systematically reviews the uses and the worries around ChatGPT in health care in a 2023 paper. ChatGPT is a conversational AI built on a large language model. Clinicians and teachers quickly saw its promise for drafting, teaching, and summarizing, alongside real concerns about errors and bias.

The review gathers early studies and expert views on three fronts: education, research, and practice. It finds hopeful signs but stresses the need for checks and clear rules. The paper serves as an early map of both the promise and the pitfalls. It also lists questions that future studies should answer.
europmc-pmc10213648:
Hassamal reviews the links between chronic stress, brain inflammation, and depression in a 2023 paper. In some patients, long exposure to stress triggers inflammation in the brain that feeds depressive illness. Inflamed depression tends to be more severe, longer lasting, and harder to treat with standard drugs.

The review explains the body pathways that connect stress to brain inflammation. It covers the signs that mark this form of depression. It then surveys anti-inflammatory treatments in development for these patients. The paper argues for matching treatment to the biology of each case.
europmc-pmc10434548:
Endale, Tesfaye, and Mengstie reviewed in 2023 how reactive oxygen drives fat damage and cell death. Reactive oxygen species are unstable bits made in cells that can attack fats. That attack, called lipid peroxidation, yields by-products such as 4-hydroxynonenal. It is a core step in ferroptosis, a form of cell death.

In ferroptosis, damage to the fat layers of cell walls helps kill the cell. Endale traces how this fat damage links to two other death forms, apoptosis and autophagy. Those links may share switches that drugs could target. The review aims to give fresh leads for diseases tied to these death paths. Much of the crosstalk map is still sketchy, the authors note.
europmc-pmc10567548:
Liu and co-authors pushed spatial gene mapping to a new scale in 2023. Their method reads proteins and the full gene set in the same tissue slice, keeping each spot's place. Past tools could map just a few dozen proteins at once. The team stained tissue with tagged antibodies, each tag a DNA code for one protein.

In mouse tissue they mapped 189 proteins plus all gene messages. In human tissue the count rose to 273 proteins. Liu used it to chart immune hubs in tonsil tissue in fine detail. At a Covid vaccine shot site in skin, the maps caught early immune firing. Pixel size sits near 10 micrometres, about one cell wide.
europmc-pmc11254748:
Chen and a large team show how a cancer waste product switches on DNA repair and blunts chemotherapy in this 2024 study. Many cancer cells burn glucose without oxygen, a trait called the Warburg effect. That habit floods them with lactate. How this metabolism affects DNA repair and drug response was incompletely understood.

Lactate tags a repair protein called NBS1 at a specific site, lysine 388, they found. The tag is required to assemble the MRN repair complex and to gather repair proteins at DNA breaks. An enzyme called TIP60 writes the tag, and HDAC3 erases it. High tag levels predicted poor response to pre-surgery chemotherapy in patients. Cutting lactate with a clinically used drug reduced repair and overcame drug resistance in their tests.
europmc-pmc11356848:
Zhu and colleagues review a gut bacterium family tied to diet and chronic disease in this 2024 paper. Muribaculaceae are bacteria in the gut, within the Bacteroidetes group that dominates the gut along with Firmicutes. They produce short-chain fatty acids, small molecules that feed the gut lining and calm inflammation. Their food sources include mucus sugars and dietary fibres.

The family cross-feeds with probiotic genera such as Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, the review notes. Plant-based diets raise its abundance, and that rise tracks with relief in bowel inflammation, obesity, and type 2 diabetes. The authors introduce the family's diversity, metabolism, and function in systematic order. They then explain the mechanisms behind the disease effects. Limitations of the field are stated plainly, including how much rests on mouse work.
europmc-pmc1185648:
Quesneville and colleagues tackled jumping genes in a 2005 methods paper. Jumping genes are DNA chunks that copy and move around genomes. They fill large shares of animal genomes. Most teams labeled them with just one search program.

The new pipeline blends results from many search methods. It mixes match-based tools with tools that find new copies unaided. A test on the fruit fly genome built cleaner labels. Quesneville aims to lift jumping gene labels to gene label quality. Careful labels matter for reading any genome well. Details are given for the fruit fly genome release used.
europmc-pmc1352348:
Ehrhart and co-authors tested a cannabinoid receptor against brain immune activation in 2005. Activated microglia contribute to Alzheimer disease, multiple sclerosis, and HIV dementia. Their inflammatory output damages nearby neurons. A signaling protein called CD40 drives harmful activation.

Cannabinoid receptor 2 stimulation was tested on cultured microglia. The cells had been activated by an immune signal. Multiple lab methods tracked CD40 expression and function. Blocking the receptor with targeted RNA tested its necessity. The team also measured how well cells swallowed amyloid peptide. Ehrhart probes a drug target for calming brain inflammation. A selective CB2 agonist was the test tool. The work used cells grown in dishes, not live mice or men. A gamma signal was used to wake the cells up first. The aim was to calm the cells and spare nerve cells near them.
europmc-pmc1584248:
Engineered nanoparticles raise health questions that tests are only starting to answer. Borm and co-authors reviewed the risks in 2006 for a European industry science body. People can meet these particles by breathing, skin contact, or swallowing, across a product's whole life.

Inhaled particles settle deep in the airways. Several kinds triggered inflammation tied to oxidative stress. Tumor effects appeared only in rats, likely under particle overload. A few reports show uptake into the brain along the smell tissue. Skin studies found little passage into the body from sunscreen particles. Borm urges more work on how much truly crosses into the blood.
europmc-pmc1613248:
A swelling signal that helps fight germs can also wreck lungs. Mukhopadhyay, Hoidal, and Mukherjee reviewed TNFalpha in 2006, a potent immune messenger. At high levels it drives the inflammation behind many diseases.

In the lung, it is implicated in asthma, chronic bronchitis, COPD, acute lung injury, and its severe form ARDS. Beyond swelling, evidence ties it to direct cell killing. Drugs that curb its production or block its action already transformed care of some inflammatory diseases. Mukhopadhyay weighs their promise for lung disease against immune side effects.  Blocking it, they add, must be weighed against its role in host defense.
europmc-pmc1660548:
A cytokine that fuels inflammation also helps tumors spread. Lewis and co-authors reviewed interleukin-1 in cancer in 2006. Tumors of breast, colon, lung, head and neck, and skin often make large amounts of it. Patients with such tumors tend to fare poorly.

IL-1 is thought to switch on spread genes, like matrix-cutting enzymes. It also prods nearby cells to release growth and vessel-building factors, including VEGF and IL-8. A natural blocker, IL-1 receptor antagonist, binds the receptor without firing it. In mouse models it shrank tumors and cut spread. Lewis frames the blocker as a candidate cancer therapy.
europmc-pmc1849948:
Navas-Acien and colleagues reviewed in 2007 the evidence tying lead exposure to cardiovascular disease in people. Lead is a toxic metal once common in paint and gasoline. Its effect on blood pressure was suspected, but the wider heart evidence had not been drawn together.

The team gathered all observational studies on lead and heart outcomes. Many studies, including ones that followed people over time and ones in uniform social groups, found higher blood pressure with higher lead exposure. Several showed a dose-response pattern, where more lead meant higher pressure. Lab models confirmed the blood pressure effect. Studies also linked lead to deaths from heart disease and stroke and to peripheral arterial disease, sometimes below five micrograms per deciliter of blood. They judge the hypertension evidence sufficient for a causal claim, the rest suggestive.
europmc-pmc1941748:
Suzuki, Nuñez and co-authors worked out in 2007 how Shigella germs trigger a fiery form of cell death in immune cells. Shigella causes dysentery and sets off caspase-1, an enzyme that switches on interleukin-1 beta and can kill the host macrophage. The wiring of that activation was unclear.

A sensor protein named Ipaf and an adaptor named ASC both proved to mediate caspase-1 activation and interleukin making after Shigella infection. Only Ipaf, though, was needed for pyroptosis, the caspase-1 driven death itself. Unlike with Salmonella and Legionella, the trigger did not depend on the bacterial tail protein flagellin. Infection also switched on autophagy, the cell's own recycling, and that cleanup surged when caspase-1 or Ipaf was missing. Autophagy needed the germ's injection system but not one single germ protein.
europmc-pmc2100048:
Kayed and co-workers raised an antibody in 2007 that recognises amyloid fibrils, the misfolded protein clumps in degenerative diseases like Alzheimer's. Different assembly states of these proteins may cause different harm. The team immunised rabbits with uniform fibrils made from the amyloid-beta 42 peptide. The resulting serum, called OC, was tested against monomers, early oligomers and fibrils of several amyloid types.

OC bound fibrils but not single molecules or prefibrillar oligomers, showing fibrils carry a distinct shape feature. That feature appeared on fibrils of other amyloids too, making it generic to the protein backbone. OC also recognised soluble fibrillar oligomers from dimer size upward. In human Alzheimer's brain it stained all amyloid deposit types. Diffuse deposits stained intensely despite testing negative with a standard dye, suggesting they are truly fibrillar.
europmc-pmc2100148:
Haesler and colleagues reduced a language-related gene in young songbirds in 2007 and watched song learning suffer. The gene FoxP2 is needed for full human speech power. Human mutations cause developmental verbal dyspraxia, a disorder of fluent word production and grammar. Patients also show changes in the basal ganglia, deep brain structures where the gene is active. Zebra finches learn song in a similar brain area, called Area X.

The team used a virus to deliver RNA interference, a gene-silencing tool, into Area X during song development. Birds with lowered FoxP2 copied their tutor's song incompletely and inaccurately. Errors appeared early and persisted into adulthood. Adult syllables varied abnormally in sound and duration, resembling word production in affected children. Normal vocal learning needs FoxP2.
europmc-pmc2125348: A medical paper on the etiology of rat-bite fever. The rodent's bite. This article preserves that infectious disease research. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2126348: A medical paper on the occurrence of Bacillus influenzae in throats and saliva. The throat germ. This article preserves that bacteriology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2131248: A medical paper with cell respiration studies, oxygen consumption comparisons. The breathing cells. This article preserves that biochemistry. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2131448: Methylene blue and other dyes changed how blood cells burned their fuel, as this first metabolism study showed. The researchers dosed the cells and measured the shift. The colored chemistry, recorded. The article preserves that biochemistry research.
europmc-pmc2131648: Cut off from the world, small communities carried their own throat microbes, which this paper surveyed in health and during colds. The team sampled noses and throats in isolation. The secluded flora, documented. The article preserves that bacteriology research for future readers.
europmc-pmc2140548: A biology paper on the stability of bacterial suspensions, a convenient cell for microscopic work. The viewing chamber. This article preserves that laboratory technique. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2180248: A medical paper with experimental epidemiology, effect of adding healthy mice to a population. The mouse epidemics. This article preserves that epidemiology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2206048:
Malinauskas and co-workers surveyed energy drink use among United States college students in 2007. Such drinks have grown in popularity since Red Bull debuted in 1997, and marketing targets young adults. Yet patterns of use on campuses were little studied. The team built a 19-item survey from focus group input and asked 496 randomly surveyed students at one state university in the Central Atlantic region about six situations.

Fifty-one percent, 253 students, drank more than one energy drink per month. Most users drank them for insufficient sleep, at 67 percent, and for general energy, at 65 percent. Over half mixed them with alcohol while partying, often three or more at once. Weekly jolt-and-crash episodes hit 29 percent of users. Headaches were reported by 22 percent and heart palpitations by 19 percent. Only jolt-and-crash showed a significant dose effect.
europmc-pmc2323748: A biology paper on the visual acuity of the honey bee. The bee's sight. This article preserves that entomology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2361848:
Taylor and Gerçel-Taylor studied tiny sacs shed by ovarian tumors in 2005. These sacs, called exosomes, are bits of cell membrane that tumors release. Similar sacs from immune cells help switch immunity on, and some teams hoped tumor sacs could serve as cancer vaccines.

The team collected the sacs from belly fluid of six ovarian cancer patients. Protein tests showed the sacs carried tumor markers and a molecule called FasL, which can trigger cell death. In lab tests with T cells, the immune cells that attack tumors, the sacs cut two key activation proteins, CD3-zeta and JAK3. They also drove many T cells into apoptosis, a form of programmed cell death. Two sac components, weighing 26 and 42 kilodaltons, carried the CD3-zeta effect. The authors warned the sacs may disarm immunity even while carrying vaccine material.
europmc-pmc2492848:
Duron and co-authors surveyed inherited bacteria in arthropods for this 2008 study. Bacteria passed from mother to offspring can act as reproductive parasites, twisting host reproduction to favor infected females. Wolbachia is the best known of these bacteria, but the team argued that others had been overlooked.

The researchers tested 136 arthropod species, sampling each one more deeply than earlier surveys had done. Counting bacteria beyond Wolbachia raised recorded infections from 33 to 57, and the share of infected species rose from 22.8 percent to 32.4 percent overall. Wolbachia caused about half of all infections found. Cardinium, Arsenophonus, and Spiroplasma each appeared in 4 to 7 percent of species, showing such bacteria live in at least a third of all arthropod species.
europmc-pmc2633048:
Madsen and Browning proposed a statistical method in 2009 for detecting disease genes whose danger comes from many rare mutations rather than one common one. Standard genotyping studies are built for common variants and cannot tag rare mutations. Yet several rare faults in the same gene may together explain much disease, each too scarce to detect alone.

Their weighted-sum method tests a whole group of mutations jointly, weighting each by how much commoner it is in cases than controls. In simulations and in real ENCODE resequencing data it proved more powerful than alternative methods. The analysis shows a resequencing study of 1,000 to 7,000 people can find such a gene. Its mutations together may account for 2 percent of disease in the population. Each mutation alone accounts for far less.
europmc-pmc2773848:
Steegers-Theunissen and co-authors reported in 2009 that mothers' folic acid use around conception is linked to higher methylation of the IGF2 gene in their young children. Women are advised to take a daily folic acid dose when planning pregnancy to prevent birth defects, and epigenetic tuning of growth genes is one suspected route. The team measured methylation at five sites in the IGF2 control region in one hundred twenty children aged about seventeen months.

Children whose mothers used folic acid showed methylation about four and a half percent higher than unexposed children. The child's methylation also tracked the mother's blood level of S-adenosylmethionine, a methylation fuel, but not the child's own level. Higher IGF2 methylation went with lower birth weight. The findings show this growth gene stays open to influence from nutrition around conception.
europmc-pmc2811148:
Dickson, Wang, Krantz, Hakonarson, and Goldstein argued in 2010 that some genome-scan hits blamed on common DNA variants may really be shadows cast by rare ones. Genome-wide scans had linked many common variants to diseases, each raising risk only a little, yet follow-up hunts for the true culprit often came up empty.

Using computer simulations of family trees of DNA, the team showed that several rare variants with strong effects can cluster by chance on one branch. A common variant marking that branch then looks guilty, an effect they call synthetic association. Such signals can stretch across wide genome regions, which would explain why fine mapping fails and why some scan hits resist confirmation.
europmc-pmc2848648:
Hyatt and colleagues introduced Prodigal in 2010, a computer program that finds genes in bacterial and archaeal genomes and pinpoints exactly where each gene starts. Automated gene prediction had improved for a decade, yet programs still missed genes, mis-called start sites, and invented false ones. Drawing on years of hand-checking genomes at the Joint Genome Institute, the team built dynamic programming software aimed at all three faults.

Benchmarks against existing tools such as Glimmer and GeneMark showed Prodigal matching or beating them on gene structure and start-site accuracy. It also predicted fewer false positives, especially in the GC-rich genomes where rivals stumble. The program runs fast, stays lightweight, and is released as open source for annotation pipelines.
europmc-pmc2852848:
Cicerale, Lucas, and Keast surveyed the evidence in 2010 that the phenolic compounds in virgin olive oil, not just its famous fats, drive much of the Mediterranean diet's health edge. Olive oil's benefits were long credited to monounsaturated fat, yet other oils rich in the same fats fail to match its record. The review gathers human, animal, and laboratory studies on how much of these compounds the body absorbs and what they do.

The phenolics proved highly absorbable and active across many systems. They improved blood fat profiles, reduced oxidative damage, calmed inflammatory markers, steadied platelet and cell function, fought microbes, and supported bone health. The authors credit this small fraction, at least thirty-six distinct compounds, with a real share of olive oil's benefits.
europmc-pmc2859048:
Coppo and the French Reference Center for Thrombotic Microangiopathies sought in 2010 a fast way to spot the most dangerous form of a rare blood disease. In these diseases, tiny clots form in small vessels and damage organs. The worst cases lack a working enzyme called ADAMTS13, which normally trims a clotting protein, and special tests for it are slow and scarce.

Comparing registry patients from 2000 to 2007, Coppo found three bedside clues pointed strongly to the severe enzyme lack. Very low platelet counts, near-normal kidney values, and certain immune markers each raised the odds sharply. When at least one clue was present, the test caught nearly all severe cases and was right in most positive calls.
europmc-pmc2898848:
Barr and colleagues measured in 2010 how widely Americans are exposed to pyrethroid insecticides, the sprays most households use against bugs. The team tested urine from over five thousand people aged six and up in the national health survey for five breakdown products of these insecticides. Urine metabolites, the body's processed leftovers, reveal recent exposure from home, food, and environment combined.

One shared breakdown product showed up in more than seventy percent of samples, meaning exposure is nearly universal. Levels crept upward between the 1999 to 2000 and 2001 to 2002 survey rounds, as these sprays replaced older pesticide classes in homes. Patterns varied with age, sex, and background, giving regulators a baseline for tracking whether use changes and safety limits protect the whole population.
europmc-pmc2908548:
Lauring and Andino explained in 2010 quasispecies theory, the population view of RNA viruses such as HIV, hepatitis C, and influenza. These viruses copy their genomes so sloppily that an infection is never one sequence but a cloud of related mutants. The cloud's members are linked by mutation and even cooperate, so the population's character belongs to the swarm rather than to any single genome.

That view upends tidy notions of viral fitness and virulence: a mediocre variant can thrive inside a strong swarm, and the swarm can cross fitness valleys no single mutant could. It also shapes therapy, since drug resistance pre-exists inside the cloud and combination drugs must suppress the whole distribution. Pushing the error rate past a collapse point is floated as an antiviral strategy.
europmc-pmc2920848:
Segrè and two large consortia asked in 2010 whether common variants across the mitochondria's genes collectively nudge type 2 diabetes risk. Mitochondria falter in the muscle of diabetic patients, and rare inherited mitochondrial DNA faults can cause diabetes outright, so a diffuse contribution from many small genetic effects was plausible. Testing it needs a method that pools weak signals across a gene set inside giant genome scans.

Their method, MAGENTA, does exactly that using only summary statistics, which is all most scan collaborations share. Applied to diabetes and blood sugar traits, the mitochondrial gene set showed no enrichment of associations beyond chance. Common inherited variation in mitochondrial genes therefore looks innocent in ordinary diabetes, pushing causation toward acquired mitochondrial decline or nuclear genes that manage the organelle.
europmc-pmc2936548:
Eierhoff and colleagues showed in 2010 that a cell surface receptor best known for growth signals helps influenza A viruses enter host cells. Flu viruses attach to sugars on the cell surface and slip inside, a step needing signals from the cell itself.

Raising or blocking the activity of the epidermal growth factor receptor, and of a related receptor called c-Met, changed how much virus got in. Virus binding gathered fatty raft patches in the membrane, switching the receptor on. The finding names a host doorway that antiviral drugs might one day block to slow infection.
europmc-pmc2946948:
Lowry and Willis showed in 2010 that a flipped chromosome segment helps drive a major life-history split in the yellow monkeyflower. Coastal plants live several years while inland ones finish in a single season, and the two forms also stay partly reproductively separate.

Experiments tied the flipped region to this annual versus perennial divide, to coping with local conditions, and to keeping the forms apart. Because a flipped segment suppresses mixing of genes inside it during breeding, helpful gene sets can stay packaged together. The study gives rare direct proof that such a rearrangement can power adaptation and separation within one species.
europmc-pmc2965748:
Peters, Shirtliff, and Jabra-Rizk surveyed antimicrobial peptides, small germ-killing molecules made by nearly all life, in a 2010 overview asking whether these ancient tools could become future drugs. Conventional antibiotics keep losing ground to resistant microbes.

The peptides are small, positively charged, and attack a broad sweep of bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa, often by tearing membranes. Their power against multidrug-resistant strains has drawn strong clinical interest. The article covers how they are built and grouped, how they kill, and what blocks their path to the clinic, from breakdown in the body to production cost.
europmc-pmc2992548:
Venselaar and colleagues built HOPE, an automatic program that explains how a single letter change in a protein may cause inherited disease, in a 2010 article. New mutations surface constantly, and judging them needs structural insight few clinicians can compute by hand.

The program gathers data from structure services, sequence databases, and prediction servers, builds a stand-in model when no measured structure exists, and reasons through the likely effects. Its output is a plain report with pictures and animations. On straightforward cases it matched trained specialists, giving life scientists a friendly route into mutation analysis.
europmc-pmc2996748:
Huang and Zou reviewed protein-ligand docking, the computer method that predicts how a small molecule fits into a protein, in a 2010 article. Docking underpins modern drug design by forecasting both fit shape and grip strength.

The review covers the three moving parts of the craft: letting the protein flex, sampling the ligand's possible poses, and scoring how good each pose looks. Each area has advanced, yet proteins that reshape on binding still fool algorithms. The authors close with the field's main challenges and likely directions, from better scoring to handling water and flexibility together.
europmc-pmc3041648:
Abramson described in 2011 an updated set of free statistics programs built for epidemiologists, the specialists who track disease in populations. The suite, called WINPEPI, runs on ordinary computers and can be downloaded at no cost. It has grown steadily and now holds seven programs with well over a hundred modules between them.

Programs cover describing data, comparing two groups, matched comparisons, and two kinds of regression for rates and odds. A finder tool points users to the right module for each task, and manuals give formulas, limits, and references. Because the tools are portable and easy to run, the author stresses their value in teaching. Students can learn core study design and analysis ideas by doing real calculations, not just reading about them. Practicing health workers gain the same benefit in the field.
europmc-pmc3080848:
Huys and coauthors dissected in 2011 how automatic, Pavlovian reactions steer deliberate choices for reward and punishment. Cues that predict good or bad outcomes trigger built in responses, such as approaching or withdrawing, which can help or sabotage the action a task actually requires. The team used a detailed learning model to split these influences into three parts: overall value, specific action pull, and general activation or shutdown.

Appetizing cues specifically boosted approach and held back withdrawal, while threatening cues did the mirror image. Those twin effects explained why approach and withdrawal tasks are not learned at the same speed. One puzzle stood out: losses taught as much as gains in the automatic system, yet people largely ignored losses when learning deliberately. The authors frame the automatic system as a helpful prior that saves effort, at the price of occasional bad advice.
europmc-pmc3100248:
Chen and coauthors solved in 2011 a supply problem for a promising cell free heart therapy: the healing parcels shed by stem cells. Parcels called exosomes from embryonic stem cell derived connective tissue cells had shrunk heart attack damage in animals. But the parent cells age and stop dividing, forcing costly fresh batches. The team immortalized the cells by adding a growth gene borrowed from cancer biology.

The transformed cells grew faster, never aged, and kept most parent traits, though they lost one defining ability and so technically stopped being the same cell type. Crucially, their parcels still protected mouse hearts from blood flow injury as well as the originals. The authors conclude the trick preserves the therapeutic product while giving an endless, cheaper cell supply. Scale up to milligram batches of parcels becomes practical, for therapy or drug delivery alike.
europmc-pmc3116148:
Miguel Araújo and colleagues tested how well European nature reserves will work as the climate warms, in a 2011 paper in Ecology Letters. Europe holds the largest reserve network in the world, but sites were picked without regard to future climate. The team modelled suitable climate for many plant and land animal species inside and outside protected land.

By late this century, well over half of the species studied would lose suitable climate inside reserves, with even larger losses in the main European network sites. Reserves still kept suitable conditions better than unprotected land in general, though the flagship network did no better than land outside it. The authors warn that current saving efforts face real risk from warming and need new policy that plans for shifting ranges.
europmc-pmc3158048:
Irina Shapiro and colleagues mapped a splicing program that helps breast cancer cells change identity in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Cancer cells can switch from orderly sheet-like growth to a wandering form, a change long studied at the gene on-off level. How alternative cutting and joining of gene messages contributes was largely unmapped, so the team used deep RNA sequencing in a cell model of the switch.

Changed splicing clustered in genes controlling cell skeleton, junctions, and movement, and a handful of splicing-factor families appeared to run the program. Breast cancer cell lines sorted into their two main subtypes by splicing pattern alone, and patient tumours showed the same switched messages. Forcing one splicing factor on wandering cells partly restored the orderly form, proving splicing alone can drive the change.
europmc-pmc3218848:
Nicola Segata and colleagues described LEfSe, a method for finding biomarkers in metagenomic data, in this 2011 paper in Genome Biology. Metagenomics profiles whole microbial communities, and a central problem is identifying which organisms, genes, or pathways reliably separate one community type from another. Their method combines several checks into one pipeline.

It first tests for features that differ between classes. Then it checks that the differences are biologically consistent. Finally it estimates the size of each effect. Results are thus ranked by importance, not by statistical significance alone. The authors tested the approach widely on several real microbiomes. They also provided a web interface, so researchers without local computing power could use the tool.
europmc-pmc3218948:
Galatea Kallergi and colleagues looked for signs of a shape-shifting process in tumor cells circulating in the blood of breast cancer patients, in this 2011 study in Breast Cancer Research. The process, called epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, is thought to help cancers spread. Earlier work had not checked whether these blood-borne cells carry its markers.

Using fluorescent staining, the team examined samples from twenty-five women with early disease and twenty-five with metastatic disease. Cells bearing the markers Twist or vimentin alongside an epithelial marker appeared in most early-stage patients and in every metastatic patient, usually in a larger share of their circulating cells. Triple staining confirmed the cells were tumor-derived, and the two markers often appeared in the same cell. The pattern supports a role for the transition in spread.
europmc-pmc3236748:
Lori Newman, Donna Korol, and Paul Gold tested the idea that astrocytes feed the brain lactate to support memory, in this 2011 study in PLoS ONE. Glucose is known to boost memory, and brain glucose dips during memory tasks. The team suspected the benefit runs through glycogen stored in astrocytes, broken down to lactate and handed to neurons as fuel.

Fine probes sampling every second showed hippocampal glucose falling and lactate rising. The rats were working through a spatial memory task at the time. Infusing lactate into the hippocampus improved memory. Blocking the breakdown of astrocyte glycogen impaired memory, and lactate or glucose rescued it. Blocking the transporter that lets neurons take up lactate also impaired memory. That second block could not be rescued. The authors conclude astrocytes regulate memory by controlling lactate supply.
europmc-pmc3251548:
Carlo Perego, Stefano Fumagalli, and Maria-Grazia De Simoni charted how the brain's immune cells change their character after a stroke, in this 2011 study in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Microglia and macrophages can adopt different phenotypes depending on local signals, but the timing, location, and overlap of their markers after ischemia were largely unmapped. The team examined mouse brains from hours to a week after blocking a major artery.

Each marker they tracked followed its own schedule and settled in its own zone of the lesion. One marker stayed at the lesion's rim early on, then surged into the core by a week. Some markers appeared only in rounded, globular immune cells, while another appeared in both rounded and branched forms. The authors read this as a complex, shifting response, and a basis for therapies that push the cells toward a protective state.
europmc-pmc3292448:
Sapone and a large international group of colleagues proposed clearer names for illnesses caused by gluten, in a 2012 consensus paper. Celiac disease had moved from a rare diagnosis to a widely known one within a decade. At the same time, far more people were choosing gluten free diets than doctors would expect from celiac numbers alone, which created confusion.

The group sorts gluten reactions into three families. One is allergic, namely wheat allergy. One is driven by the immune system attacking the body itself, covering celiac disease, a skin condition, and a nerve condition affecting balance. The third covers gluten sensitivity, where neither allergy nor self attack explains the symptoms. The paper compares how each form starts, looks, and spreads through populations.
europmc-pmc3311548:
Yuan, Cohen, Ravel, Abdo, and Forney compared ways of pulling DNA out of human associated bacteria, in a 2012 study. Reading microbe communities without growing them first always starts with extracting DNA, and a poor method can distort which species seem present. The team ran six common procedures on eleven bacterial species, alone and in an even test mixture.

Every method skewed the apparent mix of species away from the true even balance. Methods that smashed cells open with tiny beads, or used an enzyme that digs through bacterial walls, came closest to the truth. All six methods repeated well across workers and days. The authors advise that studies of human samples build in bead beating or the enzyme step to crack tough cells open.
europmc-pmc3329548:
Hospodsky and colleagues showed that people themselves fill indoor air with bacteria, in a 2012 study. Breathing in certain airborne bacteria can spread infection or worsen asthma, yet where indoor bacteria come from is poorly understood. The team sampled air and dust in a university classroom, both while it was occupied and while empty. They compared the bacteria with those outdoors, in ventilation ducts, and in floor dust.

With students present, the air carried far more particles and bacterial genomes, up to about a hundred times more in the larger particle size range. The bacteria matched types living on human skin, noses, and hair. Stirred up floor dust was a major source, though direct shedding from bodies contributed too. The findings mean people in shared rooms inhale microbes shed by current and earlier occupants.
europmc-pmc3349748:
Hemetsberger and colleagues investigated how the maize smut fungus Ustilago maydis disarms its host during infection. They focused on Pep1, a small protein the fungus secretes into plant tissue, and searched for the plant component it acts upon.

Pep1 turned out to bind and inhibit POX12, a maize peroxidase involved in generating reactive oxygen species for defence. Fungal mutants lacking Pep1 triggered strong oxidative bursts and were blocked early in infection, while the intact effector kept the plant's alarm quiet. The work identifies suppression of the oxidative burst as a decisive early step in establishing this fungal disease.
europmc-pmc3364948:
Jeon and colleagues showed that a probiotic bacterium, Bifidobacterium breve, teaches the gut immune system to calm inflammation. They compared two intestinal strains in mice and found that only B. breve, not Lactobacillus casei, generated regulatory T cells of the Tr1 type that produce the calming signal interleukin-10 in the large intestine.

The effect ran through CD103-positive dendritic cells, which responded to the bacterium via the TLR2 and MyD88 pathway by releasing interleukin-10 and interleukin-27. Those signals drove T cells to become interleukin-10 producers expressing cMaf, interleukin-21, and Ahr. Feeding B. breve eased colitis in susceptible mice, an effect lost when interleukin-10 was absent.
europmc-pmc3386248:
Jones and a large team argued in 2012 that the resting brain's network layout keeps shifting rather than sitting still. Brain scans at rest show linked regions forming modules, but the flickering of those links has blocked their use as disease markers. The team built an atlas of regions from nearly nine hundred older adults.

Tracking links over sliding time windows proved the modular pattern is genuinely unsteady. Comparing Alzheimer patients with matched healthy peers, the team found the difference lay in how long the default mode network lingered in certain strong states, not in average link strength. That dwell time, they propose, may underpin scan findings across early memory disorders.

fichte-vocation-man-1848:
The Vocation of Man, Johann Gottlieb Fichte's Die Bestimmung des Menschen of 1800, is his most widely read book. William Smith's English translation of 1848, the first in the language, is the text here. Fichte wrote it for readers beyond the schools, in dialogue form, as a journey of one mind through its own doubts.

Doubt speaks first, stripping the world to a show of images. Knowledge answers, showing the mind its own laws at work in that show. Faith speaks last, and carries the speaker to duty, freedom, and trust in a moral order. The three voices move like acts in a play. No other work of Fichte's reaches the heart so directly.
french-constitution-1848:
France wrote a new constitution in 1848 after the February Revolution toppled King Louis-Philippe. The charter founded the Second Republic in the springtime of the peoples, when thrones shook across Europe. Its makers tried to join a strong executive to the widest democracy France had known.

The text grants the vote to all adult men, the first full manhood suffrage in French history. It creates a president elected by the people for four years, facing a single elected assembly. In December 1848 the voters chose Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte as president. Within four years he seized full power in a coup and strangled the republic his office came from. The constitution remains the charter of 1848's hope and of its winter, the republic that elected its own destroyer.
frus-1861-d148:

His report belongs to the quiet counter work that kept such goods from sailing under French colors. Southern buyers in France worked through banks and brokers, hard men to track. Hard men to track were tracked all the same, by consuls, clerks, and patience. Tracked all the same, by patience and proof.
frus-1861-d248:

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d48:

Britain had now declared its neutrality and granted the South the rights of a belligerent. Adams had to accept that step while blocking any move beyond it. His end of May report shows the care with which he drew that line in talk with British ministers. Adams treated the belligerent grant as a fixed fact and fought on the ground beyond it. Beyond that line lay recognition, and on that line Adams would not yield an inch.

In May 1861 the war was a month old, and Seward was setting the terms on which foreign governments would deal with the rebellion. A note to Prussia's minister in those weeks belonged to the first framing of the Union's case. The case ran: one nation, a domestic revolt, no foreign hand welcome. The letter reaches back to the spring when all the volume's later files began.

The letter is document 248 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

The chief aim behind such orders was simple: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Every instruction from Washington served that goal in some way. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d348:
Washington's business with Britain on 31 December 1862 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 348 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Notes on this route often dealt with single ships, single cargoes, or single men. Small cases mattered, because each one tested what neutrality would allow. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d448:
A letter of 6 April 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 448 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds.
frus-1863p1-d48:
On 25 October 1862, Christopher G. Memminger wrote to James M. Mason for the second day in a row. Memminger ran the Confederate treasury; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 48 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Back-to-back letters from a treasury chief point to deals that would not wait. The South's credit in Europe hung on cotton and on faith that the new republic would last. Memminger's sheets to Mason fed that work. With its twin, this letter shows Richmond's money men writing in haste in the fall of 1862, as costs rose and the purse shrank.
frus-1863p1-d548:
In the flow of wartime mail, F. W. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 3 June 1863. F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State, writing here to Britain's minister in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them.
frus-1863p1-d648:
The 26 October 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d148: Roosevelt wrote to Stalin on November 20, 1943, two days before Cairo and eight before Tehran. The letter is Document 148 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It was among the last written approaches to a man the president had never met, from the middle of the journey itself. The record gives the date and the two leaders' names. The letter is preserved in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d248:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 22 November 1943, at three in the afternoon, open the Sextant Conference's staff work. Admiral Leahy proposed, and the chiefs agreed, that Britain's General Sir Alan Brooke chair their meetings during the conference.

The first business was order of work. Far East operations would be taken early, so the Chinese theater could be studied before Europe, and the chiefs adopted the agenda in paper C.C.S. 404/1. General Marshall read out Stilwell's brief note of Chiang Kai-shek's views, and the chiefs set times to study it and to meet the Generalissimo and his advisers the next day. They also settled conference procedure on the Quebec model, and took up relations with Soviet and Chinese military representatives.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d348:
Harry Hopkins sent a secret telegram from Tehran on 30 November 1943 to Ambassador Kirk at Cairo, addressed through him to Frank Shea of the information services. It answers a query about the background material meant to accompany the Cairo communiqué.

Shea had noted that the communiqué placed the conference only somewhere in North Africa. He asked whether the background stories could name Mena. Mena is the suburb by the Pyramids where the meetings were held. Hopkins' answer is firm: strike out or hold for later release every reference to the Mena House, to the villas occupied by any member of the party, or to Mena itself. Color stories about trips to the Pyramids and the Sphinx are allowed, so long as nothing hints at where the conference sat. The Cairo dateline stands, and the communiqué text is unchanged.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d448: An editorial note stands at Document 448 of the Cairo-Tehran volume. The State Department's historians wrote it long after the events described. Such notes supply background, clarify names, and link related papers. The volume itself gathers the record of the 1943 Cairo and Tehran conferences. There the Allied leaders argued over invasions, borders, and the postwar map. The note is a brief pause where the editors guide the reader.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d48: On October 20, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, while the foreign ministers sat in Moscow. The message is Document 48 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. London and Washington watched the Moscow talks closely, since their results would set the agenda for Tehran. The catalog record gives the date and the two names and no subject. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series as part of that anxious, hopeful week.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d548:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote again to President Roosevelt on January 16, 1944. His letters that winter ranged across the whole war, from invasion timing to relations with Moscow. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Churchill believed in working by correspondence, and his messages often arrived like small essays: argument, history, and pressure in one package. Roosevelt received more of them than any other correspondent. Mid-January found the alliance in the demanding space between deciding and doing. For readers, this letter is another stroke in the written partnership that directed the Western war effort from day to day.
frus-1944-quebec-d148:
Santa Maria airfield is the narrow subject of this State Department briefing paper, prepared for Quebec in September 1944. The American Army Air Corps was building a second Azores airfield on the island of Santa Maria, in Portugal. Washington had negotiated the facility directly with Lisbon, using Pan American Airways as a commercial cover for the government's interest.

The paper advises Roosevelt not to raise the airfield with Churchill. If Churchill raised it, the president should make clear the deal stood apart from the Anglo-Portuguese agreement of 1943 and the old alliance of 1373. The Air Corps expected to operate the field directly. No question of postwar civil aviation control, the paper stresses, was involved.
frus-1944-quebec-d248: Morgenthau gave Roosevelt his recommendation on French lend-lease at Quebec on September 15, 1944, in a single sentence: for the time being, postpone taking any action. Roosevelt had referred Hull's discretion proposal to him two days into the conference. The memorandum bears the president's endorsement in reply: "Approved: F. D. Roosevelt." Morgenthau telephoned Hopkins to report the recommendation.
frus-1944-quebec-d48:
Emory S. Land, the War Shipping Administrator, wrote to President Roosevelt on September 1, 1944. Land ran America's wartime merchant shipping program, the largest shipbuilding effort in history. His message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Shipping was the alliance's scarcest resource, and its division between theaters and allies was a standing argument that Quebec would revisit. A message from the shipping chief to the President in the conference's run-up carried tonnage, priorities, and hard numbers. For readers, it shows the material foundation beneath the leaders' strategy, counted in ships rather than speeches.
frus-1945-50-intel-d148: On 29 April 1946, the Director of Central Intelligence (Souers) put a memorandum into the files. It is document 148 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff. Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings.
frus-1945-50-intel-d248:
A memorandum from the Deputy Director (Wright) reached Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 4 November 1947. It stands as document 248 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d348:
Formal minutes cover a meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Committee, held on 16 June 1948. It is document 348 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

The pages give the meeting in the plain form staff used at the time: a topic, the sense of the talk, and the result. Staff in other offices then worked from this record, treating its lines as the settled word. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d48:
Minutes of the 168th meeting of the Secretary of State's Staff Committee are dated 20 November 1945. The numbered meetings show a standing body grinding through the department's business week by week. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A numbered run of minutes lets readers watch an institution think over time. The 168th meeting took up the department's affairs with the intelligence question at its height. What the committee agreed, deferred, or sent upward shaped the State Department's final position. The volume prints several of these committee records. Together they give the State side of the story an official spine that the letters alone would lack.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d148:
Mikolajczyk's resignation made the Polish question much more acute, Stettinius wired the President on 25 November 1944. His telegram is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It reads the fall of the one London Pole who could deal with Moscow.

Mikolajczyk fell, Stettinius explains, because his own government would not back his program of settling the territorial issue with the Soviet Union. Without him, the London government has no basis at all for talks with Moscow or with the Lublin Committee. Washington must expect the Soviets to move fast, raising the Lublin body into Poland's sole authority. That body, Stettinius notes, is backed by Moscow but has very little support inside Poland itself.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d248:
Roosevelt asked Stalin to join the war on Japan in this message of 4 October 1944. Sent through Ambassador Harriman in Moscow, the excerpts printed in the Malta and Yalta volume carry the heart of it. General Deane had already delivered the allied chiefs' statement on the Far East war.

The President says he accepts completely the assurances Stalin has given on the point. The three countries, he writes, are waging a successful war against Germany together. They can join with no less success against Japan. That nation, he is sure in his heart, is as great an enemy of Russia as she is of America's. The short message is part of the long courtship that brought the Soviet Union into the Pacific war.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d348:
Secrecy gave way to publicity in this American draft of a first press release for the Yalta Conference, dated February 6, 1945. The draft announces that the President, the Soviet Premier, and the British Prime Minister are meeting in the Black Sea area. Their stated purpose: to concert plans for finishing the defeat of the enemy and building firm foundations for a lasting peace.

The talks, it says, had not passed the early stages, yet showed unity of purpose, frankness, and friendship. Meetings ran day and night, starting with military reviews of all the European fronts. The draft is the public face the conference chose for itself, mid-stream.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d448:
Greece had asked and heard nothing, and this British paper of February 10, 1945, takes up its case. When the Hungarian armistice was signed, Moscow let Czechoslovak and Yugoslav representatives join the Hungarian control commission. That let them deal with questions touching their own governments. Greece sought like facilities in Bulgaria.

On January 23, the Greek government, backed by Britain's Moscow embassy, asked the Soviet government for the same standing. No reply, the paper notes pointedly, had yet been vouchsafed. London's concern is plain between the lines: Greek claims on Bulgaria, above all reparations, risked being shut out of the room where Bulgaria's fate was run.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d48: Another Churchill message reached Roosevelt on 9 January 1945, continuing the daily pace of that month. It is document 48 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering Malta and Yalta. By mid-January the correspondence concerned a journey already set in motion, and each new letter added detail to plans that ships and aircraft were about to carry out.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d148:
British Minister John Balfour added an agenda item in a letter to Acting Secretary Grew dated June 1, 1945. The letter is document 148 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It follows up his letter of May 29, which had delivered the British list of subjects for the summit.

Foreign Secretary Eden asks him to say this. In view of Stalin's message about the surrendered German naval and merchant ships, the British propose adding a new item. It would go in the Germany section of the agenda. The item reads simply: disposal of the German fleet and merchant ships. A note adds that Grew passed the substance to Truman on June 5. The small addition put one of the war's tangible prizes squarely on the Potsdam table.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d248:
A briefing paper favored trusteeship for Eritrea in a paper dated June 30, 1945. The paper is document 248 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Eritrea, Italy's oldest Red Sea colony, was among the territories the peace settlement would dispose of.

The United States favors an international trusteeship over the former colony, the paper states. Its data section traces Eritrea from the purchase of Assab in 1869 to its role as the base for Italy's attacks on Ethiopia in the 1890s and again in 1935. The colony held some 600,000 people in 1931, few of them Europeans. Ethiopia has historic claims to the region, which blocks her from the sea, but handing it to Ethiopia outright might endanger the Italian population and clash with the Atlantic Charter. The dilemma ran on for years after the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d348:
Aboard the cruiser Augusta on July 12, 1945, the American delegation drafted a working paper on a German import program. It proposed that the Soviet Union, Britain, and the United States order their commanders to push one step in the Control Council. The step was a single program of minimum imports for Germany as a whole.

The paper calls for fair sharing of supplies between zones, so Germany's total import bill shrinks. Ration scales and standards of need would be the same in every zone. Buying and paying for imports would be shared, on terms set in the Control Council, and early outlays repaid as a first charge on German exports.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d448:
Greek elections come up in Grew's memorandum of a conversation with Lord Halifax on July 10, 1945. The British ambassador had called that afternoon, and the Greek item is third on the record. Halifax discussed Grew's recent aide-mémoire on supervising the Greek plebiscite and elections. On several points, London was in accord with Washington.

Britain agreed on approaching the Greek government, and in time the Soviet and French governments. But London did not concur in the American recommendation on the sequence of plebiscite and elections. That, Britain felt, was a matter for the Greek government itself to determine. Grew offered detailed discussion with his officer Kohler, which Halifax declined for the time.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d48:
Only an extract survives in print of Churchill's telegram number 64 to President Truman, sent from London on June 1, 1945. It is document 48 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The surviving passage comes from a busy day when Churchill was also pressing Truman to move the Big Three meeting to an earlier date.

In the printed lines, Churchill reports that he has spent the last few days forming Britain's new and, in his words, very complicated government, and that the work is now done. He stresses that nothing in the British election will keep the three major powers from meeting at the earliest possible date. The rest of the telegram is left out of the published volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d548:
John Balfour, the British minister in Washington, wrote to Assistant Secretary of State Will Clayton on June 21, 1945. His letter is document 548 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It answers a U.S. note of April 18 about landing rights for U.S. air lines.

Balfour says Britain has no wish to oppose the United States in gaining landing rights in any country. Britain, he adds, is bound by the deals reached at Chicago in December 1944. He cites the interim civil aviation pact, under which each state may set routes and airports in its land. Charges for their use must be fair and no higher than for its own planes.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d648:
Ambassador Winant sent a personal and secret plea on Palestine from London on July 8, 1945. Addressed to the Secretary of State, it is document 648 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Winant writes of his deep concern over the situation.

Winant reports a visit from Dr. Chaim Weizmann, the Zionist leader, two days before. Weizmann had done much good in Palestine after Lord Moyne's killing, but was now ill and worn down. His only recent word from Churchill was a brief note putting a settlement off to a peace conference. A world Zionist conference was set to meet in London at the month's end. Weizmann told Winant he would feel bound to resign his post if no advance had been made by then. Winant stresses this was no threat, but the despair of a tired man who feared a more militant policy would follow him.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1048:
Stalin answered President Truman's coal memorandum from Berlin on July 29, 1945. He confirms that he has received the July 27 paper. He also has the copy of Truman's directive to General Eisenhower on German coal exports.

The question of using German coal to meet European needs, Stalin writes, will receive proper study. Washington will be told the Soviet view when it is formed. Stalin adds one caution. Steps to export German coal must not stir disturbances inside Germany, a risk Truman's own directive names. Avoiding such trouble, he says, serves all the Allied governments.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1148:
Poland's President Bierut wrote to President Truman on 23 July 1945, three days after the joint letter he had signed with his prime minister. A second appeal so soon kept up Warsaw's pressure. The summit was deciding Poland's border and standing that week.

Bierut led the government the Soviet Union had installed and backed. He wanted the United States to treat that government as Poland's rightful rulers and to deal with it as such. A letter to a president is the highest channel a foreign leader can use. This one is part of Warsaw's drive for American acceptance, pressed while the talks could still shift.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1248:
President Truman wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on 25 July 1945. The two men exchanged notes through the whole Churchill week at Potsdam. This one came on the prime minister's last full day at the talks.

The count in London the next day would end Churchill's leadership. Neither man wrote as if the partnership were ending; the work went on to the final hour. This message belongs to that last day of joint business. It is part of the closing set of letters between the president and the prime minister who had led Britain through the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1348:
The acting secretary of state sent instructions to John Winant, the American ambassador in London, on 16 July 1945. That was the day before the Potsdam Conference, where Truman, Churchill, and Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945 formally opened. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

London was Washington's closest partner and its first sounding board in 1945. Instructions sent on the eve of a summit set the line an ambassador should hold with the host government. Readers can use this message to see what Washington wanted London to know. To do. As Truman and Byrnes set out for Germany and the talks with Stalin began.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-148: An editorial note placed after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume adds the editors' guidance at a packed point in the files. Such notes in Foreign Relations volumes cite sources and tie papers together. They may also admit where the record is silent. This one helps readers judge the strength of the evidence around it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-48:
A United States delegation memorandum sets the agenda for the foreign ministers' meeting of July 21, 1945, at noon. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Five items of business are listed in order.

First came the date for formally setting up the new Council of Foreign Ministers. The Big Three had left that choice to the ministers the day before. German economic questions came second, on the subcommittee's first report after days of work. Poland came third, on the liquidation of the London government and the carrying out of the Yalta agreement. Fourth came the same Yalta declaration as applied to liberated Europe and the satellite states. The U.S. was presenting a new paper spelling out the steps it believed should be taken there. Italy and the other satellites closed the list.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d748:
Document 748 is a proposal the United States delegation tabled at Potsdam on July 21, 1945. It dates from the conference's fifth day. By then each side knew the others' opening lines. New texts were drafted to probe and to trade. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Mid-conference proposals carry the marks of contact. They answer points made across the table. Readers can line this text up with rival drafts of the same week. The comparison shows bargaining as a written duel. The document adds one dated step to the path from first claims to the final protocol.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d848:
Document 848 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 16, 1945. It was drafted before the conference formally opened. Teams arrived in Germany with paper ready for the first sessions. This draft was kept in the delegation files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A pre-opening draft shows the summit before the summit. Staff had war-gamed the talks and written for them. Readers can measure the plan against the event. The document honors the foresight, and the misses, of the planners. It opens the working-paper run at its true start: in the quiet days when everything was still expected to go as written.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d948: Seymour Rubin wrote to his deputy Covey Oliver on July 29, 1945, about a British worry over Soviet republics filing separate reparation claims. Rubin had read the Department's telegram passing the idea to Pauley. He reports it has not happened so far. The Soviet Union seems set on treating its claims as a whole. In any case, Rubin argues, the zonal plan now taking shape makes the question moot. Soviet and Polish claims would be met from the eastern zone, plus a set amount from the west.
frus-1948v02-d548: A 1948 FRUS editorial note from the Germany and Austria volume on the Clay-Sokolovsky exchange. The Berlin crisis was brewing. This note preserves that context. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
frus-1950v01-d148: Another 1950 FRUS document on national security and foreign economic policy. The Cold War's economic front mattered. This document holds that record. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
frus-1977-80v06-d248: A 1977-1980 FRUS editorial note on the Carter-Brezhnev relationship. The two leaders. This note provides that context. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
gao-gaoreports-b-298248: Triple H Services doubled its August 2006 protest — two case numbers, one service fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
