gao-gaoreports-b-306748: Customs and Border Protection's moving expenses got a fiscal ruling in this July 2006 GAO call, which tests the relocation spending. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the moving dollars were legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-310548: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Cornell Companies, Inc. The December 3, 2007 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-316048: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Applicability of the Congressional Review Act to Letter on State Children's Health Insurance Program. Decided April 17, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-248: The Ticket to Work program needed better planning in 2005, and GAO's report says the disability employment effort could be more effective. The review writes the roadmap. The disabled workers deserved the real chance. The planning had to improve. The disabled workers deserved the real chance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-348: Troops' money troubles needed more Pentagon action in 2005, and GAO's report says further steps were required on personal finances. The review pushes for the follow-through. The young soldiers deserved the financial shield. The actions had to come. The young soldiers deserved the financial shield.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-548: Joint military training transformation needed enhancing in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were required for the program. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the warfighters deserved good training. The actions had to be taken. The warfighters deserved good training.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-748: Medicaid financing games got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says states' use of contingency-fee consultants highlighted oversight needs. The findings demand the watch. The report warns that the federal dollars deserved guarding. The need had to be addressed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-148: Lead in drinking water needed stronger action in 2006, and GAO's report says EPA should strengthen efforts to protect consumers. The findings demand the vigilance. The report warns that the tap water should not poison. The efforts had to be strengthened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-348: The Battle Monuments Commission's books got audited for 2005 and 2004, and GAO's 2006 report delivers the financial opinion. The findings grade the statements. The report shows the war memorials' money got counted. The audit kept the books honest. The memorials' books stayed open.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-648: VA hospital credentialing mostly passed in 2006, and GAO's report says selected requirements were met at seven facilities, though one privileging aspect lagged. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the veterans deserved fully vetted doctors. The privileging had to be complete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-248: The land-border ID system was struggling in 2007, and GAO's report says the US-VISIT program faced strategic, operational, and tech troubles at the crossings. The findings list the woes. The report warns that the digital eye at the border was half-blind. The gates needed better glasses.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-48: Military families outside the managed-care fold needed access in 2007, and GAO's report examines care for those who skipped TRICARE Prime. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the uniformed deserved care however they enrolled. The access had to follow the family.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-448: The Government Accountability Office dug into defense Acquisitions: Progress Made in Fielding Missile Defense, but Program Is Short of Meeting Goals in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-548: GAO published its findings on employment and Training: Most One-Stop Career Centers Are Taking Multiple Actions to Link Employers and Older Workers in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-748: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at financial Audit: Material Weaknesses in Internal Control over the Processes Used to Prepare the Consolidated Financial Statements of the US Government. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
hume-enquiry-human-understanding-1748:
David Hume published An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding in 1748 in London. Hume, a Scottish philosopher, recast the hard arguments of his earlier Treatise in a clearer, shorter form. The Enquiry became his most read statement of empiricism, the view that knowledge rests on experience.

Hume argued that we never see causes, only events following each other, yet the mind expects the pattern to hold. He tested miracles, free will, and belief in God against that standard and found them wanting. His calm, polite style carried radical doubts. The book still sets the terms for debates on reason, belief, and what the mind can know.
israeli-declaration-independence-1948: Israel's 1948 Declaration of Independence, read by Ben-Gurion, founded the state. Armies invaded at once. The Tower library holds the full text. It declared a home. Ships came. Wars began. State stood. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-albert-10:
Albert Meyer, a Danish tenor born at Sorö in Zealand on October 29, 1839, is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer, published in 1906. He began in the chorus of Copenhagen's Royal Theater in 1860, studying under H. Rung, before war service in 1864 interrupted his start.

A concert on his return paid for a year of study under Lamperti in Milan, and from 1866 he sang as soloist at the Folketheatret. In 1873 he turned to teaching, publishing a singing method grounded in the physiology of the voice and opening his own Copenhagen school. He also conducted the synagogue chorus from 1882 and compiled its Sabbath melodies in 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minden-lob-b-mo:
Löb ben Moses Minden, born Judah of Selichow in Lesser Poland in the seventeenth century, was a cantor and poet who took his name from the town where he sang. Herman Rosenthal and Meyer Kayserling wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He served as ḥazzan at Minden-on-the-Weser and died, very old, at Altona or Hamburg in 1751.

His Shire Yehudah set Hebrew songs beside German translations with music, opening with drinking-song lines addressed to dear brothers and companions. An epilogue printed at Amsterdam in 1696 scolds rabbis who let people chatter through services, a cantor's complaint from inside the pulpit. A second songbook, Zemer wa-Shir, was printed at Frankfurt in 1714 by Solomon London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monis-judah-109:
Judah Monis was Harvard's Hebrew instructor for thirty-seven years — and a convert who kept the Jewish Sabbath all his life, as Crawford Howell Toy and Frederick T. Haneman write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Algiers about 1683 and educated, it is said, in Italy, he reached Boston early in the eighteenth century. His first firm record is his baptism, in College Hall at Cambridge, in 1722.

At the baptism Monis preached and printed his own confession of faith, then threw himself into his new religion's cause — while never giving up Sabbath observance. Harvard appointed him in 1722; he resigned in 1759, on his wife's death, and withdrew to Northborough, where he died a few years later. The entry weighs Hannah Adams against Harvard's historian Quincy for his dates.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-8-1848:
Book Eight of the Antiquities of Mexico came out in 1848. Lord Kingsborough had died in debt in 1837, and the set had stalled for years. The full work runs to nine books in all. This book takes the long run of plates toward its close.

Texts and plates on the towns, gods, and past of old Mexico fill the book. The copies in the set save the look of books now lost or worn. Kingsborough's wild claim on the roots of the Mexicans drove the whole work. The set stands as a great store in spite of that claim.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-9-1848:
Book Nine ends Lord Kingsborough's Antiquities of Mexico. The last book came out in 1848, long past his death in 1837. The full set runs to nine books of plates and text. Kingsborough had spent his whole fortune on the work and died in a debt jail.

The last plates round out the store of codices and town views. Text in the set backs his claim that Mexico's folk came from the lost tribes. That claim has few friends now, but the plates endure. The set is a chief source for the art of old Mexico.
lowell-biglow-papers-1848:
James Russell Lowell published the first series of The Biglow Papers in 1848, during the Mexican-American War. Lowell, a young Massachusetts poet and abolitionist, wrote them as newspaper pieces in Yankee dialect. His farmer-poet Hosea Biglow speaks, while the learned Parson Wilbur adds mock-serious introductions.

Biglow's verses attack the war as a slaveholders' land grab and mock the politicians who sold it. A recruiting officer gets a famous dressing-down in rough, funny, perfectly rhymed dialect. Lowell based the speech on real New England talk, then sharpened it into a weapon. The papers became the masterpiece of American comic verse and the ancestor of all later dialect poetry in the United States.
lowell-fable-for-critics-1848:
James Russell Lowell published A Fable for Critics in 1848, the same year as The Biglow Papers made his name. Lowell was twenty-nine, brilliant, and unafraid of judging his elders. He cast the poem as a tour: the god Phoebus brings a visiting critic to meet America's living writers one by one.

Poe, Emerson, Hawthorne, Longfellow, Whittier, and Lowell himself each get a galloping verse portrait, praise and puncture mixed. Phoebus complains that American letters are all promise and brag. The judgments are so apt that many stuck to their subjects for life. The poem is the founding document of American critical reputation-making, and still the liveliest survey of the era's literature.
lowell-vision-sir-launfal-1848:
James Russell Lowell published The Vision of Sir Launfal in 1848, his telling of the Grail quest as a moral allegory. Lowell was in his great early burst, issuing the Biglow Papers and A Fable for Critics the same year. The poem's prelude, The Present Crisis, outgrew the poem itself in fame.

Sir Launfal rides out from his castle in pride, searching the world for the Holy Grail. He returns old and broken, and finds the Grail's lesson at his own gate, in sharing his last crust with a beggar. The Present Crisis, written against slavery's expansion, gave abolitionism a battle cry: truth forever on the scaffold, wrong forever on the throne. Generations of reformers quoted it, and Launfal's winter and summer landscapes remain lovely.
macaulay-history-england-vol-1-1848:
Thomas Babington Macaulay published Volume 1 of his History of England in 1848. The History became the best-selling work of history of the 1800s. Volume 1 opens with a survey of England from Roman times to the Restoration. It then focuses on the reign of Charles II and the accession of James II.

Macaulay writes Whig history: the story of liberty advancing through Parliament against kings. His famous third chapter paints the state of England in 1685 in rich detail. Markets, roads, alehouses, and clergy all come alive. The narrative art is brilliant and confident. Macaulay aimed to replace the novel in the reader's hands, and often succeeded.
macaulay-history-england-vol-2-1848:
Thomas Babington Macaulay published Volume 2 of his History of England in 1848, alongside the first. This volume covers the reign of James II in depth. James's push for Catholic power and standing armies alarms the nation. The trial of the Seven Bishops and the birth of a royal son spark crisis.

William of Orange lands in 1688, and James flees to France. Macaulay tells the road to revolution with narrative art at full power. His sympathies are clear: he honors those who defended law and Protestant liberty. Critics fault his partisanship, yet few deny his skill. The volume ends with William and Mary on the throne.
marx-manifesto-1848: Marx and Engels' 1848 Communist Manifesto calls workers to unite and overthrow capital. Its specter haunts still. The Tower library holds the full text. It shook thrones. Workers read. Revolutions burned. Ghosts lingered. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
mill-principles-political-economy-vol-1-:
John Stuart Mill published Principles of Political Economy, Volume 1, in 1848. For fifty years the Principles served as the dominant textbook of economics in English. Volume 1 treats production: labor, capital, land, and the laws that govern their cooperation. Mill restates classical economics in a clear, final synthesis.

He studies large and small farming, cooperation, and the limits of growth in output. Mill writes with unusual care for the human side of industry. His sympathy for workers and for reform sets the book apart from colder texts. The stationary state, treated later, already casts its shadow. Volume 1 lays the base for the whole system.
mill-principles-political-economy-vol-2-:
John Stuart Mill completed Principles of Political Economy with Volume 2 in 1848. This volume treats distribution and exchange: wages, profits, rent, money, credit, and trade between nations. Mill argues that the laws of distribution are human-made and can be reformed. That claim opened economics to social reform.

He also develops the theory of value and of international trade in classic form. Chapters on the functions of government weigh taxes, education, and poor relief. Mill's hope for a stationary state of capital, paired with rising human culture, closes the work. The two volumes formed generations of economic thought. They remain readable and humane.
montezuma-s-daughter-pg1848: H. Rider Haggard's 1893 Aztec epic: an Englishman in Mexico loves Montezuma's daughter as Cortés destroys an empire. Sweeping, tragic, and full of Haggard's energy, it brings the conquest to vivid life. Adventure on the grand scale.
needham-observations-generation-1748:
John Turberville Needham, an English priest and man of science, read this paper to the Royal Society in 1748. He claimed to have seen life spring up where none had been. His claim dealt with the birth, make up, and break down of living stuffs. The theme drew heat, since it bore on how life first came to be on earth.

Needham boiled broth, sealed it, and found tiny forms in it days later. He took this as proof that dead stuff holds a force that makes new life. Pasteur and Spallanzani spent the next age of work to show where his trials went wrong.
openalex-w1586227748: Multimorbidity got LMIC-impacted, and this health article covers low middle income countries. The pages detail the impact findings. The researchers get their paper. The impact was of-multimorbidity. The paper was researcher. The doe were countries. The mental were physical.
openalex-w1800605248: One drug, many targets — the 'skeleton key approach' to medicine. Talevi's 2015 review explores multi-target pharmacology: its possibilities and limitations from a medicinal chemist's perspective. The review weighed the promise of multi-target drugs against their design challenges.
openalex-w1971699048: Early dengue diagnosis saves lives — and NS1 tests promise speed. Guzmán and colleagues' 2010 multi-country study evaluated the sensitivity and specificity of two commercial NS1 ELISA assays for dengue diagnosis. The trials tested whether the rapid tests earn their place in clinics.
openalex-w2004015348: A rapid TB test promised much — but cost gave pause. Vassall and colleagues' 2011 cost-effectiveness analysis examined rapid TB diagnosis with the Xpert MTB/RIF assay in high-burden countries. The study weighed the test's price against its life-saving speed.
openalex-w2102203148: Tall trees hold more carbon — biomass estimates caught up. Feldpausch and colleagues' 2012 study integrated tree height into tropical forest biomass estimates. The work measured 37,625 height-diameter pairs across 327 plots worldwide — plus 1,816 harvested trees.
openalex-w2132582148: Air conditioning beat dengue in Texas. A 2003 study found Texas lifestyle limits transmission of dengue virus. The Laredo–Nuevo Laredo comparison showed screens, AC, and sealed homes blocked the mosquito — lifestyle as vector control, proven in the border cities.
openalex-w2140941348: Sleeping sickness and Chagas aren't the whole story. A 2013 review covers atypical human infections by animal parasites. The review documented cases from other species beyond the classical two — parasites crossing over, reviewed.
openalex-w2308892148: Severe respiratory illness hospitalizes countless children, and flu's share of that burden was long unclear. This 2016 PLoS Medicine systematic analysis estimates influenza's role in pediatric respiratory hospitalizations worldwide from 1982 to 2012. As surveillance and testing expanded globally, the study gives the clearest picture yet of how much childhood suffering flu causes — and where vaccines could help most.
openalex-w2511044748: The 2015–2016 El Niño rivaled the monster event of 1997–98, and the Amazon felt it brutally. This 2016 Scientific Reports paper documents record-breaking warming and extreme drought across the rainforest as the oscillation peaked. The study captures how the planet's largest tropical forest copes — or fails to — when heat and drought strike together.
openalex-w2804430248: Deforming a two-dimensional quantum theory by the TTbar operator yields something remarkable: a solvable theory of gravity. This 2018 Journal of High Energy Physics paper computes the deformed partition function by coupling to flat-space Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity. The result illuminates one of the few exactly solvable corners of quantum gravity.
openalex-w2889449548: A cow's rumen is a fermentation vat run by microbes — anaerobic bacteria, protozoa, fungi, methane-making archaea, and phages — that digest what humans can't. This 2018 Frontiers in Microbiology review surveys the rumen microbiome's past, present, and future. Understanding this ecosystem is key to feeding livestock efficiently while curbing methane emissions.
openalex-w4317716348: This 2023 Archives of Virology paper summarizes the ICTV Bacterial Viruses Subcommittee’s work from March 2021 to March 2022: abolishing morphology-based taxa and moving to binomial species names. The update overhauls how bacterial viruses are classified.
openalex-w4366482848: Pollution, overconsumption, urbanization, inequality, habitat loss — climate change worsens them all. This 2023 Science paper reviews the links among the climate and biodiversity crises and their societal impacts. The synthesis argues the twin emergencies must be overcome together.
openalex-w4392193048: Adapted large language models can now outperform medical experts at clinical text summarization. This 2024 Nature Medicine paper — by Van Veen, Van Uden, Blankemeier and colleagues — tests LLMs against physicians on the task. The result signals AI’s arrival in clinical documentation.
openalex-w588204548: This 2015 European Physical Journal C paper combines all inclusive deep inelastic electron-proton scattering cross sections from HERA’s H1 and ZEUS collaborations — neutral and charged current, at multiple proton beam energies — with a QCD analysis. The combination is a cornerstone of proton-structure physics.
openalex-w7128707048: Robots are entering the chest surgeon's toolkit. This paper reports Juntendo University's experience with robot-assisted lung cancer surgery since 2017: safety and benefits. The authors tracked the program's growth past 15 percent of cases. A surgical report from the robotic frontier.
openalex-w7204260448: Energy drinks promise focus but may frazzle the brain. This integrative review studies what the science says about these beverages' effects on the central nervous system. The authors screened Portuguese and English research from 2021 to mid-2025. A timely review of the can behind the buzz.
openalex-w7204448948: Artificial intelligence is entering biology classrooms, promising new tools and raising new worries. This paper reviews the potential and the pitfalls of AI in teaching biological sciences: what it can do for learning, and the teaching, ethical, and academic challenges it brings. The authors aim for balance over hype. A timely guide for biology teachers facing the AI question.
openalex-w7204987148: In 2025, the Brazilian state of Paraiba logged 7,122 poisoning cases, and this study profiles the ones caused by medicines. The authors break down who was poisoned, by which drugs, and in what settings, using plain case counts. The numbers show patterns, accidental, on purpose, and work-related, that point to ways of stopping future cases. A fact-based snapshot of a quiet public-health problem.
openalex-w7204991548: Blood pressure often drops during surgery, and kidneys are among the first organs to suffer. This study examines how the depth and duration of intraoperative hypotension affect the risk of acute kidney injury after operations. The authors analyze the link between low blood pressure on the table and kidney outcomes in recovery. A precise clinical investigation with a direct message for anesthesiologists: pressure matters, and minutes count.
openalex-w7205000548: College pressure drives some students to study drugs like lisdexamfetamine and methylphenidate, hoping for better grades. This paper reviews the risks of that misuse: health harms, dependence, and the false promise of smarter performance. The authors focus on why high-achieving students reach for pills and what it costs them. A cautionary review aimed at campuses where the medicine cabinet doubles as a study aid.
openalex-w7214311248: Undoing an ileostomy can leave a hernia where the stoma was. This study of 194 patients hunted risk factors for these hernias, with focus on what thread closed the muscle layer. The team counted how often they struck. A surgery study of closing bellies cleanly.
owen-archetype-homologies-1848:
Richard Owen, Britain's leading anatomist, published his study of the vertebrate skeleton in 1848. Owen compared bones across fish, reptiles, birds, and mammals. He saw one hidden pattern beneath their many shapes.

Owen calls that pattern the archetype, an ideal plan of the backbone and skull. Bones that match across species, he names homologies, a term science still uses. His scheme came before Darwin and pointed to a rival cause, yet it framed the debate. Darwin later used Owen's own facts to argue for descent with change. His terms let anatomists compare skeletons across the whole animal kingdom.
plos-pbio-0020248:
Robert L. Hammond and Laurent Keller reviewed a conflict inside insect societies in PLOS Biology in 2004. In ant, bee, and wasp colonies, workers are often related more to some males than to others. That skew creates conflict over which males get raised and whose sons the queen's mates produce.

Theory predicts workers should favor their closest kin, yet colonies mostly run smoothly. The authors weigh how workers police each other and how queens limit strife. Their review sorts strong evidence from neat but untested ideas. Social insects are a test bed for the whole theory of cooperation. A clear account of their one big conflict sharpens that theory.
plos-pone-0000048:
Matthias Nahrendorf, Ralph Weissleder, and Georg Ertl asked in 2006 whether a clotting factor is needed for the heart to heal. After a myocardial infarction, a heart attack, the dead muscle is replaced by scar tissue. Factor XIII helps stabilize blood clots, and the team tested whether lacking it impairs wound healing in the heart.

The question links bleeding biology to recovery: a repair process that starts with a clot may falter if the clot is weak. Their title poses the question plainly, and the study answers it in the injured heart. For patients born without factor XIII, or treated in ways that lower it, the answer bears on how well the heart can mend.
plos-pone-0000148:
Chunyi Li, Jo-Ann L. Stanton, Tracy M. Robertson, and colleagues published this deer biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Red deer regrow their antlers every year, one of the fastest examples of organ regeneration in mammals. The authors measured nerve growth factor messages in the regenerating antler tip of Cervus elaphus.

Nerves must regrow along with bone and skin for a new antler to form. Tracking where and when nerve growth factor is expressed shows how that regrowth is guided. Antlers are a prized natural model of regeneration, so findings here interest biologists who study how tissues rebuild themselves.
plos-pone-0000248:
Jonathan S. Friedlaender, Françoise R. Friedlaender, Jason A. Hodgson, and colleagues published this population genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies the mitochondrial DNA of Melanesian peoples, the populations of the Pacific islands northeast of Australia. The title flags the theme: their mtDNA shows striking complexity.

Melanesia was settled in layers over tens of thousands of years, and its DNA carries that history. The authors untangle patterns of maternal lineages across the region. The work helps reconstruct how humans spread through the Pacific, one of the last great chapters of human migration.
plos-pone-0000348:
David Lusseau published this dolphin behavior paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In the bottlenose dolphin population of Doubtful Sound, New Zealand, male social relationships are unusually complex. The author asks why, examining the social network of males in this isolated fjord population.

Male dolphins elsewhere form alliances with clear tiers; Doubtful Sound's pattern differs. Working out what drives that difference tests general theories of animal society. The study uses long-term observation of known individuals, the strength of this small, well-watched population. Doubtful Sound's isolation makes it a natural test case, since what holds there may not match busier coasts.
plos-pone-0000448:
Philippe Boucher and colleagues described a blood vessel protein that gathers growth signals, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The protein, LRP1, functions as an atheroprotective integrator. It helps protect arteries from the plaque buildup of atherosclerosis. It does this by combining signals from TGFβ and PDGF, two growth factors in the vascular wall.

The team drew out implications for Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder that weakens the aorta. A protein that both reads growth signals and guards the vessel wall sits at a crossroads of several diseases. Work of this kind helps explain how one signaling fault can produce widespread damage in arteries.
plos-pone-0000548:
Yang Liu and colleagues solved the structure of a fish antifreeze and traced its origin, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Herring survive icy water with a type II antifreeze protein that stops ice crystals from growing, and the protein needs calcium ions to work. The team determined the structure and evolutionary origin of this Ca2+-dependent protein.

Antifreeze proteins evolved several times independently, making them a natural experiment in invention. A structure shows exactly how the protein grips ice, and its ancestry shows which ordinary protein was reshaped into antifreeze. Both views matter for designing synthetic antifreezes for medicine and industry.
plos-pone-0000648:
Todd A. Sangster, Adam Bahrami, Amity Wilczek and co-authors lowered a protective protein in Arabidopsis plants and watched the variety that emerged. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study concerns HSP90, a molecular chaperone that helps select proteins mature correctly. Many of its client proteins sit in key signal pathways. Its role had been studied mostly in animals and fungi.

With reduced HSP90, the plants showed wider phenotypic diversity, a broader spread of visible traits. Their ability to adjust to the environment changed too. The result supports the idea that HSP90 buffers hidden genetic variation, letting it surface when the chaperone weakens. Evolution researchers prize such mechanisms for explaining sudden trait changes.
plos-pone-0000748:
Martin Weinberger, Li Feng, Anita Paul and colleagues tied the stress of copying DNA to how long yeast cells live, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Chronological lifespan in budding yeast means how long non-dividing cells survive. Mutations that switch off conserved growth-signaling pathways extend that lifespan. Those pathways regulate entry into and progress through the cell cycle.

The authors show that DNA replication stress is a determinant of this lifespan. Copying damage accumulated earlier seems to set a clock on later survival. Aging research prizes such links, because growth pathways and replication stress also appear in human aging and cancer. Yeast offers the fast, cheap system for testing them.
plos-pone-0000848:
Basilis Zikopoulos and Helen Barbas mapped two kinds of wiring between the brain's executive region and its relay station, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pathways linking the thalamus and cortex mediate our daily shifts from attention to quiet rest or sleep. Little was known about their architecture in high-order systems tied to cognition, emotion, and action. The prefrontal cortex is the seat of those high-order functions.

The authors provide novel neurochemical evidence for parallel driving and modulatory pathways linking prefrontal cortex and thalamus. Driving pathways carry the main message; modulatory ones tune it. That division, proven for sensory systems, apparently extends to the circuits of thought itself.
plos-pone-0000948:
Gerald Lim, Greg Huber, Yoshihiro Torii and colleagues modeled the fission yeast nucleus as if it were a tiny fluid sac, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fission yeast divides with its nuclear envelope intact. During that closed division, the nucleus stretches through a striking series of shapes as the spindle inside it grows.

The authors argue that vesicle like mechanics, the physics of a soft membrane sac, govern much of that geometry. Treating the nucleus as a physical object, not just a bag of genes, explains shapes that pure biology leaves puzzling. The approach links cell biology with soft matter physics in a testable way.
plos-pone-0001048:
Christopher Smith, Michael Gill, Janet May and colleagues showed how a mouse herpesvirus hides from dendritic cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dendritic cells start adaptive immune responses, so viruses that infect them gain a strong advantage. Murine gammaherpesvirus-68 infects dendritic cells during normal colonization of its host.

The team report the virus inhibits antigen presentation by those cells, weakening the alarm they should raise. A virus that mutes its host's sentries can persist for life, as herpesviruses do. Studying the trick in a mouse virus reveals principles that apply to human relatives, including ones tied to cancer.
plos-pone-0001148:
Flaxseed has been shown to improve blood lipids in people, and a flaxseed compound called lignan improved blood sugar control in animals. An Pan and colleagues put the lignan to a human test in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their trial involved patients with type 2 diabetes.

The study was randomized, double-blind, and used a cross-over design, so each patient served as their own comparison. It measured the supplement's effects on blood sugar control, lipid profiles, and insulin measures. The paper adds controlled human evidence to a question mostly studied in animals before.
plos-pone-0001248:
Soil ecology has produced a huge body of results on soil organisms and the processes they control. Sébastien Barot, Manuel Blouin, and Sébastien Fontaine argue that the field still lacks theory tying those results together, in a 2007 PLOS ONE essay. They frame the problem as a tale of four stories: soil ecology, theory, evolution, and the publication system.

Some soil scientists think the field is short of modeling and evolutionary thinking, the authors note. Their essay examines why, including how publishing incentives reward description over synthesis. It is an opinion and analysis piece aimed at the field's habits as much as its data.
plos-pone-0001348:
Thymopentin, or TP5, is a small peptide used to stimulate the immune system by contacting T cells. Zuojia Liu and colleagues modeled how it binds to HLA-DR molecules, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The molecular basis of how TP5 achieves its immune triggering remained incompletely understood.

HLA-DR molecules present peptide fragments to T cells, so a TP5 complex with them is a plausible trigger mechanism. The authors carry out a molecular analysis of that binding. Understanding the complex could guide the design of peptide immunomodulators with more predictable effects.
plos-pone-0001448:
Craig Bennett and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study that used yeast to find partners of a breast cancer gene. The gene, BRCA1, is tied to many DNA repair paths that keep the genome sound. Which of its jobs stops tumors was still obscure. The team screened yeast for the most kept, core links of BRCA1.

Their screen flagged the tail of the main gene copying enzyme and a partner factor as key targets. Yeast and human cells share these core parts. Hits that survive that long span of evolution are likely central. The work helps narrow a wide field to the BRCA1 jobs that matter most.
plos-pone-0001548:
Stuart Sandin and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on coral reefs in the Northern Line Islands. Good guard work needs a true picture of a reef left alone. Most reefs are worn down by fishing, waste, and other human acts. The team surveyed reefs that range from near pristine to heavily used.

Their data set a base line for what a sound reef holds in fish, coral, and microbes. Reefs near people show clear drops from that base. A firm base line lets managers judge if guard steps work. It also shows what is lost, step by step, as use grows.
plos-pone-0001648:
Kathryn L. Lipson, Rajarshi Ghosh, and Fumihiko Urano studied stress inside insulin-making cells for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Insulin is built in the endoplasmic reticulum, a cell compartment where new secretory proteins are folded. When folding goes wrong, the cell feels ER stress and switches on a set of rescue pathways called the unfolded protein response.

The team focused on IRE1α, one sensor of that stress, in pancreatic beta cells. Their work shows this sensor plays a part in breaking down insulin's gene message when stress hits. The full text gives the cell tests and message levels they measured. The finding links ER stress to falling insulin output, a core fault in diabetes, and names a protein that future drug work may target.
plos-pone-0001748:
James T. Mandel, John M. Ratcliffe, David J. Cerasale, and their co-authors tested side preferences in flying swallows in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Many vertebrates favor one side of the body, a result of brain hemispheric specialization. Side bias can speed responses and help multitasking, but it can also bend body shape into asymmetries.

The team ran concurrent tests of side bias and optimality in flying tree swallows. They asked whether the birds favor a side, and whether that side is the better one for flight tasks. The full text gives the flight tests and the turning data. Swallows feed on the wing at high speed, so their choices test how lateralization works under real aerodynamic pressure.
plos-pone-0001848:
Matthias Vömel and Christian Wegener mapped amine signaling systems in the fruit fly larva's nerve cord in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Biogenic amines are important signaling molecules in the central nervous systems of vertebrates and invertebrates alike. In Drosophila melanogaster, amines help regulate feeding, learning and memory, and other vital processes.

Their paper gives the neuroarchitecture of aminergic systems in the larval ventral ganglion: which neurons make each amine and where their fibers run. The full text gives the staining maps cell by cell. A wiring atlas of the larva's amine systems is reference material for the many labs that use fly larvae to study behavior genetics.
plos-pone-0001948:
Klaus Stark and co-authors tested a gene's link to two ills at once, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The gene, GLUT9, moves uric acid in the body. Two large genome scans had tied common forms of it to uric acid levels in Italian and British groups. High uric acid is the cause of gout and often comes with metabolic syndrome.

In a large case and control study, the team asked whether those same gene forms track with gout. They also asked about coronary artery disease, a heart illness. As the title states, they found a link to gout but not to heart disease. Such splits help sort cause from mere company.
plos-pone-0002048:
Michael Bryan and co-authors traced a gene that jumps between sea viruses, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. S-PM2 is a virus that infects Synechococcus, a one-celled cyanobacterium common in the oceans. Like kin viruses, it carries genes that look bacterial, picked up from hosts at some point in its past.

One such gene makes a MazG-like protein, present in high copy. As the title states, the evidence points to intense exchange of MazG among marine cyanophages. The route is horizontal gene transfer, genes passed sideways rather than from parent to offspring. Sea viruses, it seems, trade tools freely.
plos-pone-0002148:
Roberto Galán studied the patterns that brain circuits produce on their own, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Even with no sensory input, networks in the neocortex, the brain's outer sheet, fire in complex patterns. These patterns are thought to reflect how the network is built, including how it is divided into modules.

Galán asked how the layout of connections shapes which patterns take over. His work connects wiring to activity: the same neurons can settle into different dominant rhythms depending on how they are linked. That link helps explain how a resting brain can hold ready-made patterns for thought and action.
plos-pone-0002248:
Yusuke Ohnishi and co-authors improved a way to silence one faulty gene copy while sparing the healthy one, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Many diseases come from a single bad allele, one copy of a gene, while its twin copy is normal. RNA interference can silence genes, and allele-specific silencing aims to hit only the bad copy.

The team found that adding deliberate single-letter mismatches to the silencing RNA sharpens the contrast between copies. That makes the treatment cut the disease allele's output while leaving the normal allele closer to untouched. Finer control like this is vital if RNA drugs are to be safe.
plos-pone-0002348:
Eric Mooshagian, Jonas Kaplan, and Eran Zaidel studied how fast the brain answers when a stimulus appears twice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Processing several stimuli in parallel is critical for dealing with a busy world. One test of that ability measures reaction times to redundant targets, multiple copies of the same stimulus, which people answer faster than to one.

The team asked what role the right temporo-parietal junction, a region where the temporal and parietal lobes meet, plays in that speed-up. Their results tie this brain hub to fast visuomotor processing of redundant targets. The finding helps explain how the brain turns several signals into one quick action.
plos-pone-0002448:
Siroux and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Valérie Siroux, Emmanuelle Bouzigon, Marie-Hélène Dizier, and others. Its subject is replication of Association between ADAM33 Polymorphisms and Psoriasis. Polymorphisms in ADAM33, the first gene identified in asthma by positional cloning, have been recently linked to psoriasis.

No replication study of this association has been published so far. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002548:
Led by Gu, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Peili Gu, Jeffrey G. Reid, Xiaolian Gao, and others. Its subject is novel MicroRNA Candidates and miRNA-mRNA Pairs in Embryonic Stem (ES) Cells. MicroRNAs (miRNAs: a class of short non-coding RNAs) are emerging as important agents of post transcriptional gene regulation and integral components of gene networks.

MiRNAs have been strongly linked to stem cells, which have a remarkable dual role in development. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002648:
Research from Hiroaki Takagi and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers functional analysis of spontaneous cell movement under different physiological conditions. Authorship is credited in the record to Hiroaki Takagi and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Cells can show not only spontaneous movement but also tactic responses to environmental signals. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002748:
Work by Renhai Cao and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with Hypoxia-Induced retinal angiogenesis in zebrafish as a model to study retinopathy. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Renhai Cao, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Mechanistic understanding and defining novel therapeutic targets of diabetic retinopathy and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) have been hampered by a lack of appropriate adult. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002848:
Work by ZhiFang Dong and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was coincident activity of converging pathways enables simultaneous Long-Term potentiation and Long-Term depression in hippocampal CA1 network in vivo. The catalog record names ZhiFang Dong first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Memory is believed to depend on activity-dependent changes in the strength of synapses, e.g. The authors add a further point. Long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD), which can be determined by the sequence of coincident pre- and postsynaptic activity, respectively. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002948:
Fang He, Dong-Dong Wu, Qing-Peng Kong and co-authors sequenced a limb-control region in human DNA in 2008. Intron 5 of the gene LMBR1 acts as a switch for the sonic hedgehog gene, a master guide for limb growth. Changes in this non-coding region are tied to extra fingers present from birth.

The authors report signs of balancing selection on that region, meaning natural selection kept more than one version in people. Such a pattern hints the variants affect survival in opposing ways. Published in PLOS ONE, the study links a limb switch to human evolution and skeletal development.
plos-pone-0003048:
Naoki Yamanaka, Sachie Yamamoto, Dušan Žitňan and co-authors catalogued neuropeptide receptors in insects in 2008. Neuropeptides guide much of animal development and daily balance. Insects are ideal models for studying them, and the past decade's focus had been on identifying the peptides themselves.

A transcriptome survey of their receptors reveals unidentified neuroendocrine pathways, per the title. Receptors are the receiving half of the system and the usual drug target. Published in PLOS ONE, the catalog opens routes to insect control that act on signaling rather than broad poisons. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003148:
Shlomit Gilad, Eti Meiri, Yariv Yogev and colleagues report that small RNAs in blood may serve as disease markers in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Nucleic acids that circulate in body fluids offer a chance for early diagnosis. MicroRNAs are a family of small non-coding RNAs that regulate genes and play roles in human growth and disease.

The team show that microRNAs are present in body fluids and can act as new, effective markers, as the title claims for serum samples. Readers see an early case for blood tests based on microRNA patterns. Such tests could one day flag disease without invasive sampling.
plos-pone-0003248:
Philip Barnes and Kerrie L. Thomas link a protein cleavage to memory formation in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. It is essential to understand the molecular processes underlying long-term memory to provide therapeutic targets for aberrant memory that produces pathological behaviour in humans. Under conditions of recall, fully consolidated memories can undergo reconsolidation or extinction.

The title reports that proteolysis of proBDNF is a key regulator in the formation of memory. Readers learn that cutting a precursor protein, not just its amount, decides a memory step. Such switches could be targets in disorders of too much or too little memory.
plos-pone-0003348:
Zi-Huan Yang and co-authors study a plant compound for constipation in rats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Constipation is very common, above all in old age, and good treatments are still needed. The team test naringenin, a herbal flavonol, for two effects: making the gut secrete more fluid, and easing passage as a laxative.

They trace the cell steps behind the laxative effect in a rat model of constipation, in gut lining cells. Readers see how one compound drives gut secretion at the cell level. That detail lifts the work above a simple folk cure claim.
plos-pone-0003448:
César Mattei and co-authors tested a natural compound against seafood poison in this 2008 study. Ciguatoxins come from tiny sea algae and build up in reef fish. They cause ciguatera, a nasty food poisoning of the nerves. A related compound, brevenal, was known to block a sister toxin.

The team used hormone-making cells from cattle for their tests. Pacific ciguatoxin-1B made those cells release far too much content. Brevenal curbed that toxin-driven release. The result hints at a treatment path for a poisoning that now has none. Ciguatera sickens many thousands of people in tropical regions each year.
plos-pone-0003548:
Maria A. Croyle and co-authors delivered a vaccine through the nose in this 2008 mouse study. Many people already have immunity to adenovirus type 5. That virus is a popular carrier for vaccine genes. Prior immunity can blunt a vaccine built on it.

The team compared muscle, nose, and oral delivery routes in mice. The vaccine expressed an Ebola surface protein for the tests. Nasal delivery bypassed the pre-existing immunity problem. It also improved the immune response over other routes. The nose route also avoids needles, which could help mass vaccine drives.
plos-pone-0003648:
Tomoyasu Wakuda, Hideo Matsuzaki, Katsuaki Suzuki, and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Lack of oxygen around birth is a suspected risk factor for schizophrenia later in life. The team used rats to test how such an oxygen loss affects the brain.

Pups that went through perinatal asphyxia grew fewer dentate granule cells, a type of neuron in the hippocampus. As adults, the same animals also showed stronger overactivity when given methamphetamine. The work supports the idea that a hard start at birth can leave lasting marks on the brain.
plos-pone-0003748:
Pedro José Barbosa Pereira, Nuno Empadinhas, Luciana Albuquerque, and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Tuberculosis remains a serious threat, worsened by drug-resistant strains of its bacterium. Few new compounds against it have been developed. The team solved the structure of one of its enzymes.

The enzyme builds a sugar needed for the bacterium's methylglucose lipopolysaccharides, a part of its outer chemistry. Knowing its atomic structure hands drug designers a concrete target. A drug that jams this key step could weaken Mycobacterium tuberculosis where current drugs fail.
plos-pone-0003848:
Rosana D. Meyer, David B. Sacks, and Nader Rahimi published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. VEGFR-2 is the main receptor for the growth factor that builds blood vessels. Its signaling is required for normal development and feeds pathological vessel growth in cancer and eye disease.

The team found a signaling pathway dependent on the scaffold protein IQGAP1. That pathway regulates endothelial cell proliferation and angiogenesis downstream of the receptor. The result names a control point in the vessel-building machinery that tumors hijack to feed themselves. Blocking that point is one route drug makers can test.
plos-pone-0003948:
Michael G. Wallach, Udi Ashash, Amnon Michael, and co-authors field-tested a chicken vaccine in 2008. Coccidiosis is a gut disease that hits intensively reared chickens worldwide. Parasites of the genus Eimeria cause the disease. A subunit vaccine was made from purified proteins of one species, Eimeria maxima.

Their PLOS ONE article reports use of that vaccine under field conditions. The vaccine aimed to prompt hens to pass protection to their chicks. Farm-level evidence matters more than lab results for poultry disease control. A working subunit vaccine could cut losses without heavy drug use. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004048:
Yves Gingras, Vincent Larivière, Benoît Macaluso, and co-authors measured how aging affects researchers in 2008. The average age of a first NIH grant in the U.S. rose over decades. It climbed from 34.3 years in 1970 to 41.7 in 2004. That trend raised questions about older scientists' output.

Their PLOS ONE article drew on a sizable sample of researchers. They tracked publication and citation patterns across career ages. Whether impact fades, holds, or grows with age matters for funding policy. Evidence can counter easy assumptions about aging and creativity. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004148:
Francesco Bonadonna, Samuel Caro, and M. de L. Brooke published this bird study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chemical signals can tell an animal another's identity, rank, or sex. Birds were long thought to barely use smell, yet recent work shows several species use chemical cues to find food and recognise each other.

The team asked whether Antarctic prions, seabirds that breed in burrows, can tell male from female by scent alone. Testing this sense in a wild seabird pushes against the old view of birds as poor smellers. Whatever the birds reveal, the study widens what we know about how animals read sex from smell.
plos-pone-0004248:
Nathaniel Sowa, Kunjumon Vadakkan, and Mark Zylka published this pain study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Prostatic acid phosphatase, or PAP, is made by pain-sensing neurons and works as an ectonucleotidase, an enzyme that processes nucleotides outside cells. Injected human and bovine PAP proteins produce strong, long-lasting pain relief that depends on A1-adenosine receptors.

The team made the mouse version of PAP in the lab and tested it. They report that its enzyme activity depends on pH and that it relieves pain through the same A1 receptors. The work supports PAP as a possible long-acting, non-opioid pain treatment.
plos-pone-0004348:
Jonathan Foley and colleagues published this genome engineering study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Customised zinc finger nucleases form the basis of a broadly applicable tool for highly efficient genome modification. They are artificial restriction enzymes: a non-specific nuclease domain fused to a zinc finger array engineered to recognise a chosen DNA sequence.

The team applied nucleases made by oligomerized pool engineering, called OPEN, to rapidly mutate endogenous zebrafish genes. Editing a fish's own genes in place, rather than adding copies, made the method practical. The study helped turn zinc finger editing into a routine laboratory tool.
plos-pone-0004448:
Two ancient millets look nearly alike once burned, and Houyuan Lu, Jianping Zhang, Naiqin Wu, and co-authors found a way to tell them apart in PLOS ONE in 2009. Foxtail millet and common millet are the oldest farmed dry-land crops in Eurasia. Their grains survive at dig sites mainly when charred, which makes them hard to identify.

The team turned to phytoliths, tiny silica shapes that plants leave behind and that outlast the grains themselves. By comparing the silica patterns of the two species, they built a test archaeologists can use on old remains. Knowing which millet early farmers grew, and where, sharpens the story of how farming spread. It also helps trace the roots of two crops still eaten today.
plos-pone-0004548:
What it costs to prevent disability in leprosy, and whether the money is well spent, is reviewed here. Natasja van Veen, Paul McNamee, Jan Hendrik Richardus, and co-authors did that review in PLOS ONE in 2009. Prevention of disability is one of the key aims of leprosy programs. Coverage and access had recently been named the priority issues in that work.

The authors carried out a systematic review, gathering all studies on the cost-effectiveness of such interventions. Judging value for money is highly relevant to understanding the barriers and opportunities programs face. Leprosy is curable, but late care leaves lasting disability that shapes a person's whole life. Evidence on which prevention steps give the most benefit per unit of cost helps programs protect more people.
plos-pone-0004648:
A single-letter change in a cholesterol-scavenging receptor alters how it works, show Silvia Biocca, Mattia Falconi, Ilaria Filesi, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The receptor is LOX-1, the major scavenger receptor for oxidized low density lipoprotein in endothelial cells, the cells lining blood vessels. Oxidized LDL is the harmful form of cholesterol that drives artery disease.

The change, K167N, swaps one building block of the receptor for another. The team combined functional analysis with molecular dynamics simulation, a computer model of the protein's motion. Together these reveal an alteration of receptor activity. Knowing how a natural human variant changes the receptor helps explain why some people's arteries handle bad cholesterol worse than others.
plos-pone-0004748:
Jonathan Alberts built a computer model with true to life filament bending for cell simulation, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Agent based models track small local contacts among many parts over time. They can show how complex cell behavior grows out of simple molecular rules, which is hard to see in the lab alone.

Thin filaments inside cells bend as they push and pull. Alberts added bending physics that match real filament stiffness and flex. More true physics makes model results safer to trust. Other builders can reuse the method for cytoskeleton studies. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004848:
Nicholas Haley and colleagues detected chronic wasting disease prions in urine and saliva of deer by transgenic mouse bioassay, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chronic wasting disease is a prion disease affecting captive and free ranging cervids such as deer, elk, and moose. Mechanisms of transmission are poorly understood, though bodily fluids are thought to play an important role in spread among animals sharing ranges and social groups.

Finding infectious prions in urine and saliva confirms shedding. Noninvasive tests and environmental spread become plausible. Management can target contamination hotspots. Wildlife agencies gain evidence for policy. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here.
plos-pone-0004948:
Measles clears from the body and leaves lifelong immunity. Yet infection is followed by a strange immune shutdown. Caroline Sellin and colleagues explored this paradox in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on two kinds of T cells. Effector cells attack the virus directly. Regulatory T cells, marked by Foxp3, calm the immune system down.

The study examines how the balance between these cells shapes measles. It also looks at the suppression that follows infection. Understanding that balance helps explain a puzzle. Measles leaves children briefly open to other infections. At the same time, it protects them against measles for life.
plos-pone-0005048:
Ancient DNA unlocks the genes of long-dead creatures. Insect specimens are precious and often unique. Sampling them usually destroys part of the specimen. Philip Francis Thomsen and colleagues offered a gentler way in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their extraction protocol gets DNA from insect remains. It leaves no visible damage to the specimen's form.

The method opens museum drawers to genetic study. Curators can allow sampling without losing specimens. Scientists gain access to collections once considered untouchable. The DNA can reveal how species changed over time. It can also identify remains that morphology alone cannot. Non-destructive sampling widens ancient DNA work considerably.
plos-pone-0005148:
A protein folds into one working shape. Its energy landscape holds many almost-shapes, called decoys. Kanagasabai Vadivel and Gautham Namasivayam counted them in PLOS ONE in 2009. They estimated the number of low-energy structures in that landscape. They also estimated how densely the decoys pack it. A comprehensive count is difficult to make.

The count guides protein-structure prediction. Predictors must find one native shape among countless near-misses. Knowing the crowd's size sharpens the search. It also sets realistic expectations for algorithms. The energy landscape is a central metaphor in folding science. Putting numbers on it makes the metaphor useful. This estimate gives modelers a scale to design against.
plos-pone-0005248:
People moving to music tend to sync the downward phase of a gesture with the beat. Why that pattern feels natural has been debated, with gravity as one suspect. Carson and colleagues used artificial gravity to test the idea in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Changing the gravity field changed how stable the coordinated movements were. The results point to economy of action: the system settles on the pattern that costs least under gravity. The work reveals a physical reason behind a very human habit of moving with music. The same pull toward cheap motion may shape how we walk, row, and play sports, not just how we wave a hand to a beat.
plos-pone-0005348:
Aldehyde oxidase is a liver enzyme that breaks down a wide range of molecules, including many drugs. The mouse form, AOX1, belongs to a family marked by a sulfur-bearing molybdenum center. Schumann and colleagues altered its active site piece by piece in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Site-directed mutagenesis swaps single amino acids at chosen spots. Changing residues at the active site shows which ones grip substrates and drive the reaction. Maps like this help predict how the enzyme will handle new drugs in people and animals. Liver enzymes like this one decide how long a drug stays strong in the blood, so a map of its grip helps set dose. Flags drugs that may fail in some patients.
plos-pone-0005448:
Elise Mok and colleagues ran a drug trial for boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. Boys with the disease lose muscle strength over time. The amino acid glutamine, taken by mouth, had been shown to slow the breakdown of protein in the whole body.

In the trial, boys took glutamine and a dummy treatment in turn, without knowing which was which. After months of treatment, the team checked walking and other daily functions. Glutamine gave no clear gain in function over the dummy treatment. That honest result helps families avoid false hope and guides care toward what works.
plos-pone-0005548:
Michal Schweiger and co-authors sequenced cancer tissue kept in wax blocks, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Most hospital tissue samples are fixed and stored in paraffin wax, not frozen fresh. Cancer gene programs have mostly relied on the rarer frozen samples.

The team showed that modern high-speed sequencing can read DNA from the wax blocks well enough to find copy number changes and mutations. That unlocks vast hospital archives for cancer research. Old samples with known patient outcomes are among the most valuable material a study can use. Archived blocks also let workers test new markers on cancers whose outcomes are already known in full.
plos-pone-0005648:
Jessica Perkins, Kashif Khan, and S V Subramanian mapped HIV patterns across India in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. National estimates of HIV in India had been revised downward a year earlier. How the infection is spread across people and states stayed unclear, though.

The authors examined how HIV status links with personal wealth, schooling, and state of residence for men and women. Uneven patterns show where prevention money will do most good. They also caution against treating India as one uniform epidemic. State-level gaps also hint at how migration and city growth shape the spread of infection across India.
plos-pone-0005748:
Nuno Fonseca, Cristina Vieira, and Jorge Vieira tackled a sorting problem in gene families in 2009. The DLX genes help pattern bodies during development, and their family tree spans many species. Picking just the wanted sequences out of huge public databases can be slow and error prone.

The team built a method that sorts genes by short amino acid motifs and key residues. Motifs act like barcodes for each family branch. With them, hundreds of sequences can be classified cleanly and fast. The DLX case serves as the test bed. The method suits any family where members look alike but do different jobs.
plos-pone-0005848:
Ravindresh Chhabra and co-authors reported in 2009 that a cluster of small RNAs can drive human kidney cells to self-destruct. MicroRNAs tune gene activity, and their misbehavior is common in cancer and other diseases. The cluster studied, miR-23a through miR-24-2, sits together on one chromosome stretch.

Raising the cluster's levels triggered apoptosis, programmed cell death, by more than one route. Some death ran through caspase enzymes, some did not. A single RNA cluster commanding death pathways is a powerful lever. It may help explain growth control gone wrong in tumors where the cluster is altered.
plos-pone-0005948:
A virus that copies itself inside a cell often remodels the room it works in. Teemu Ihalainen, Einari Niskanen, Juulia Jylhävä and colleagues watched that remodeling in 2009, using parvovirus infection as their case. Their PLOS ONE paper tracks how the virus alters the layout and motion of the host cell nucleus.

The nucleus holds the cell's DNA in a packed web, plus many small work zones. The team reports deep changes to that inner layout as infection proceeds. Knowing how a small DNA virus rebuilds its work space helps explain how it copies so well, and it may expose weak points that future antiviral work could aim at.
plos-pone-0006048:
In diabetes, excess fatty acids in the blood are tied to kidney damage, but the chain in between was murky. Hong-Mei Zhang, Howard Dang, Chih-Ko Yeh and colleagues traced one link in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies linoleic acid, a common fatty acid, and its effect on mitochondria, the power plants of kidney cells.

The acid forces mitochondria to release their calcium, the title reports, and that release sparks peroxynitrite, a harsh chemical that marks proteins with nitro groups. Each step is a place where the damage chain might be cut. The work gives diabetic kidney disease a concrete sequence to test, from fat in the blood to chemical harm in the cell.
plos-pone-0006148:
Ras proteins are small switches that must gather in clusters to speak loudly. Thomas Gurry, Ozan Kahramanoğulları and Robert Endres modeled that gathering in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper builds a biophysical model of Ras nanocluster formation and signaling in the plasma membrane, where electron microscope images had long shown the lipid-anchored proteins segregated into tiny domains.

Several models had tried to explain the clusters; a physical one can be tested against measured numbers. Clustering controls how strongly Ras signals, and Ras is among the most common drivers of human cancer. The model ties a membrane's physics to a cancer signal's volume, a link drug design increasingly tries to use.
plos-pone-0006248:
Enzymes that cut proteins must be watched closely if drugs are to control them. Taeyun Kwon and colleagues built a tiny mechanical sensor for that job, reported in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The sensor tracks cathepsin B, a cutting enzyme involved in several diseases, as it snips a peptide chain.

The device is a resonator whose vibration shifts as the peptide is cut. Watching the cut happen in place and in real time beats taking samples at intervals. Drug hunters can use such sensors to test blockers quickly. The method may extend to many other cutting enzymes.
plos-pone-0006348:
The factor that switches genes on in low oxygen may also set how long an animal lives. Yi Zhang and colleagues studied HIF-1 in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. HIF transcription factors implement most gene changes that let animals adapt to hypoxia during development and disease.

HIF-1 modulates lifespan in the worm, the authors report. The oxygen response system and the ageing clock are thus connected. That link could cut both ways, helping or harming depending on setting. Worm results often guide ageing research in more complex animals.
plos-pone-0006448:
Caroline Blais, Daniel Fiset, Martin Arguin, and colleagues studied how skilled readers read words, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Good adult readers, unlike beginners, barely slow down as words grow longer, up to about seven letters. How they pull information from a word so fast was still largely unknown. The team looked at what the eyes take in between saccades, the quick jumps eyes make while reading.

Their work probes the strategy behind fast word recognition. Readers seem to grab more than one letter at a time. Understanding that strategy helps explain skilled reading and its failures. It also informs models of how the brain turns print into words.
plos-pone-0006548:
Ricardo Hattori and co-authors studied sex determination in a South American fish for PLOS ONE in 2009. Gonadal fate in many reptiles, fish, and amphibians is modulated by temperature during a critical early period. This is called temperature-dependent sex determination. Pejerrey is a teleost fish with such a system.

The team asked whether cortisol-induced masculinization interacts with thermal stress. Cortisol is a stress hormone, and their title asks whether thermal stress affects gonadal fate. If stress hormones mediate temperature effects, pollution and climate may shift sex ratios. That has direct consequences for fisheries managing this species.
plos-pone-0006648:
Alexandre Tromas, Nils Braun, Philippe Muller, and colleagues studied a hormone binding protein in plant roots in PLOS ONE in 2009. In plants, the phytohormone auxin is a crucial regulator sustaining growth and development. At the cellular level, auxin is interpreted differentially in a tissue- and dose-dependent manner. The team examined the auxin binding protein 1, ABP1.

Their title reports ABP1 is required for differential auxin responses mediating root growth. Roots read auxin gradients to decide where to grow. A required sensor makes ABP1 central to that reading. Root architecture determines crop access to water and nutrients.
plos-pone-0006748:
Helit Cohen and colleagues studied control switches for immune recognition genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The genes are the MHC class I genes. Their proper regulation is critical for immune surveillance. The team looked beyond the promoter region in front of each gene. They found elements downstream that the genes need in living animals.

One element was a novel barrier element. It protects the MHC class I gene from surrounding influences. Without that protection, expression in vivo goes wrong. Barrier elements act like fences between gene neighborhoods. Finding one here refines how scientists picture immune gene control. It may also explain some failures of artificial gene constructs.
plos-pone-0006848:
Annarita de Luca and colleagues watched cerebellar neurons change growth style as they develop in PLOS ONE in 2009. The neurons are Purkinje cells, the cerebellum's main output cells. Developing neurons first elongate a main axon toward its target. A growth cone drives that extension. Later they switch to branching, forming a terminal arbor for synapses.

The study describes distinct modes of neuritic growth at different stages. It also examines cellular mechanisms regulating the switch. Timing the switch matters for correct wiring. Errors could leave Purkinje cells connected to wrong targets. The work adds detail to how the cerebellum assembles itself.
plos-pone-0006948:
Vince Davies, Kerrie Vaughan, Rohini Damle, and colleagues took stock of immune epitope research in PLOS ONE in 2009. PubMed then held more than eighteen million scientific articles. A large share concerned immune responses to microbes, allergens, transplants, and cancer antigens. The Immune Epitope Database was built to organize that work.

The authors classified the epitope literature as a whole. They described how the field is represented in the database. They also pointed out clear knowledge gaps in the record. Their map helps database curators and researchers see which agents and responses still lack solid epitope data.
plos-pone-0007048:
Shilpak Chatterjee, Ananda Mookerjee, Jayati Mookerjee Basu, and colleagues tested a copper compound against tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Early in cancer, T cells can block tumor growth and protect the body. Tumor associated macrophages can undercut that defense. These macrophages often suppress the immune response instead of helping it, giving young tumors room to grow.

The team used a new copper chelate to reprogram those macrophages. Treated macrophages stopped shielding the tumor. T cell attacks against the tumor grew stronger in response. Turning a tumor's own support cells against it is an attractive therapy idea, and this study gives it early support.
plos-pone-0007148:
Fred Kippert and Dietlind Gerloff improved a protein pattern search in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many eukaryotic proteins contain repeated blocks called HEAT and ARM repeats. These repeats often diverge so much that spotting them is hard. Finding them one by one, rather than in blocks, is essential except in the clearest cases.

Their method combines two tools, HHpred and COACH, for sensitive detection. Better repeat maps reveal how these proteins are built. Repeats often form the arms that grip partner proteins. Missing them can hide a protein's whole working shape from researchers.
plos-pone-0007248:
Chien-Hui Ma, Aashiq H. Kachroo, Anna Macieszak, and colleagues studied how a DNA-cutting enzyme reacts with modified DNA in 2009. The enzyme is Cre, a site-specific recombinase from a virus that infects bacteria. Related enzymes include Flp and vaccinia topoisomerase, studied with similar modified substrates before.

The team uses DNA containing methylphosphonate, a chemical change in the backbone. Earlier work with the related enzymes revealed how they cut and rejoin DNA strands. The authors compare Cre's reactions, noting similarities and contrasts. Their results clarify the electrical features of these molecular steps.
plos-pone-0007348:
Huey-Jen Lai, Szecheng J. Lo, Eriko Kage-Nakadai, and colleagues studied DNA-chewing enzymes in a roundworm in 2009. DNase II enzymes are acidic enzymes tied to apoptotic DNA degradation. Breaking down the DNA of dying cells is a critical final step in programmed cell death across animals.

The worm Caenorhabditis elegans carries three DNase II relatives, named NUC-1, CRN-6, and CRN-7. Their expression patterns and roles were unclear. The authors examine where each acts and what each does in DNA degradation and development. Their work assigns separate jobs to similar enzymes.
plos-pone-0007448:
Agnieszka Juncker and colleagues published a large-scale study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the proteins that feed the immune system's display system. Immune cells show fragments of proteins on surface molecules called MHC, like flags announcing what is inside the cell. Those displayed fragments, or ligands, trigger immune responses. Where their source proteins sit in the cell was the team's question.

They catalogued the cellular location and abundance of proteins that supply MHC ligands. Knowing which proteins are plentiful, and where they live, helps predict which fragments get displayed. That knowledge is directly useful for vaccine design. Designers can favor targets the immune system is most likely to notice. The study turns a basic catalogue into a practical guide for immunology.
plos-pone-0007548:
Jun-Li Liu and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how fear is unlearned. In the lab, a tone paired with shock teaches animals to fear the tone. Repeating the tone without shock slowly extinguishes that fear. Extinction is new learning, and like other learning it must be consolidated to last. NMDA receptors were suspected to play a part in that process.

The team blocked those receptors with the drug MK-801 in a Pavlovian fear model. Blocking impaired the consolidation of extinction. The rats kept more of their fear, as if the safety lesson never set. The result confirms the receptors are needed to let fear go, not only to form it. That matters for therapies that retrain fear, such as treatments for phobias and traumatic stress.
plos-pone-0007648:
Ravi Kavasery and colleagues published a trial report in PLOS ONE in 2009 on HIV testing in a women's jail. Ten million Americans pass through jails each year, making them an important venue for finding undiagnosed infections. New CDC guidelines recommended routine opt-out testing: everyone is tested unless they decline. The team ran a prospective, controlled trial of that strategy among newly incarcerated women. They also examined the best timing for offering the test.

Routine opt-out testing in the jail setting caught infections that risk-based testing would miss. Timing mattered: when in the intake process testing happens changes participation. The results give jail health services a tested playbook. Short stays mean the chance to test may not come again. The study treats a correctional setting as the public health opportunity it plainly is.
plos-pone-0007748:
Anne-Lise Pitel and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines the brains of people with Korsakoff's syndrome. The syndrome is a severe memory disorder tied to heavy alcohol use. It is often missed during life and confirmed only after death.

Earlier scans had looked at only a few brain regions. This team compared brain structure and glucose use across the whole brain. They analyzed patients as a group and one by one. The broader map revealed abnormalities beyond the usual suspect areas. Better brain markers could help doctors diagnose the syndrome earlier and more accurately.
plos-pone-0007848:
Sylvaine You and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines a signaling pathway that helps drive autoimmune diabetes in mice. In such diseases, harmful T cells and regulatory T cells talk past each other. That cross-talk decides whether the disease advances.

The team targeted the GITR and GITRL pathway, used by both cell types. They found it plays a key role in the development of murine autoimmune diabetes. A pathway with that much influence is a natural drug target. Blocking or tuning it might slow the attack on insulin-making cells.
plos-pone-0007948:
Constance Schultsz and colleagues checked bird flu exposure among poultry workers in Vietnam, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Outbreaks of the H5N1 virus in Ho Chi Minh City in 2005 put cullers and farm staff close to sick birds. Blood tests can show past infection through antibodies, the body's memory marks.

Few of the workers carried those marks. That low count suggests that careful culling and farm work, while risky on its face, led to few true infections. The news was welcome for health teams planning how to handle the next outbreak without undue fear.
plos-pone-0008048:
Audrey Dayon and colleagues placed a fat-handling enzyme at the heart of prostate cancer's hormone habit in PLOS ONE in 2009. Prostate tumors grow in answer to androgens, male hormones, and care often cuts that supply. The enzyme, sphingosine kinase-1, makes a fat signal tied to cancer growth.

The enzyme's activity rose and fell with androgen signals, and blocking it cut tumor growth and survival. That makes it a linchpin between the hormone and the cancer's will to live. Drugs against this enzyme could join hormone therapy for men whose disease no longer obeys it.
plos-pone-0008148:
Avinash Abhyankar and colleagues compared the control stretches of mitochondrial DNA across lab rat strains in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mitochondria, the cell's power plants, carry their own small genome. Its non-coding stretches hold the switches that set how the rest of that genome is read.

Inbred rat strains, each nearly uniform within itself, made the comparison clean. The switches varied between strains in ways that may tune how hard their power plants work. Since rat strains differ in disease risk, those quiet switch changes may explain part of the gap.
plos-pone-0008248:
David H. Tompkins and colleagues studied a gene in mouse airways in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Small airways called bronchioles are lined by ciliated, Clara, and goblet cells. Together these cells form a barrier and clear mucus. They also defend the lung against inhaled threats. Keeping that lining healthy is vital for the lung.

The team showed that the Sox2 gene is required for these cells. Without it, the three cell types were not maintained or produced properly. That finding identifies a master control for airway lining cells. It may guide research on lung repair and disease.
plos-pone-0008348:
Debra A. O'Leary and colleagues screened for muscular dystrophy drug helpers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a severe inherited muscle disease. One therapy idea uses antisense oligonucleotides to skip a faulty exon. Skipping converts the disease pattern toward the milder Becker form. Such trials were recently entering the clinic when the paper appeared.
