The team ran high-throughput screening for modulators of exon skipping. Both small molecules and genetic modulators were sought. Boosters of skipping could make the therapy work better. The screen provides leads for combination treatments.
plos-pone-0008448:
Georgia Schafer and co-authors test a receptor in tuberculosis in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The germ that causes tuberculosis is Mycobacterium tuberculosis. How it meets and enters host cells is complex and not well known. Many receptors may play a part. The team focus on one called scavenger receptor B1. It had been found to have some role in sensing the germ.

They study infection in a mouse model that lacks or holds this receptor. They check how the germ load and disease change. The results clarify what this receptor does and does not do. That helps map the first steps of infection.
plos-pone-0008548:
Ikuko Teramitsu and co-authors study a language gene in songbirds in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Mutations in FOXP2 cause developmental language disorders in humans. Accompanying brain abnormalities point to cortico-striatal circuitry. Part of the behavioral phenotype likely reflects organizational deficits there. Songbirds learn vocal patterns much as children learn speech. The team examine FoxP2 in the striatum during song learning.

They find striatal FoxP2 is actively regulated during sensorimotor learning. Levels shift as young birds practice and refine their songs. That dynamic regulation ties FoxP2 to vocal learning in real time. Birds thus model a core aspect of human speech development.
plos-pone-0008648:
Yang Zhao and co-authors track an immunity protein in mouse cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Irgm1, also called LRG-47, is an interferon-inducible GTPase associated with the Golgi membrane. Its disruption causes susceptibility to many intracellular pathogens. Irgm1 has been variously interpreted as a regulator of related effector GTPases. The team examine its localisation in mouse cells at rest and after interferon. They also study what happens when it is mislocalised to wrong compartments.

Proper localisation proves key to Irgm1's protective function. Mislocalised protein fails to defend cells against intracellular germs. The study clarifies where this GTPase must sit to work. It refines models of the interferon-induced immunity system.
plos-pone-0008748:
Michael Poulsen and Cameron Currie looked for friction inside a famous farming partnership. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fungus-growing ants raise fungi for food in underground gardens. A second fungus partners in the same gardens. Both fungi gain from the ants, yet they share one home. Partners in mutualisms often clash even while cooperating.

The authors probed whether the two fungi antagonize each other. Tests checked growth effects when the fungi met. Any hostility would complicate the picture of a harmonious farm. The work shows how cooperation and conflict mix in a three-way partnership.
plos-pone-0008848:
Vera Huang, Yi Qin, Ji Wang, and colleagues checked whether a gene-boosting RNA trick works beyond human cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Small double-stranded RNAs usually silence genes. A newer finding showed some can instead activate genes, a process called RNA activation. Until then it had been shown only in human cells. Conservation across mammals would make it a general tool.

The team triggered RNA activation in other mammalian cells successfully. The mechanism appears to be an old, shared feature of mammalian biology. A conserved activation route widens the RNA toolbox for research. It may also matter for future gene-boosting therapies.
plos-pone-0008948:
Susanne Frykman and co-authors mapped where an Alzheimer's-linked enzyme works in rat brain, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, gamma-secretase, cuts proteins inside cells. One of its cuts produces amyloid beta, the fragment that clumps in Alzheimer's disease. The enzyme is built from four parts, including presenilin and nicastrin.

The team located the active enzyme at synapses, where nerve cells connect. They also found it on endosomes, the sorting sacs inside cells. Knowing the enzyme's exact addresses helps explain how amyloid beta forms near synapses. That detail matters for drugs meant to block the enzyme without wrecking its other jobs.
plos-pone-0009048:
Jan-Michael Kugler, Christopher Lem, and Paul Lasko watched fruit fly egg making go wrong without one enzyme, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drosophila egg development is a classic window on stem cells and tissue shaping. Ubiquitin, a small tag, marks proteins for recycling or new duties. Cul-5 is part of one tagging machine in the fly's ovary.

Lowering cul-5 activity distorted the follicles that cradle each egg. Germ cells, the future eggs themselves, were also lost. The follicle's shape and the egg supply both depend on this tagging step. The study links protein recycling to the basic architecture of reproduction.
plos-pone-0009148:
Laurent Beck and co-authors found a phosphate pump gene that mouse livers cannot grow without, in PLOS ONE in 2010. PiT1 ferries phosphate into cells across their outer membrane. Phosphate is a basic need for DNA, bones, and energy handling. The pump was treated as a plain housekeeping supplier.

Mice lacking the gene during development failed to build normal livers. The defect showed PiT1 does more than top up phosphate. A routine supplier turned out to be an essential developmental gene. The finding warns against assuming housekeeping genes are boring.
plos-pone-0009248:
Vincent Gache and co-authors published this frog egg study in PLOS ONE in 2010. When an egg divides, it builds a spindle of microtubules to split its chromosomes. Many helper proteins run that machine, and many remain unknown. Frog eggs from Xenopus are a classic system for studying the process.

The team pulled the proteins bound to microtubules out of Xenopus eggs. Using mass spectrometry, they identified the full set present during meiosis. The result is an interactome: a parts list of the spindle's supporting cast. That catalogue gives cell biologists new candidates for the proteins that keep division accurate.
plos-pone-0009348:
Alessandro Bertolino and co-authors published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A form of the gene DRD2 is tied to risk of schizophrenia and to weak working memory. DRD2 builds the D2 receptor, which catches the brain signal dopamine. The gene form shifts the mix of two receptor types a person makes.

The team read D2 signals in a deep brain area, the striatum, from each person's genes. They then scanned the front of the brain while people did memory tasks. The gene-based D2 measures foretold how active the front brain area was. That chain links a gene to brain work in plain steps.
plos-pone-0009448:
Shyamasree De Majumdar and colleagues wrote in PLOS ONE in 2010 on the germ that causes tuberculosis. Inside the body the germ faces low oxygen. A control protein named DevR helps it adapt to that stress. DevR also helps the germ stay able to cause disease. The team made germs that produced DevR plus a cut down form of it.

With both forms present, the germs adapted poorly to low oxygen. They also became less able to cause disease. The findings show how much the germ leans on one control circuit. Jamming that circuit is a possible route to weaken the tuberculosis germ.
plos-pone-0009548:
Kristin Nichol, Kate Tummers, and Alanna Hoyer-Leitzel modeled flu on a college campus in PLOS ONE in 2010. Students catch flu at high rates and can gain much from vaccination. Shots can be given before the season or during it. Breaks and holidays empty the campus and then refill it. The team modeled an outbreak in a closed campus with those features.

The model tested how timing of shots changed the size of the outbreak. It also weighed the effect of students leaving and returning. Results like these give campus health teams a practical playbook. Flu planning can now match the rhythm of the school year.
plos-pone-0009648:
Sean Stromberg and Jean Carlson proposed a gentle theory of immune control in PLOS ONE in 2010. Immune disorders arise when the system attacks the body or overreacts. Most treatments suppress the immune system broadly, with real costs. The authors model a different idea, called passive attrition. In it, harmful immune responses fade as their cells wear out without renewal.

The model explores when such slow wearing down could suppress a disorder on its own. It suggests patience might sometimes beat force in immune therapy. The framework is theoretical, so its worth must be tested in practice. It offers a fresh way to think about calming autoimmunity.
plos-pone-0009848:
Tuberculosis is hard to confirm quickly in patients who also carry HIV. Keertan Dheda and colleagues tested a commercial urine and sputum test for that job. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Urine is far easier to collect than most samples.

The test is a LAM-ELISA assay, which hunts for a molecule shed by TB bacteria. Clinical utility means whether a test actually helps real diagnosis. The team judged the assay in HIV-infected patients, whose TB often hides. A fast, simple test would matter most where labs are scarce.
plos-pone-0009948:
A virus found in some prostate tumors and chronic fatigue patients drew wide attention in 2009. Ila Singh and colleagues tested whether an HIV drug could stop it. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The virus's role in disease was debated at the time.

The virus is XMRV, a retrovirus implicated in both conditions named above. Raltegravir proved a potent inhibitor of the virus in lab tests. The drug was built to block HIV's integration into DNA. A ready-made drug with this power gave researchers a fast lead. It gave the XMRV debate one concrete test result.
plos-pone-0010048:
The authors were Arun Konagurthu, Cyril Reboul, Jason Schmidberger, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper presented a web server for protein structure work. Proteins with related jobs often share similar shapes. Finding that shared core shape is a step in comparing and solving protein structures.

The server, called MUSTANG-MR, automates a sieving step based on that shared core. Users can run structural analysis and crystallography tasks through it online. Putting the tool on a server saves each lab from building the same pipeline on its own. It is offered as a free tool for other research groups.
plos-pone-0010148:
The authors were Vladimir Novitsky, Rui Wang, Hermann Bussmann, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study measured HIV levels in Botswana. It covered 4,348 HIV-positive people who had not yet taken antiviral drugs. All were infected with HIV-1 subtype C, the dominant form in southern Africa, and joined clinical studies there.

The team mapped how viral load, the amount of virus in blood, was spread across people. They highlighted those who keep a high viral load over time. Such people may be key targets for test-and-treat programs, which treat early to cut transmission.
plos-pone-0010248:
Catalina Alfonso-Parra and Keith Maggert studied a chromosome-binding protein in fruit flies in 2010. Turning a gene on comes with changes in how the nucleus is organized. Active genes shift near other active genes and distinct nuclear domains. Chromosomes are tethered to an inner nuclear scaffold, and those anchors may help set activity patterns across the genome.

Their PLOS ONE paper covered SAF-B, a protein linking the nuclear matrix, chromosomes, and gene activity. It sits at the junction of structure and transcription in Drosophila cells. Such links help explain how a cell's architecture shapes which genes it uses.
plos-pone-0010348:
David Montaner and Joaquín Dopazo presented a new data method in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gene studies produce long lists of changes, but lists alone do not explain biology. Researchers want to know what those changes do as a group. Standard tools test sets of genes that share a job or pathway. Montaner and Dopazo argued such tests miss part of the picture.

Their method looks at gene sets along more than one dimension at once. That gives a fuller view of how whole modules behave in an experiment. Better summaries can change which leads a lab follows up. The paper is aimed at analysts drowning in genomic output. It offers a way to turn thousands of gene readings into clearer claims.
plos-pone-0010448:
Magaly Blas and colleagues tested whether online videos could raise HIV testing among men in Peru for PLOS ONE in 2010. Many Peruvian men who have sex with men do not know their HIV status. The same group uses the internet heavily, making it a promising outreach channel. The team ran an online randomized trial comparing video-based promotion with standard material. Men were assigned by chance, keeping the comparison fair.

If short videos move men to test, clinics gain a cheap outreach tool. Testing is the gateway to treatment and to protecting partners. Reaching hidden populations online avoids some stigma of clinics. The study measured clicks and stated intent as first signs of effect. It stands as an early trial of internet health promotion in the region.
plos-pone-0010548:
Simon Patrick, Ed White and Holly Shiels studied how stretch feeds back on the electrical life of fish hearts in PLOS ONE in 2010. In hearts, mechanical squeezing and electrical signals influence each other. Stretch can open special channels and change the beat's timing. That feedback had never been studied in fish heart muscle. Fish hearts can swell greatly in volume, making the question pointed.

Their work gives fish a place in a field dominated by mammal studies. Feedback that steadies a mammal heart may act differently in a fish. Comparative data keep general theories honest. The study also matters for fish health in farming and warming waters. A small heart, here, tests a universal claim.
plos-pone-0010648:
Martina Lari and colleagues read a brain gene from Neanderthal DNA, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, microcephalin, helps control brain size. A newer version of one section spread widely in living people within the last tens of thousands of years.

Some researchers had proposed that the newer version entered our lineage from an archaic human group. The team recovered the older version from a Neanderthal individual. Finding the ancestral form there, and not the newer one, narrows the possible histories. Each gene read from fossil DNA sharpens the story of how modern humans and Neanderthals relate.
plos-pone-0010748:
Sujatha Venkataraman and colleagues studied a tiny RNA that fights a childhood brain tumor, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood. MicroRNAs are short RNAs that dial down specific genes. One of them, microRNA-128a, is often scarce in these tumors.

Restoring the RNA raised harmful oxygen radicals inside tumor cells. It did so by dialing down Bmi-1, a gene that helps cells stay young. The tumor cells then aged fast, a state called senescence, and stopped growing. A natural brake that tumors lose could be given back as a drug-like treatment.
plos-pone-0010848:
Sigeng Chen, Geoffrey Owens, Helen Makarenkova and co-authors published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nerve cells must haul cargo, including mitochondria, along long internal tracks, and the protein HDAC6 helps control that traffic by editing tubulin, a track building block. The authors asked how HDAC6 fits into a known serotonin-driven pathway that speeds mitochondria up.

Blocking HDAC6 with a specific drug sharply boosted mitochondrial movement in rat hippocampal neurons, while a near-identical inactive drug did nothing. Treated neurons carried more edited tubulin, and more of the motor protein kinesin-1 was attached to their mitochondria. Chen and colleagues place HDAC6 as a brake within the pathway. Releasing that brake on demand could matter for brain diseases where failing transport starves distant parts of a neuron.
plos-pone-0010948:
Blake Matthews, Luke Harmon, Leithen M'Gonigle and co-authors published this stickleback evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Parasites push their hosts to evolve, and different parasite communities in different habitats might even split one species into two. The authors examined MHC immune genes, which vary fast under parasite pressure and influence mate choice, in threespine stickleback fish.

They sampled fish from paired lake species that feed in open water or on the bottom, plus fish from lakes where the species live apart. Comparing immune gene variation across these settings tests whether divergence follows habitat, geography, or both. Matthews and colleagues use a classic speciation model to ask if parasites leave fingerprints on the immune system. Their answer bears on how quickly new species can form in neighboring habitats.
plos-pone-0011048:
Raad Gharaibeh, Joshua Newton, Jennifer Weller and co-authors published this microarray methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gene chips using fifty-letter probes are widespread, but how those probes behave with near-matching targets was poorly charted compared with shorter probe platforms. The authors used physics-based equilibrium models of DNA binding to predict and interpret that behavior.

Arrays carrying probes with one, two, or three central mismatches were tested across a range of target concentrations. The models' percent-bound values discriminated perfect matches from mismatches, and in the mid concentration range even predicted which kind of mismatch was present. Gharaibeh and colleagues show that solution chemistry models transfer to chip design, helping researchers choose probes and read results with fewer costly empirical trials.
plos-pone-0011148:
De Jong, Xie, Onsongo and colleagues searched saliva for cancer signs in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mouth cancer does far better when caught early, yet there was no easy test to tell risky spots from true cancer. The team measured proteins in saliva from patients with both kinds of lesions.

Two proteins, myosin and actin, stood out as promising marks that separate the two states. A spit test would be painless and cheap compared with cutting tissue. Such a test could raise survival by speeding treatment decisions. The marks now need larger trials before dentists or doctors can rely on them.
plos-pone-0011248:
Imada, Hoki, Suehiro and colleagues watched pairs of small fish in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fish schools move as one, but the building blocks start with just two fish. The team showed both fish the same moving stripe pattern, triggering a shared reflex to swim with the motion.

Under that shared stimulus, the pair moved in a coordinated and cohesive way. That simple setup reveals how group order can arise without a leader. It gives behavior researchers a clean way to study schooling from its smallest unit. The same principles may guide robot swarms that must move together.
plos-pone-0011348:
Nisebita Sahu and co-workers built a mouse model in 2010 to explain why some animals resist allergic airway disease while others develop it. Mouse models of allergic asthma have taught scientists much, and gene knockouts have named many molecules involved. Yet those tools had not fully explained why genetic background decides who gets sick.

By comparing strains that differ in their response, the team found that a signaling enzyme called Itk helps set the balance between sickness and resistance. Adjusting that enzyme shifted how the airway disease played out. The model gives asthma researchers a cleaner way to separate cause from side effect. It also marks Itk as a possible drug target for allergic disease, where calming one enzyme might spare patients broader immune suppression.
plos-pone-0011448:
Marta Epeldegui and co-authors reported in 2010 that HIV particles can switch on a mutating enzyme inside human B cells. B cells make antibodies, and an enzyme called AID normally edits their antibody genes under tight control. The team found that HIV virions carrying a host protein, CD40 ligand, on their surface push B cells to make that enzyme.

Switching on a gene-editing enzyme at the wrong time can scramble B-cell programming and weaken antibody defense. The result suggests HIV harms immunity by more than killing T cells; it also misdirects the B cells it touches. That angle helps explain the odd antibody patterns seen in HIV infection, including high antibody levels that protect poorly. For researchers, the virus's passenger protein becomes a suspect worth blocking.
plos-pone-0011548:
Surender Khurana and co-authors reported in 2010 a bacteria-grown flu vaccine that protected ferrets from the pandemic virus. The 2009 H1N1 pandemic demanded vaccines faster and cheaper than egg-based production allows. The team grew pieces of the virus's surface protein, hemagglutinin, in bacteria, and showed the pieces folded into the correct shape, a step earlier attempts often failed.

Ferrets vaccinated with the properly folded head and outer sections of the protein were protected against the pandemic strain. Ferrets are the standard stand-in for human flu, so protection there is a meaningful milestone. A bacterial method promises quicker, cheaper production that can scale in ordinary factories worldwide. For the next pandemic, speed of manufacture is measured in lives, and this study is about buying that speed.
plos-pone-0011648:
Marion Liberloo and co-authors checked whether bioenergy crops still help the climate as carbon dioxide rises, in PLOS ONE in 2010. For biofuels to replace fossil fuels, they must keep cutting net emissions under future air conditions. Higher carbon dioxide does boost plant growth, yet it was unclear whether the climate benefit would survive the change.

Their analysis finds that bio-energy keeps its mitigation potential under elevated carbon dioxide. In other words, the carbon savings do not wash away as the atmosphere changes. That reassurance supports keeping sustainably grown bioenergy in long-term climate plans.
plos-pone-0011748:
Hélène Falentin and co-authors read the full genome of a cheese-ripening germ, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Propionibacterium freudenreichii is a key culture for ripening Swiss-type cheeses and is also studied for probiotic use. The species grows slowly, needs few nutrients and stays hardy in many places.

Their full genetic text covers the type strain used as the species reference. It shows the basis of the germ's toughness and its dairy performance. Cheese-makers and probiotic designers gain a parts list for improving flavour, texture and health-linked uses of this useful microbe over time.
plos-pone-0011848:
Melanie Ruffner and Paul Robbins tested in 2010 whether reprogrammed immune cells could delay type 1 diabetes in mice. They worked with nonobese diabetic mice, a strain that develops the disease on its own. Their tool was dendritic cells, the immune system's teachers, altered in the lab to make interleukin-4, a calming signal molecule.

Giving these altered cells reduced the onset of diabetes both in mice still showing normal blood sugar and in mice already partway toward disease. Earlier work had shown similar cells easing arthritis-like illness, so the diabetes result extends the approach to another self-attack disease. It supports the idea of using a patient's own retrained cells to quiet a harmful immune response.
plos-pone-0011948:
Amit Kapoor and colleagues told the world in 2010 about a virus no one had seen before, found in gorillas in the wild. The virus is a bocavirus, a small member of the parvovirus family. The team found its DNA while testing the stool of western lowland gorillas that had fallen ill with a gut complaint, and they then read the new virus's full gene set.

The gene set has three main reading frames and differs enough from known bocaviruses to count as a new species. Sick apes are not the only reason to care: kin of this virus infect people, and apes so close to us can trade germs with us. A firm record of what flows through wild gorillas gives health watchers a head start and helps guard the apes as well.
plos-pone-0012048:
Inês de Oliveira and co-workers mapped in 2010 bacterial mutations that defeat a cell division policeman. In Bacillus subtilis, division must happen exactly at midcell. Two systems enforce that: one blocks division over the chromosome, and the Min system, whose MinC protein stops the division ring from forming in the wrong place.

The team characterized changes in ftsZ, the protein that builds the division ring, which make the bacterium resistant to MinC. Escape mutations reveal exactly where the policeman grips its target. That knowledge completes the picture of how a cell guarantees one division, in the middle, a control problem every bacterium must solve.
plos-pone-0012148:
Nil Emre, Jason Vidal, Jeanne Elia, and co-authors improved a lab method for human embryonic stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. These cells can become any tissue, but they are fragile: sorting them with a laser-guided machine often kills so many that experiments fail. The team wanted a reliable way to sort them using several surface markers at once.

Adding a compound that blocks a certain enzyme greatly improved how many cells survived sorting and grew afterward. Their protocol hands other labs a sturdier recipe for picking out chosen cell types. Better survival means cleaner experiments, which every stem cell project, from basic study to therapy design, depends on.
plos-pone-0012248:
Geoffroy Nourissat, Amadou Diop, Nathalie Maurel, and co-authors tested stem cell therapy for tendon-to-bone repair in rats, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The junction where tendon meets bone wears away with age, and surgery to reattach torn tendons there often disappoints because older tissue heals poorly. The team used a degenerative rat model of this repair to test whether added mesenchymal stem cells could rebuild the junction.

Treated repairs regenerated a junction closer to the natural one, rather than weak scar. Restoring the original graded tissue, from soft tendon to hard bone, is what makes such repairs durable. Shoulder surgeons face this failure daily in older patients, so a cell boost that works in animals earns attention.
plos-pone-0012348:
Anne Visscher, Anna-Lisa Paul, Matias Kirst and colleagues grew a small mustard-family plant in Mars-like soil in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Soil on Mars holds large amounts of a magnesium salt that could poison crops. Crews on long Mars missions may need to grow food in local soil, so the team asked how the plant copes and which genes switch on or off.

Plants grew in soil dosed with the salt at levels like those found on Mars, and the team read growth plus root gene activity. The plants survived but grew less, and their roots reshaped which genes they used. The results point to both limits and hope for farming on Mars with treated local soil.
plos-pone-0012448:
Kevin Watt, Erica Waddle and Ravi Jhaveri reviewed how serious bacterial infections in feverish infants have changed, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Babies with fever but no clear source worry doctors greatly, and rules for which babies need full testing have shifted over the years. Vaccines and new tests changed the odds that such a fever hides a dangerous germ.

The review tracks which bacteria now cause these infections and how their shares moved over time. Updated odds help doctors decide when blood and spinal tests are worth the pain and cost. Guidance built on old germ patterns can overtest some babies and miss the real risks in others.
plos-pone-0012548:
Lee Cooper, David Gutman, Qi Long and colleagues mined brain tumor genome data for a survival-linked pattern, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The Cancer Genome Atlas had gathered vast molecular data on glioblastoma, the deadliest common brain tumor, and sorted tumors into expression subtypes. One pattern, called proneural, stood out in a related tumor family, the diffuse gliomas.

The proneural signature was enriched in oligodendrogliomas and predicted improved survival among diffuse glioma patients. A signature that sorts patients by outlook can guide how aggressively to treat and whom to enroll in trials. It also hints that proneural tumors run a distinct, somewhat less vicious biology.
plos-pone-0012648:
Zhang, Liu, Ding and co-authors improved a method for predicting an animal's breeding worth from its DNA. Modern chips read hundreds of thousands of gene markers at once, making genome-based selection real for farms. Their 2010 paper refines the prediction method known as BLUP, best linear unbiased prediction.

Their twist builds the family links between animals from markers tied to the trait itself, not the whole genome. Trait-focused links can sharpen accuracy where it counts, in meat, milk and other farm traits. Better predictions mean faster gains from each round of breeding.
plos-pone-0012748:
Mallet, Barriere, Ermund and co-authors placed a heat-sensing channel in the brain at the centre of how paracetamol eases pain. The drug, also called acetaminophen, is among the most used pain and fever medicines on earth. Yet its exact way of working stayed debated for decades.

Their 2010 study shows the TRPV1 channel in the brain is needed for the drug's pain relief in their tests. A brain site of action overturns the old view that the drug works only in the body. It may also explain some of the drug's risks.
plos-pone-0012948:
Christakis and Fowler proposed using well-connected people as early sensors for outbreaks. Standard outbreak detection only reports a disease once it is already spreading. People near the centre of a social network, though, tend to catch contagious illnesses earlier than average members.

Their 2010 paper shows that monitoring such central people, or their friends, can give advance warning of an epidemic's course. Even a few days of warning lets hospitals and officials prepare. The method uses friendship data that surveys already gather, at little extra cost.  The authors ground the idea in data from a college social network study.
plos-pone-0339248:
Jacinta Thorne and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It reports on the Concussion Recovery Study, known as CREST, in an Australian community cohort. The authors work on predicting recovery outcomes after mild traumatic brain injury, the medical name for concussion.

Most concussions clear within weeks, but some people struggle for months, and doctors struggle to say in advance who they will be. Prediction built from a community cohort, not just hospital patients, reflects the injuries people actually get in sport and daily life. Clinicians and insurers planning follow-up care are the readers for such forecasts.
plos-pone-0340348: Conic intersections — easily computed via the common self-polar triangle. This paper showed how. The elegant geometry simplified a classical problem. The findings served the pure mathematics — beauty in the service of computation.
plos-pone-0340748:
Khan and colleagues combined gut microbe gene data with protein modeling in Crohn's disease in a 2026 study. Crohn's inflames the gut, and microbe shifts are well known, but changes inside the microbes' own genes were little explored. Three helpful gut bacteria were less common in Crohn's and in a related condition.

Hundreds of gene variants were specific to Crohn's samples. One change in a starch-using protein of a key bacterium weakened its grip on a test starch molecule in modeling, while the molecule stayed in place during simulations. A weaker grip could alter how the bacterium feeds in the gut, offering a fresh angle on Crohn's biology.
plos-pone-0343448:
Jiamin Zhang and colleagues optimised the water passages of a large vertical pump station by testing many factors at once rather than one by one. Single factor tuning misses how settings interact. Orthogonal test design plus fluid simulation scored options on water loss, flow evenness, and inflow angle, for both entry and exit passages at a drainage station.

Best entry design cut loss to a trickle and delivered near ideal upright inflow with high evenness. Best exit design flowed smoothly without separation and fit the station layout. Model tests matched simulations closely, with unit efficiency above seventy seven percent at design load. Multi factor tuning finds pump gains that single dial experiments miss.
plos-pone-0344048:
Haoxian Shi and fellow engineers studied clogged screens in offshore gas hydrate wells in 2026. Hydrate, an ice-like mix of gas and water, blocks the sand screens in wells set in soft silt, and output falls. Flushing the screens with spinning water jets is one fix.

Tests weighed jet tool type, tool speed, screen mesh, and whether a pierced pipe sat inside. A high pressure tool that forms tiny bursting bubbles cleaned best, slower movement beat faster, and coarser screens flushed better than fine ones. Pierced pipes made cleaning worse. The rankings give crews a practical recipe for restoring flow in hydrate wells.
plos-pone-0346348:
Beth Nichol and colleagues present a protocol, published in 2026, for a realist evaluation of Healthy Conversation Skills training. This coaching sits behind Britain's Making Every Contact Count initiative. The initiative asks frontline workers to slip health behavior conversations into everyday encounters. Training is widespread but delivery is patchy. Nobody knows which ingredients work for whom.

The evaluation will survey trainees before, right after, and two months following training. It will interview them in depth. Community sector workers and volunteers will be compared against pharmacy undergraduates. Realist method hunts context and mechanism, not just outcomes. It asks what fires change, in which setting, for which trainee. The refined theory produced should tell trainers which elements are sacred and which can flex.
plos-pone-0346948: de Paula Ferreira and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on knee osteoarthritis pain. Using gene activity data, they found a program in the joint lining that resembles a process called epithelial-mesenchymal transition. They describe it as a stromal-remodeling program tied to pain. Early discovery work like this can point to why some knees hurt more than scans suggest, and where new drugs might act.
plos-pone-0347048:
Large bone gaps need scaffolds that invite new bone while bearing load. Vahid Khademi Ardakani and colleagues printed scaffolds from a plastic and mineral blend enriched with helpful ions, then coated them with a zinc-bearing crystal layer, in this 2026 PLOS One materials study.

The best recipe, carrying forty percent mineral, reached useful strength while slowly dissolving over a month at stable acidity. In body-like fluid it quickly grew the mineral crust real bone forms, releasing calcium, magnesium, silicon, and strontium steadily. Bone-related cells stuck, multiplied, and laid down mineral far better on coated scaffolds than plain ones. The team sees a biodegradable implant that coaches the body to rebuild.
plos-pone-0347748:
Shrawan K. Patel and co-workers design a small microwave part that splits signals cleanly across a very wide band of frequencies. Such couplers steer signals in communication gear, and wideband versions are hard to keep even and well directed. Their 2026 study builds a three-section design from short-ended paired lines and checks it by calculation, simulation, and bench tests on a built prototype.

The prototype held its coupling nearly level from low to high test frequencies, a five-to-one span. Signals passed with low loss, unwanted leakage stayed down, and direction quality beat the usual design. The layout also scales: adding sections can set other bandwidths. Better couplers support the fast, crowded networks that phones and sensors now depend on.
plos-pone-0347848:
Josephine Mensah and Pauline Boachie Ansah led talks with health workers at a big teaching hospital in Ghana. The topic was hydroxyurea, a key drug for sickle cell disease. Many patients there fail to get it or to stay on it. The team spoke with six doctors, nurses, and pharmacists in 2022. They also asked staff about a phone app built to aid sickle cell care.

Cost was the top block, workers said. Stock-outs and slow paperwork also hurt. Parents forget doses or fear side effects. Making a liquid form for young children adds cost and time. Staff backed more patient teaching, faster buying, and state aid with drug costs. Few knew the app well, so the team urges training.
plos-pone-0348348:
Wikan Danar Sunindyo and colleagues automated the reading of electrical signals used to detect troponin, a protein that leaks from injured heart muscle. Clinicians measure troponin with electrode tests whose wavy traces drift, buzz with noise, and usually need a trained eye to interpret. Their software cleans each trace with the fitting method suited to its type, then measures the peak height above the corrected baseline as the signal of interest.

Automated reading found the characteristic peaks reliably and separated stronger from weaker heart-marker responses against a set threshold. Results matched the reference analysis software closely. By removing operator judgement from the routine reading, the authors aim to make bedside and low-resource heart screening faster and more consistent. The aid could help catch heart attacks early where specialists are scarce.
plos-pone-0348948:
Darren Cook and colleagues present a protocol for a study testing whether language-processing software can help analyze Domestic Homicide Reviews, the official inquiries held after abuse-related deaths in England and Wales. Reviews are legally required, yet studying many of them at once is rare because reading long narrative reports by hand is slow and costly. Lessons that cross cases therefore stay buried.

The planned study will assess whether computers can extract the patterns while practitioners guide and check the work, balancing speed with expert judgment. Natural language processing here means software that reads text for themes and facts. If feasible, the approach could finally let researchers learn from the full archive of reviews rather than small samples.
plos-pone-0349148:
Ahmad Zambri Ilham, Mohd Noor Norhayati, and Ismail Shaiful Bahari studied loneliness among older residents of a Malaysian nursing home in 2026. Loneliness in care homes carries real health risks, yet it is rarely studied in depth in the region.

Twenty-three residents of a home in Taiping took part in interviews and a short loneliness scale. Every participant scored as lonely, and most fell at the loneliest end. Interviews traced causes such as loss, distance from family, and few meaningful activities, alongside the ways residents cope. The findings argue for care that treats company and purpose as health needs, not extras.
plos-pone-0349448:
Chancy Skenard Chimatiro and co-authors mapped what is known about how health systems in Sub-Saharan Africa respond to a warming climate. Their 2026 PLOS One scoping review searched four databases for studies published between 2011 and 2025, in a region hit harder by climate change than most.

From more than eleven thousand records, only eight studies qualified. Most described responses in care delivery, staffing, information systems, and leadership. Few covered how services are paid for or how medicines reach clinics. No study spanned all six building blocks the World Health Organization uses to describe a health system. The thin evidence itself is a warning, the authors suggest.
plos-pone-0349548:
Shadrack Ayanku and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about blood safety in Ghana. It covers the Volta Region and looks back over four years of records. The authors report seroprevalence, the share of blood donors whose blood shows signs of infections that can pass through transfusion.

Tracking these infections over time shows whether the donor blood supply is getting safer or facing new risks. Transfusion-transmissible infections can harm patients who receive blood during surgery or emergencies. Blood service managers in Ghana and similar settings can use trend data like this to improve donor screening and testing.
plos-pone-0349748:
Mariann Eilertsen and colleagues traced how the eyes and brain of Atlantic salmon rewire their light sensing during smoltification, the spring change that prepares young fish to leave rivers for the sea. Longer days trigger the shift through light-sensitive pigments in the eye and brain and through the body's daily clock. The team sequenced gene activity across the transition.

A dramatic switch appeared in the color-vision genes: the balance between green-sensitive and red-sensitive pigments changed as the fish prepared for ocean light. Nonvisual light sensors and clock genes shifted too, retuning the fish to a new daily rhythm. Understanding this internal calendar matters for fish farming, where artificial light schedules are used to control when smolts are ready for seawater.
plos-pone-0349848:
Heather Cuevas, Jeeyeon Kim, and Shenell Wood wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on type 2 diabetes and the mind. It studies maintaining cognitive gains, keeping improvements in thinking that patients had achieved. The authors map the barriers people meet, the supports they find, and how their strategy use falls into patterns, among people working to hold those gains.

Diabetes threatens memory and thinking over time, so gains won through training or care are worth defending. Knowing which strategies people actually keep using, and what knocks them off course, guides programs beyond their first success. Diabetes educators and neuropsychologists are the readers for this maintenance view.
plos-pone-0349948:
Going home after heart bypass surgery can feel abrupt, and Melanie Rushton, Michelle Howarth, and Heather Iles-Smith asked patients how ready they felt. Their 2026 PLOS One qualitative study interviewed eleven patients at a hospital in northern England, four to six weeks after surgery.

Four themes stood out. Many patients avoided asking for help, not wanting to make a fuss. Many felt unready to leave. A printed booklet proved genuinely useful. Care felt too standard, with too little tailoring to each person's home life and worries. The authors argue discharge planning should be shaped around the individual, not the ward routine.
plos-pone-0350048:
Victor Beaucoté, Marc Fischler, and co-authors reanalyzed data from more than nine thousand surgical patients to refine how low blood pressure during an operation predicts a long hospital stay afterward. No universal danger threshold exists, though guidelines cluster around a standard pressure range. Their 2026 reanalysis modeled three pressure measures against prolonged stay, splitting results by age and sex.

One measure, the lowest average pressure reached, showed a clear activation point: risk rose steadily once it fell below a level notably above the usual guideline floor. Swings in pulse pressure raised risk with no safe threshold at all. Women showed lower risk and lower thresholds than men, while patients over sixty-five carried higher baseline risk with no clean threshold. The authors say age and sex belong in any definition of dangerous pressure drops.
plos-pone-0350148:
Qian Li and colleagues built a model for deciding where to place depots of emergency rescue supplies before an earthquake strikes. A depot in the wrong spot wastes the first hours after a quake, when rescue matters most. Their model scores candidate regions using four parts of disaster risk: the hazard itself, what stands exposed, how fragile it is, and the local capacity to respond.

Weights for the scores come from the data rather than opinion, and map data feeds the regional comparisons. The model also separates what can be judged before a disaster from the losses expected after one, so depots match both everyday readiness and likely damage patterns. For planners in quake-prone regions, the work turns depot siting from habit into a defensible calculation, tested here on the earthquake case.
plos-pone-0350548:
Nermin Kukuksonmez, Abdullah Kocak, and Nuh Akcakaya surveyed nearly twelve hundred university students across twelve Turkish universities on cinema habits and motives, read through a class lens. Students reported how often they attend, what draws them, and their social and economic background with three standard tools.

Going with others to socialise led all motives. Cinema was rarely a cure for loneliness; company was the point. Screen and sound quality also drew crowds. Richer students attended more, poorer students less, and motives varied by class. Cheap tickets alone will not equalise cinema culture while social and class gaps shape the night out.
plos-pone-0350648:
Dala Daraghmeh, Leen Kahla, and Noor Taqatq surveyed four hundred pharmacists across Palestine about probiotics and prebiotics, the live-culture and culture-feeding products crowding pharmacy shelves. Pharmacists are the most reachable health professionals for most people, so their grasp of these products shapes what customers buy. A scored questionnaire sorted knowledge into poor, moderate, and high bands and probed attitudes and counseling habits.

Most pharmacists landed in the moderate band, about a third scored high, and one in ten scored poorly. Nearly nine in ten believed the products help health and four in five were willing to recommend them. Formal training on the topic, age, and prescription volume nudged knowledge up modestly. The gap between enthusiasm and evidence access, pharmacists citing trouble reaching good sources, is the fixable problem this survey exposes.
plos-pone-0350748:
Ningjing Guo and colleagues reviewed twenty one English language studies on large language models in weight loss surgery care. Uses clustered into patient education and questions, decision support for clinicians, and testing professional knowledge. Searches spanned eight databases through November 2025 under standard scoping rules.

Models answered information questions well, yet agreed poorly with experts on complex, personal surgical advice. One leading model generally scored best, while surgery tuned models showed promise. Accuracy, reading level, and clinical fit remain weak spots. Chatbots can draft patient guidance, the authors conclude, but surgeons must vet every answer before it reaches a patient.
plos-pone-0351248:
Yoshiaki Zaizen and colleagues examined skin biopsies from twenty two patients with dermatomyositis, an autoimmune disease that inflames skin and muscle, against thirteen control skin samples. Stains tracked immune deposits and a virus sensing protein in the surface skin layers where rash forms.

Diseased skin held far more complement and two antibody types at the rash border zone than control skin, a pattern that fits immune complex injury. The sensing protein sat strongly in upper skin layers in both groups, yet appeared in deeper inflammation cells and tiny vessels only in diseased skin. Immune deposits at the skin junction may help pathologists confirm this elusive rash.
plos-pone-0351548:
Gribaudo and colleagues, in a 2026 modeling study, compare ways of giving treatment to patients with a form of breast cancer marked by the HER2 protein in Italian cancer centers. Drugs for this cancer can be given by drip into a vein or by injection under the skin. The route changes how long patients and staff spend, and what care costs.

A decision tree model played out five pathways, from standard practice to a fully optimized route, tracking staff time, chair time, patient time, and direct and indirect costs. Switching to under-skin delivery cut times a great deal. In the best pathway, savings per hundred patients each month reached dozens of staff hours, well over a hundred chair hours, and hundreds of patient hours. Every new pathway saved money against standard practice. The authors argue centers should match the pathway to their own layout and staffing.
plos-pone-0351748:
Eric Margenau, Petra Wood, and Christopher Ryan survey songbirds along pipeline and powerline corridors in West Virginia forests, asking which scale of habitat shapes them most, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The corridors were managed with forestry treatments, and bird counts at each point were compared against vegetation immediately around the point and across the wider surrounding landscape.

Landscape won. The amount of young forest nearby and the size of the nearest young-forest patch influenced birds more than anything measured up close; of the local factors, corridor width mattered most. Species within the same habitat guild sometimes pulled in opposite directions, complicating one-size management. Planners, the authors argue, must design corridor work with the whole neighbourhood in view.
plos-pone-0351948: Psammophilic — sand-loving — scarab beetles radiated across ancient dunes. This phylogeography of Geopsammodius traced that radiation of endemic beetles. The evolutionary history reveals how life diversifies in Earth’s most shifting habitats.
plos-pone-0352148:
James Barton and colleagues measured two antibody types, IgA and IgM, in people whose genes load their bodies with iron. The condition, hemochromatosis tied to two copies of a variant in the HFE gene, also raises infection risk, yet antibody levels in such patients had not been reported. The team compiled levels from seventy-three patients at diagnosis and tested links with age, drinking, blood counts, and iron measures.

Average levels sat within ordinary ranges, and most patient traits showed no link with either antibody. IgM fell as age rose and climbed a little with daily alcohol intake. Set beside published European averages, the values give doctors a baseline for a group where immune questions are often raised but rarely measured. The study fills a small, concrete gap rather than claiming a new immune defect.
plos-pone-0352248:
Courtney Slegers and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study on whether what a breastfeeding mother eats changes the inflammatory signals in her milk. The team collected day-long diet records from about one hundred healthy nursing mothers, scored each diet's inflammatory tendency, and measured thirteen immune markers in their milk using a bead-based laboratory panel.

Every mother's diet landed on the anti-inflammatory side, so the planned comparison between diet types collapsed into a narrower question. Milk turned out to be dominated by three messenger chemicals tied to immune cell traffic, found in nearly all samples. Only one marker showed a weak link with diet score. The authors, reporting the first study of its kind, call for work with more diverse eaters before drawing conclusions about infants.
plos-pone-0352348:
Sangtaek Oh and colleagues asked a simple question with long reach. Does having diabetes in the family speed up the slow rise in blood sugar that comes before the disease? Most past work counted who got sick. This team tracked how sugar levels moved over time. They used repeat health checkups from tens of thousands of Korean adults. People with and without a family history were matched so the groups began alike.

Across two and four year windows, the family history group worsened faster. Both fasting sugar and long-term sugar control drifted up more quickly. Three different statistical methods gave the same answer. Family history is not just a warning about some distant day. It marks people whose sugar is already climbing, and who may need earlier checks.
plos-pone-0352648:
Francis Ssenkuba and four colleagues survey snails and other molluscs in small volcanic lakes of East Africa. Their 2026 study covers three lakes in Uganda and two in Rwanda. These barrier lakes sit inside a famous biodiversity hotspot. Yet scientists have mostly studied the great Rift lakes instead. The team combined shell identification, DNA barcoding, and ecological analysis.

Diversity in the small lakes was surprisingly high. Most species were widespread forms with affinities to the Nile basin fauna. Worryingly, communities across lakes are growing more alike. Invaded lakes showed the tightest clustering of similar assemblages. Suspected drivers include invaders like the North American crayfish and an Asian snail line. The authors stay cautious: their data cannot fully separate invasion effects from other lake differences. The baseline still matters, since change is clearly underway.
plos-pone-0353348:
Saadia Malik, Muhammad Hamid, and Muhammad Saleem teach a computer a hard judgement call. How much work will a software task take? Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Agile teams describe work as short 'user stories'. Guessing their effort is notoriously unreliable. The authors gathered thousands of real stories from many sources. They cleaned them down to about four thousand sound examples. Then they trained a hybrid model. One part reads language with a pre-trained transformer. The other tracks word order with a memory network.

On held-out stories the model beat conventional methods. Its error was clearly lower. Its scores were then mapped onto the point scale. That is the scale planning teams actually use. Reliable estimates mean fewer blown deadlines in software projects.
plos-pone-0353748:
Rekha Timalsina and four colleagues survey three hundred older adults attending daycare centres in Kathmandu, Nepal, about their psychological well-being, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Face-to-face interviews combined a standard well-being scale with questions on family, money, and health. Nepal has little local evidence on what keeps older people psychologically well, despite a rapidly ageing population.

Being married and living with a spouse, being literate, and having worked earlier in life each raised the odds of high well-being substantially. Receiving the state old-age allowance was also associated in early analysis. Money and marriage mattered, but literacy's strong showing suggests adult education in earlier life pays emotional dividends decades later — a case for investing in today's middle-aged.
plos-pone-0354148:
Momahhed and Haghighathoseini, in a 2026 study of Iranian insurance claims, build a machine learning model to spot typhoid patients who stay in hospital longer than they need to. Long stays cost patients and systems, and in Iran's split insurance system patients pay much of the bill themselves. Claims for one year were grouped into about thirteen thousand hospital stays.

The model sorted patients well, beating a standard statistical method. It flagged more than a third of stays as potentially shorter, adding up to thousands of recoverable bed-days subject to clinical review. In a costed subset, earlier discharge cut spending by nearly a quarter, and most savings landed with patients as lower out-of-pocket payments. Freed beds could take well over a thousand extra admissions. The strongest predictor of a long stay was not illness severity but the patient's insurance class, a structural flaw the authors highlight.
plos-pone-0354248:
Brahms and colleagues, in a 2026 study, compare two huge families of blood pressure drugs for a possible link to cancer. Both families are mainstays of heart and kidney care, yet their long-term safety on cancer has stayed unsettled. Using records from Israel's largest health service, the team followed adults with high blood pressure who stayed on one family only.

From a pool of over a million people, rules left about three hundred fifty thousand users of one family and seventy-seven thousand of the other. Over long follow-up, cancer appeared less often among users of the first family, the ACE inhibitors, than among users of the second, the receptor blockers. The pattern shifted by cancer type, favoring the first family for several common cancers. The authors stress the design cannot prove cause, since doctors choose drugs for reasons that may track with cancer risk.
plos-pone-0354348:
Zheng Li and colleagues engineered a grout that can be held in place by magnets. It seals leaks and stabilizes ground underwater, where ordinary slurry washes away. Their 2026 study loaded a cement slurry with magnetic iron oxide powder at several doses. It measured how the slurry flows under magnetic fields of different strengths. It imaged the particle chains that form inside. It also blasted the slurry with flowing water to test retention.

More powder magnetized the slurry in a straight-line relationship. Its resistance to flow rose with field strength, as physics predicts. Particles lined up into short chains, long chains, and bundles. In moving water at a brisk clip, the magnetic slurry stayed put nearly nine times better than plain slurry. The work gives underwater construction a controllable new material.
plos-pone-0354748:
Christos Charalambous builds in 2026 a computer model of how people decide about vaccination during an outbreak. Fictional agents learn from results, feel expected regret, watch what others do, and face unclear information. Spread of illness follows a classic pattern where people move between being at risk, ill, and recovered.

Middle levels of careful choice worked best when learning stood alone. Adding social norms steadied behaviour and softened the cost of very precise choices, while great noise stayed harmful. Moderate regret helped agents correct course, but too much regret or greed upset choices. Norms based on approval mattered most when information felt shaky.
plos-pone-0355048:
Jie Cao and colleagues simulated management choices for the snapper-grouper fishery off the southeast United States coast. Many species are caught together there, yet rules usually target one species at a time, which wastes fish. Their 2026 study modelled time and area limits on fishing effort for six commonly caught species.

The simulation scored each option on spawning stock, landings, discarded fish, and money for commercial and recreational fleets. Some effort controls beat others, but none was best for every species and both fleets at once. Gains for conservation often traded against harvest or income. Cao and colleagues present the framework as a way for managers to see those trade-offs clearly before choosing.
plos-pone-0355548:
Hao Zhang and co-authors searched for shared molecular signals between Alzheimer's disease and HIV-related brain disorder. Both conditions erode thinking over time, yet common mechanisms and early markers are lacking. Their 2026 study combined gene activity data from several brain and blood cohorts and tested machine learning classifiers.

One gene, a known regulator of cell ageing and survival, stood out as the top marker for both diseases. It sorted Alzheimer's samples very well and HIV-related samples fairly well. Two further regulators joined it in a small panel that worked in blood, which would allow easier testing. Pathways for cell survival and inflammation ran through the results. The authors stress the panel needs testing in fresh clinical groups.
plos-pone-0355848:
Tinghui Huang and co-authors built an interpretable machine learning model to predict frailty in hospital patients who have both heart failure and an acute infection. Frailty worsens outcomes, yet its drivers in this exact group were little studied. Their 2026 study enrolled about fifteen hundred patients at a Nanjing hospital and screened many candidate predictors.

Frailty proved strikingly common, affecting about four in five patients. Selected predictors included use of a common water pill class, blood protein level, kidney function, and immune cell share. Eight algorithms were compared, and explanation graphics showed how each factor pushes a prediction. The title question, whether thiazide diuretics belong on the risk list, is answered as one signal among several, not a lone cause.
plos-pone-0355948:
Harya Hermawan and colleagues evaluated a rapid bedside test for bacterial vaginosis in pregnant women at an Indonesian hospital. The infection is common in pregnancy and is linked with early birth and other complications. Their 2026 study compared the rapid test against a standard clinical scoring method in over a hundred women.

About six in ten women tested positive under the reference method. The rapid test caught nearly all true cases and was especially strong when it read negative. Repeat infection and secondary infection raised the odds of a positive result, while more schooling lowered them. Hermawan and colleagues judge the test a reliable, fast option where laboratory diagnosis is hard to reach.
plos-pone-0356148:
Xintong Wang and colleagues studied what quitting a cancer-causing chemical exposure does inside early mouse lung nodules. Smoking is known to slow after quitting, but changes inside precancerous tissue were unclear. Their 2026 study exposed mice to a tobacco-related carcinogen, confirmed early nodules by scanning, then withdrew the exposure for set periods.

Withdrawal brought fewer new nodules and shrank existing ones. Tissue looked less abnormal, and inflammation eased. Immune cell mixes shifted toward defender cells and away from inflammatory types. Several growth and stress genes quieted, while heat-shock defence genes rose. Wang and colleagues say the cell-level detail helps explain why stopping exposure still helps after damage has begun.
plos-pone-0356548:
Alfredo González-Espinoza and Joshua Plotkin measure how harmony changed across four centuries of Western classical music in this 2026 study. They turned each piece into a bar-by-bar sequence of musical keys, using an algorithm that judges the most likely key for each stretch of notes. From those sequences they computed measures of uncertainty, variety, and how surprising each key change is.

The measures confirmed several trends musicologists had long described, with some disagreements around the Classical period. Harmonic innovation dipped early in that era, then rose steeply later, a pattern the authors explain in line with music theory. Composers also clustered neatly by historical period when compared by their habits of moving between keys, and their closest matches lined up with documented influences. The authors note that richer score data would be needed to extend the method across cultures.
plos-pone-0356748:
Seiichiro Ito and colleagues mapped how close residents of Aichi Prefecture, Japan, actually live to pharmacies, hospitals, and clinics, using census data and geographic software. Their 2026 study drew walking and driving catchments around every facility across eleven healthcare regions and calculated the share of residents, and of elderly residents, covered at several distances.

In the Nagoya region nearly everyone lived within a short drive of all three facility types. In the northern Higashimikawa region, coverage collapsed, with only about a third of residents within reach of a hospital, and elderly coverage ran lower still. Transit access split the same way. The maps quantify a familiar rural penalty and show officials exactly where medical deserts persist.
plos-pone-0357048:
Samir Regmi and colleagues dunked seven rice varieties, including local Nepalese landraces, under deep water for ten days to learn which survival strategy works when fields flood completely. Their 2026 trial measured survival after a recovery week along with shoot growth, leaf greenness, and chlorophyll, comparing two philosophies: race upward for air, or sit still and save energy.

Sitting still won. The landraces that barely elongated kept their leaves green and survived best, while the fastest stretcher piled up growth underwater and then died at the highest rate. Statistical grouping cleanly separated the patient conservers from the reckless escapers. Two local varieties emerged as promising breeding material, and the study confirms energy thrift, not heroics, as the trait flood-prone rice needs.
plos-pone-0357448:
Rachel A. Roston, Nicholas J. Tustison, and A. Murat Maga published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on aligning medical images when anatomy is strikingly abnormal. Registration, warping one image to match a template, underpins modern morphometrics, but standard tools align by brightness alone and fail when organs are rearranged. Their label-informed approach lets experts supply segmentations declaring which regions correspond, guiding the warp by biology rather than pixels, inside a widely used open ecosystem.

The demonstration was dramatic: mouse embryos lacking a key developmental gene develop severe spinal curvature scrambling their organs, and ordinary registration failed to match them to a normal template. With label guidance, the knockout embryos registered properly, restoring correspondence organ by organ, raising the power of measurements drawn from the alignment. The method is offered as a general fix for developmental and comparative studies, where the interesting subjects are those breaking ordinary registration.
plos-pone-0358248: Xiong and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on teaching computers to name Chinese dishes from photos. Many dishes look nearly alike, so the task is fine-grained. Their learning method sharpens how the system separates one dish class from its close rivals. The test set is CNFOOD-241, a large named collection. Better dish naming helps calorie apps and menu tools read a photo correctly.
plos-pone-0358348:
Linan Sun, Boyang Fu, and Wenwen Liu built sentiment into stock portfolio design, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Investor mood moves markets, sometimes beyond what company facts justify. The team used the Black-Litterman model, a standard portfolio framework, and wove investor sentiment into how portfolios are constructed.

Sun's sentiment-aware portfolios aim to ride the crowd's emotions profitably rather than be blindsided by them. The Black-Litterman model is a natural home for this, since it already blends market data with investor views. Adding a measured mood signal tests whether sentiment can be used with discipline, not just chased. Fund managers and researchers gain a worked example of behavioral finance applied inside a mainstream tool.
plos-pone-0358648:
Jian Zhang and three colleagues trace how university teaching becomes joined up professional and entrepreneurship skill, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Five hundred eighty-four students rated their courses, teachers, drive, and campus resources, plus what they had truly taken in from the experience. The authors arranged the factors as a process: resources go in, students build understanding, drive turns it into behavior, and results emerge at the end.

Teacher competence, course content, engaged students, and links with enterprises all associated positively with integrated outcomes. The pathway ran mainly through instructional practice, the lived quality of teaching, which acted as the key middle step. Policy support showed no direct association at all, surfacing only through indirect routes. The authors advise universities to spend less faith on policy declarations and more on the classroom processes and industry links that the data truly connect to learning.
plos-pone-0359348: Zhao and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on tracking desert spread on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau. They combined two satellite signals: surface albedo, how bright the ground is, and a glow from plants that shows how green they are. Watching both over time maps where land is turning to desert. The plateau feeds major Asian rivers, so its land health matters far beyond its borders.
plos-pone-0360048:
Masayuki Kato and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on hospital hygiene. After gastrointestinal endoscopes are cleaned by automated reprocessing, germs can remain or return. The authors run microbiological surveillance, regular germ testing, in routine clinical practice, in a prospective randomized study design.

Endoscopes are hard to clean because of their long, narrow channels, and lapses have caused infections worldwide. Surveillance after reprocessing checks whether routine cleaning in real hospitals, not ideal ones, keeps scopes safe. Infection control teams and endoscopy units are the readers who must decide how much testing is enough.
pmc-10048148:
Sallam published a systematic review in 2023 on what ChatGPT, the conversational AI built on a large language model, can do in health care. The review gathers published studies and reports on the tool's use in teaching, research and everyday medical practice. It weighs hopeful findings against the worries raised about accuracy and safety.

Across the collected work, the tool helped with tasks like drafting, summarising and answering study questions, while authors kept flagging errors and bias as live risks. A balanced map of promise and concern is useful as hospitals and schools set rules for AI use.
pmc-13251348: Bipolar disorder patients often skip medications with serious consequences. The authors studied clinical and sociodemographic correlates of poor adherence. The findings guide adherence interventions. Understanding non-adherence improves outcomes. Adherence research improves bipolar care. Correlate identification enables targeted support. Bipolar adherence research guides interventions.
pmc-13397648: lymph cancer translational hematologists in full pick out telling apart angiogenic growth factor dock expression patterns on harmful B cells from mantle cell lymph cancer patients. The team with care profile tumor blood vessel talking. The 2026 Europe PMC paper in full reports the dock expression. It suggests hopeful anti-angiogenic treatment targets. Angiogenic receptors drive tumor vascularization. Mantle cell lymph cancer remains incurable. Target expression becomes therapeutically identified.
pmc-13402648: Can D-limonene help testes recover after testicle surgery for undescended testicles in rats? Arman Norouzi‐Ghalehbala, Mohammadjavad Rezaei‐Varmaziar, and others test the treatment effects. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is andrology drug research. It tests D-limonene after testicle surgery in the rat cryptorchidism model, checking healing results with care.
pmc-13402848: 3D-printed surgery guides for precise sacral tumor removal and reconstruction. Yansong Liu, Yinghua He, and others apply them. pmc-2848648:
Hyatt, Chen, Locascio, and co-authors present Prodigal, a program for finding genes in microbes. Automated gene prediction had improved steadily over the previous decade, yet errors remained common. Prodigal aims to raise the number of genes found correctly, including each gene's exact start site.

Getting start sites right matters because a shifted start changes the predicted protein. Fewer false genes also means cleaner genome annotation for every later study. Prodigal became a standard first step in analysing new bacterial genomes, valued for speed and accuracy on ordinary computers.  Gene starts it reports match hand-checked genomes more often than rival tools.
pmc-3218848:
Segata, Izard, Waldron, and co-authors describe a method for metagenomic biomarker discovery. Their approach compares microbe communities between classes, such as sick and healthy people, then checks steadiness and effect size. The challenge is finding organisms, genes, or pathways that truly explain the differences.

Many apparent differences shrink once steadiness and size are demanded. Their checked method, known as LEfSe, ranks features that separate groups robustly. It helps microbiome studies move from long lists of loose links toward short lists of credible markers to guide care.  Cancer and ageing studies both adopted the method for community comparison tasks.
pmc-3764148:
Salzman, Chen, Olsen, and co-authors study cell-type specific features of circular RNA expression. Thousands of loci in human and mouse genomes produce circular RNA transcripts. At many of those places, the circle is in fact the main RNA form produced.

Using an improved computational approach for finding circles, the team also reports widespread circular RNA expression in the fruit fly. Circles vary by cell type, suggesting regulated roles rather than accidents. Their findings deepened the puzzle of what circular RNAs do inside cells.  Different brain cell types carry distinct circle profiles, the data show clearly.
pmc-4237348:
Walker, Abeel, Shea, and their colleagues introduced Pilon in 2014, a tool for improving microbial genomes. Modern sequencers can produce data for hundreds of bacterial genomes in a single day from one machine. That flood of data calls for fully automated ways to build high-quality assemblies.

Pilon combines variant detection with assembly repair in one integrated tool. It uses the reads themselves to find errors, fill gaps, and fix local mistakes in a draft genome. Better assemblies mean gene calls and outbreak tracking rest on solid ground. The automation lets small labs polish genomes without hand editing each one.
pmc-4978148:
Gorgolewski, Auer, Calhoun, and their colleagues introduced the Brain Imaging Data Structure in 2016. Magnetic resonance imaging had defined modern neuroimaging, with tens of thousands of studies of the living brain. Yet each lab organized its data in its own way, which blocked sharing and reuse.

The structure, known as BIDS, is a format for organizing and describing the outputs of neuroimaging experiments. A common layout lets software read any compliant dataset without custom code. That makes large joint analyses and replication far easier. BIDS became the standard that brain imaging needed as datasets grew and teams merged their work.
pmc-5592248:
Shi, McAllister, O'Brien, and their colleagues estimated the disease burden in 2017 of respiratory syncytial virus in young children. This virus, known as RSV, is a major cause of acute lower respiratory infections in children under five. The team had previously linked it to a large share of severe episodes and many deaths in 2005.

With major research activity in the past five years, they updated global, regional, and national estimates for 2015 through a systematic review and modeling study. RSV is the leading cause of infant hospital admission for breathing infections in many countries. Firm burden numbers guide investment in vaccines and antibody treatments that were then in development.
pmc-5805548:
Linlin Chen, Huidan Deng, Hengmin Cui, and coauthors reviewed inflammation and the diseases tied to it in 2018. Inflammation is the immune response set off by germs, damaged cells, or toxic substances. Short bursts help healing, but long-lasting inflammation harms organs.

The review walks through how this response plays out in the heart, liver, lungs, brain, and other organs. It links common pathways to diseases that look unrelated on the surface. Readers see why swelling, pain, and tissue damage share roots across conditions. The broad survey helps students connect basic immune science with everyday clinical problems.
pmc-6030848:
Andrew Waterhouse, Martino Bertoni, Stefan Bienert, and coauthors described SWISS-MODEL in 2018. The method predicts a protein's shape from a related protein with a known shape. Such models help close the gap between known sequences and known structures.

SWISS-MODEL runs the whole task on a server, from finding a template to building and scoring the model. Clear reports show where the model is firm and where it is shaky. Structural biologists use the models to plan experiments and interpret mutations. The update covers new template libraries and quality checks that keep pace with growing data.
pmc-6324048:
Rolf Nilsson, Karl-Henrik Larsson, Andy Taylor, and coauthors described the UNITE database for fungi in 2018. UNITE supports naming fungi from DNA, using the standard barcode region of ribosomal DNA. It holds around a million public fungal sequences.

Many sequences come from fungi with no formal name, the so-called dark taxa. UNITE gives such sequences stable placeholder labels so studies can still talk about them. The system also handles rival classifications side by side. Ecologists sequencing soil or air samples rely on it to turn raw reads into usable fungal names.
pmc-7095448:
The Coronaviridae Study Group of the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses named the COVID-19 virus in this 2020 paper. The outbreak was the third major spillover of an animal coronavirus into humans in two decades. Naming the virus correctly mattered for clear science.

Comparing genomes across the family, the group placed the new virus within the species of SARS-related coronaviruses. They gave it the name SARS-CoV-2, stressing kinship without equating it to the earlier virus. The disease name, COVID-19, was set separately by the World Health Organization. The paper explains the reasoning that settled both labels.
pmc-7506548:
Haijun Yu and colleagues reviewed in 2020 efforts to treat disease by targeting the NF-kappaB pathway, one of the body's central inflammation switches. The pathway comes in two forms, a fast acting canonical route and a slower non-canonical one. It controls genes tied to inflammation and sits at the crossing point of many other signaling routes.

Because this switch is involved in so many conditions, from arthritis to cancer, blocking it has long tempted drug developers. The authors explain how the pathway works, then survey clinical studies that tried to bend it toward healing. They also weigh the risks, since a switch this central is hard to dampen without weakening normal immune defense.
