podcast-dannyjones-QGCxNo5X348:
Julian Dorey hosts a wide-ranging interview podcast and joins Danny Jones, host to host, to discuss what he calls the deadliest conspiracy theory in the world. The two compare the claims that circulate through their shared world and settle on the one Dorey believes has killed the most people and done the deepest damage.

The conversation works as an industry summit: two men who interview everyone, believers and generals alike, comparing what they have heard off the record. Dorey's choice and his argument for it are the episode's payload, and listeners should treat the ranking as his judgment, not a measurement. The recording's interest is the peer-to-peer candor. Podcasters who usually ask the questions answer them here, and their map of which theories matter, and which merely entertain, differs from the audience's in instructive ways.
podcast-joerogan-Wi0nMTtLr48:
Boxing champion Terence Crawford visits Joe Rogan's MMA Show for number 145. Crawford had just beaten Errol Spence Jr. in a clash of unbeaten champions. Fans and judges had long denied him full credit.

Crawford says he always felt he was the man, long before others agreed. Rogan notes how hard it was to make the dream fight happen. They talk about control, pace, and the joy of finally getting his flowers. The episode lets a quiet champion explain his rise in his own calm words, with respect earned the hard way.
poe-eureka-1848:
Edgar Allan Poe called Eureka a prose poem when it came out in 1848. He held it the great work of his life. The book sets out his view of how the cosmos was made and how it will end. Poe gave the core of it first as a talk in New York.

One prime burst, he holds, flung all stuff out through space. That stuff now draws back, grain to grain, to one mass once more. His view of a world that grows from one start struck fans as a flash of the Big Bang thought. The book is Poe's bold leap at the whole of things.
rhazes-smallpox-measles-greenhill-1848:
The Persian doctor Rhazes, known in Arabic as al-Razi, wrote on smallpox and measles around the year 910. William Alexander Greenhill translated his treatise into English for the Sydenham Society in 1848. Rhazes was the first clinician to set the two diseases clearly apart. Generations of doctors had mixed their fevers and rashes together.

He describes each illness day by day: fever, pains, and the rising of the spots. Treatment follows his wide experience in Baghdad's hospitals. The work shows medieval Islamic medicine at its most observant. Its distinction between the diseases held for centuries. The translation made a classic of Eastern medicine open to English readers.
seidel-pneumatologia-1648:
Abraham Seidel sets out the lore of souls in Pneumatologia, his Latin work of 1648. The name means the study of spirits. Seidel was a church sage in the German lands in the midst of the great war that tore them. His book sorts the kinds of souls: angels, demons, the ghosts of the dead, and the strange forms that plague houses, fields, and the dreams of men in that torn age.

He weighs tales of marvels by the Good Book's rule. Wild claims get a strict sift. The text, in Latin, is a late sum of its school. It shows its age's fears.
seneca-falls-declaration-1848:
Elizabeth Cady Stanton and her allies adopted the Declaration of Sentiments in 1848. The Seneca Falls meeting launched the fight for women's rights. Stanton took the Declaration of Independence as her direct model.

All men and women are created equal, her bold rewrite declares. A list of grievances then charges men with a long tyranny. Denied votes, wages, schooling, and legal standing fill the counts. The call for the ballot shocked even many friends of reform. American feminism counts this short text as its founding manifesto to this day. Its grievance list reads like a mirror held up to 1776 itself.
sperling-de-magia-1648:
Johann Sperling set out ten short claims about magic in this Latin work, printed in 1648. It took the form of a school debate, held at the town of Wittenberg. Such debates let scholars test ideas in public, point by point.

The ten claims deal with magic and with demons, and what each one is said to do. Readers get a clear view of how a trained mind of that age sorted real acts from false ones. Short and plain, it shows the old schools at work on a dark theme.
squier-davis-ancient-monuments-1848:
Surveyors with chains and compasses gave the mound debate its first hard facts in 1848. Ancient Monuments of the Mississippi Valley, by Ephraim Squier and Edwin Davis, was the first book the Smithsonian issued. The two men mapped and dug the great earthworks of Ohio and beyond.

Their plans and measures of forts, mounds, and sacred rings are exact and rich in detail. Claims about the builders could now be tested against drawn proof for the first time. Every later fight over the mounds cites this volume, for or against. It stands as the founding record of American field archaeology.
stearne-confirmation-discovery-witchcraf:
John Stearne backs his mate's hunt in A Confirmation and Discovery of Witchcraft, his book of 1648. Stearne worked by Matthew Hopkins in the great East Anglia hunt. Towns paid them to quiz, watch, and search the charged. Here Stearne prints the words of folk hanged since 1645, as proof the craft is real and the hunt was just in its harsh work.

He meets foes of the hunt point by point. His tone is prim, firm, and free of doubt. The book is the hunt's full case from its next chief hand. It is a hard read.
sydenham-works-vol1-1848:
Thomas Sydenham was a seventeenth-century English doctor famous for watching patients closely instead of trusting medical theory. Because he followed the example of Hippocrates, people called him the English Hippocrates. R. G. Latham translated his Latin works for the Sydenham Society, and this first volume came out in 1848.

The writings cover fevers and the great epidemics that swept through London in his lifetime. Sydenham sorted diseases by their steady symptoms, much as a botanist sorts plants by their form. He also recorded exact case notes and cures that he had tested at the bedside. His method helped start modern clinical medicine.
the-little-duke-richard-the-fearless-pg3: Charlotte Yonge's 1854 Little Duke: Richard the Fearless of Normandy. The beloved children's history, noble and true. Childhood's Middle Ages. Normandy's boy duke, nobly told, childhood's classic, noble and true for young readers, noble and true for young readers.
the-poor-clare-pg2548: Elizabeth Gaskell's haunting story about the Poor Clare: a curse, a drowned lover, and the supernatural. Dark and moving, it is her great ghost story. Victorian terror at its finest. The drowned lover's curse is genuinely chilling.
the-winter-s-tale-pg2248: Time turns his hourglass in this edition: sixteen years pass between Leontes' jealousy and Perdita's return. The bear chases Antigonus off, and Hermione's statue comes alive. The most magical of the romances, grief transfigured into wonder.
tob-0148:
Farid ud-Din Attar, a Persian poet of the twelfth century, sent thirty birds on a quest in the Conference of the Birds. The hoopoe leads them across seven valleys to find the Simorgh, the king of birds. Most fall away; thirty reach the mountain at last.

There the pun at the poem's heart opens: si morgh, in Persian, means thirty birds. The seekers find themselves. Attar fills the road with tales of lovers, madmen, and saints that mirror each stage of the soul's path. The poem is Sufism's greatest allegory. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-4148:
J. M. Rodwell's 1861 translation of the Koran was the first widely read English version made by a scholar who arranged the suras in what he judged chronological order. That innovation shaped Western study of the Quran for a century, letting readers trace the preaching's development from Meccan to Medinan periods. Rodwell's language is dated Victorian English.

His method, though, was pioneering, and his notes reflect serious engagement with Muslim tradition. Modern translators order the text traditionally and dispute some of Rodwell's judgments, but students of reception history still consult him. The volume stands as the Victorian doorway into Islam's scripture, learned, opinionated, and historically important.
treaty-of-guadalupe-hidalgo-1848:
The treaty that ended the Mexican-American War was signed in 1848 at Guadalupe Hidalgo, near Mexico City. Defeated in war, Mexico gave up a vast share of its northern territory to the United States. The land included California and much of what became Nevada, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado.

In return, the United States paid Mexico fifteen million dollars and took on some claims owed to American citizens. The Rio Grande became the border for Texas, and Mexicans living in the ceded lands could choose which country to join. The treaty completed the map of the continental United States, but it left a lasting wound in Mexican memory.
treaty-of-westphalia-1648:
Signed at Münster in 1648, the treaty between the Holy Roman Emperor and France formed one half of the Peace of Westphalia. Envoys for Emperor Ferdinand III and the French crown negotiated it while a companion treaty was settled at Osnabrück. Together the two deals closed the Thirty Years' War, a conflict that had torn central Europe apart since 1618.

The terms redrew borders, settled which faiths could be practiced in German lands, and confirmed that princes could run their own states with far less imperial control. France gained ground along its eastern border. Later writers often treat the peace as the starting point of the modern system of sovereign states dealing with each other as equals.
truman-eo-9981-1948:
Harry S. Truman signed Executive Order 9981 in 1948, by his own hand. The order demands fair treatment for all in the armed forces. Race, color, faith, or origin shall not bar a soldier's fair chance.

Segregation in uniform was to end under the order's firm terms. Truman acted over his generals' doubts and the South's loud anger. The order changed the American military more deeply than any since. Black troops gained a legal claim their service had long earned. Between Lincoln and Johnson, no president struck a bolder rights blow alone. Full integration took years, but the order made it the law's clear aim.
udhr-1948:
The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris in December 1948. Eleanor Roosevelt led the committee that drafted it, drawing on traditions from many countries. The declaration came in the shadow of the Second World War and the Holocaust, when the world had seen where contempt for human rights could lead.

Its thirty articles proclaim rights held by every person, including free speech, fair trials, education, and freedom of religion. The declaration is not a treaty and binds no court, yet it has guided laws and constitutions across the globe. It remains the foundation stone of modern human rights work and the most translated document in history.
un-ga-res-448:
News from the Netherlands shapes Resolution 448, adopted by the General Assembly on 12 December 1950. The Dutch state wrote in June of that year with a change. It would no longer send facts on Indonesia to the UN under Article 73 of the Charter, save for West New Guinea. The reason was plain: the Republic of Indonesia now stood fully free, and had just joined the UN as a member.

The Assembly takes note of the Dutch letter with pleasure. It recalls its 1948 stand on two points. Growth of self-rule in lands not yet free is welcome. And the UN must be told when a land's status changes so much that reports are no longer owed. A short set of requests to its study team follows.
un-ga-res-48:
One more winter of want faced war-torn lands as the General Assembly passed Resolution 48 on 11 December 1946. The relief agency UNRRA was winding down. The Assembly notes that some states would need cash aid in 1947 to import food and other bare needs of life. World bodies and private aid, it fears, may not cover that need in full.

Where such aid fails to come, the text warns, hunger and suffering will follow through winter, spring, and early summer. The leftover relief need must be met at speed, and without waste or doubled effort. Member states had voiced their will to do their part. The vote is a bridge from wartime relief to the great aid plans of the years ahead.
un-ga-res-a-69-48:
Step by step is the path urged in Resolution A/69/48, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Its subject is the cut of the nuclear threat by stages. The text recalls the first vote on the plan, in 1994, and the chain that has run each year since. It restates the world pledge: the total end of nuclear arms, and a world free of them for good.

Two older pacts are held up as guides on the road: the 1972 ban on germ arms, and the ban on chemical arms that came after it. Each shows, the text argues, that a whole class of arms can be wiped out by pact. The nuclear class, it holds, must meet the same end, by steps that can be checked.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 448 (V) was adopted on 12 December 1950. It concerned the growth of self-government in Non-Self-Governing Territories. The Assembly noted word from the Government of the Netherlands, dated 29 June 1950. The Netherlands said it would no longer report on Indonesia under Article 73 e of the Charter, West New Guinea aside. Indonesia was now fully free and a United Nations member. The Assembly took note with pleasure. It asked its information committee to keep reviewing such reports.

General Assembly Resolution 48, adopted on 11 December 1946, planned relief for 1947 as UNRRA wound down. The Assembly warned that some countries would face hunger through the winter and spring without help buying food and other basics. It restated the rule that relief must never serve as a political weapon. Relief must not be handed out by race, creed, or belief.

A Special Technical Committee of ten finance and trade experts was set up to study least needs and report by 15 January 1947. Members were called on to rush their own aid plans and credits. The Secretary-General was asked to weigh a worldwide appeal. The appeal would be built on one day's earnings from people everywhere.

Resolution 69/48 of the General Assembly is the annual comprehensive call for nuclear disarmament. It urges the nuclear-weapon states to halt the improvement, development, production, and stockpiling of warheads and delivery systems, to de-alert and deactivate their weapons as an interim step. It urges step-by-step reductions leading to total elimination within a set timeframe. It seeks a joint no-first-use undertaking and legally binding security assurances for non-nuclear-weapon states, alongside early entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty.
un-sc-res-1248: Security Council Resolution 1248 was adopted in June 1999. The catalog lists its year as 1248, which merely repeats part of the number and predates the United Nations by centuries, so the date in the record is wrong. Beyond the number and the true year, this record names no subject, and none should be invented for it. It is a formal decision of the council, kept as official record text, from a year when the council's agenda ran from Kosovo to East Timor.
un-sc-res-1348: Listed under 2001, Resolution 1348 preserves formal action taken by the United Nations Security Council. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1448:
Angola's sanctions regime came to an end in December 2002. On 9 December 2002 the Security Council lifted the last measures on UNITA. The civil war had closed with a peace deal that April. A monitoring team still owed reports on the sanctions years. The Council said it would give those reports full attention. It restated Angola's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The lifted measures dated from resolutions 864, 1127, and 1173. They had barred UNITA's travel, offices, and diamond trade. The Council also dissolved its Angola sanctions committee at once. That committee had policed the measures since 1993. The text closes a sanctions era that had tried to starve a rebel army of funds.
un-sc-res-1548:
Cyprus again needed its peacekeeping force in the summer of 2004. On 11 June 2004 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 December 2004. The government of Cyprus agreed the force should stay. Weeks earlier, voters on the island had rejected a settlement plan in referenda. The Secretary-General planned a full review of the mission's size and tasks.

The Council welcomed that review and promised to act on it within a month. It repeated its call to address the fate of missing persons with urgency. It urged the Turkish Cypriot side to lift all limits on the force. It also demanded the old military position at Strovilia be restored.
un-sc-res-1648: Resolution 1648, from 2005, is a Security Council decision preserved here in its official-record text. English Wikisource supplied the transcription the collection holds. The act follows the body's classic layout: a preamble that recalls and weighs, then numbered paragraphs that settle the matter. Its preservation keeps one more link in the Council's chain intact.
un-sc-res-1748:
The probe into a Beirut bombing that killed a former prime minister gained more time in 2007. Rafiq Hariri died in the February 2005 attack. An international commission was tracing those behind it. On 27 March 2007 the Security Council welcomed the commission's latest report. It extended the commission's mandate until 15 June 2008. The Council said it could end the work early if the probe finished sooner.

The commission had to report on progress every four months. It could report sooner whenever it saw fit. The Council restated that those behind the attacks must face justice. Other bombings in Lebanon since October 2004 fell under the same demand. Within months, the investigation fed into plans for a special tribunal.
un-sc-res-1848: Resolution 1848, adopted in 2008, is a formal act of the Security Council kept here through English Wikisource. The members vote such texts at headquarters in New York, and the record of the vote is the document itself. This entry holds that document entire: the grounds the Council stated and the steps it voted to require.
un-sc-res-1948:
Bosnia and Herzegovina came before the Security Council in Resolution 1948, adopted on 18 November 2010. Fifteen years after the Dayton peace deal, much of it still lacked full effect. Elections on 3 October 2010 had drawn a strong turnout and passed off in order. Citizens had just won visa-free travel to most of Europe.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the European Union force, called EUFOR, for twelve more months. The NATO headquarters in Sarajevo also stays. Both may use force to uphold the peace deal's military terms. Bosnian leaders must form governments fast, drop divisive talk, and settle open questions like state property. Quarterly reports keep the Council informed.
un-sc-res-248: The catalog's entries for 1967 include Resolution 248 of the United Nations Security Council. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-348:
A thaw between Iran and Iraq was welcomed by the Security Council on 28 May 1974. The Secretary-General's report of 20 May described talks held through his special representative. Both countries had agreed to calm the border situation and improve their relations. The Council recalled its consensus of 28 February 1974 on the dispute.

The two states had accepted four points. They would respect the cease-fire of 7 March 1974 strictly. Troop concentrations along the whole border would pull back jointly and promptly. Hostile acts would halt in full. Early talks without preconditions would seek a settlement of all bilateral issues. The Council voiced the hope that both would act on the deal as soon as possible. It invited the Secretary-General to give any help the two countries asked for in applying it. The opening led the next year to the Algiers Agreement on the Shatt al-Arab.
un-sc-res-448:
Rhodesia's regime staged elections in April 1979 to keep minority rule. The vote was meant to dress up the illegal government in Salisbury. On 30 April 1979 the Security Council condemned the whole effort. It called the elections a manoeuvre to extend racist rule. They were held, it said, to block Zimbabwe's path to independence and true majority rule. African states and the Patriotic Front had addressed the Council.

The so-called elections and their results were declared null and void. No state could recognize any body or representative they produced. Mandatory sanctions on Rhodesia had to be observed strictly. France, Britain, and the United States abstained. Within a year, real elections brought majority rule to Zimbabwe.
un-sc-res-48:
A truce in Palestine needed supervisors on the ground in 1948. The Council had set truce terms in its resolution 46 that April. On 23 April 1948 it created a Truce Commission for Palestine. The commission would be drawn from Council members with consular officers in Jerusalem. Syria said its government was not ready to serve. The others formed the body without it.

The commission's job was to help the Council and the truce parties keep the peace. It worked in Jerusalem at the height of the fighting over the city's future. Its consuls reported on breaches and tried to calm local clashes. The body was an early experiment in field supervision. It fed into the truce machinery that followed the 1948 war.
un-sc-res-648: Catalogued with a 1990 date, Resolution 648 forms part of the Security Council's official record at the United Nations. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording.
un-sc-res-848:
Security Council Resolution 848, adopted on July 8, 1993, recommended Andorra for membership in the United Nations. Andorra, a small land in the Pyrenees between France and Spain, had been ruled jointly by two co-princes since the 1200s: the French head of state and a Spanish bishop. A new constitution in 1993 recast it as a modern sovereign state.

The Assembly seated Andorra on July 28. The council's text is the standard short form, but the setting is rare: a medieval arrangement, kept alive for seven centuries, stepping into the modern system of states. Andorra's admission came in the same season as Monaco's, as Europe's smallest lands took their places.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Kiribati is recommended for United Nations membership in Resolution 1248, adopted on 25 June 1999. The Council had examined the Pacific republic's application, document S/1999/477. Kiribati, a chain of low atolls scattered across a vast stretch of the central Pacific, had been independent from Britain since 1979 but had waited twenty years to join.

The resolution asks the General Assembly to admit Kiribati, following the Charter's standard sequence. When the Assembly voted that September, Kiribati joined alongside Nauru and Tonga in a small Pacific wave. Membership gave a country of under one hundred thousand people, threatened even then by rising seas, a formal voice in world affairs.

Sanctions against Angola's UNITA rebel movement, and the experts who checked whether they were being broken, are the subject on 19 April 2001. A small expert body, called the monitoring mechanism, reported to the Council's sanctions committee. Its final report and a written addendum were now before the Council.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended the mechanism's mandate for six months, ending on 19 October 2001. Up to five experts were to serve on it. They would report to the sanctions committee as they worked and deliver a fuller report by the end date. All states were called on to cooperate fully with the experts' checks.

Angola's sanctions era formally ended with Resolution 1448. It was adopted unanimously on 9 December 2002. The civil war had closed that April. UNITA was disarming and entering politics. A joint commission had finished overseeing the peace terms. Only the leftover sanctions machinery remained in place.

Members wiped out the remaining measures from 1993, 1997, and 1998. The old Angola sanctions committee was dissolved on the spot. A UN trust fund for the file was ordered closed. Contributing states would get their unused shares back, in proportion. The monitoring experts' last reports were still to be read. Even so, the message was clear: Angola's file was moving from punishment to peace.

Niger, a vast landlocked territory in West Africa, left French rule on 3 August 1960. Twenty days later its UN application was before the Council. Resolution 148 was adopted unanimously on 23 August 1960. The vote came at the marathon 891st meeting. Several new African states were recommended that same day.

The Council advised the General Assembly to admit the Republic of Niger. The Assembly approved the admission in September. Niger was desperately poor and mostly desert. Still, its seat counted equally in Assembly votes. The resolution formed part of the 1960 intake. That wave transformed the UN from a club of victors into a near-universal body.

Weeks after Cypriot voters split over a UN reunification plan, the Council paired a renewal with a review. On 11 June 2004, it adopted Resolution 1548 without dissent. One side in the twin votes backed the plan. The other side turned it down. The Secretary-General's May report urged fresh thought on the force itself.

The text welcomes his review of the mandate, size, and methods. It extends the Cyprus mandate to 15 December 2004. The Council vows to act on the review within a month of getting it. Turkish Cypriot forces must lift all curbs on the peacekeepers at once. The status quo at Strovilia must go back to how it stood before mid-2000. Missing persons get a pointed mention too.

The Golan Heights observer force is renewed for six months on 21 December 2005, until 30 June 2006. UNDOF continues to watch the separation between Israeli and Syrian forces. The parties are called on to carry out resolution 338 of 1973 at once. The force's work to enforce the zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse is welcomed. A report is asked for at the end of the period.

Guides that link this text to Nepal have the wrong file. Its world is Lebanon. A huge bomb had killed past prime minister Rafic Hariri on 14 February 2005. A world probe team was digging into the hit. Beirut's prime minister wrote on 21 February 2007 to ask for more time. Resolution 1748 passed on 27 March 2007.

The probe team's term grew to 15 June 2008. The Council praised its fine work in hard times. The team had warned it could not close the case by the old date. Word on the probe was due each four months, or more if the team saw need. The grant could end early if the work wrapped up. The aim stayed stark: find the truth of the blast, and see the guilty held to account.

The Golan Heights observer force is renewed for six months on 12 December 2008, until 30 June 2009. UNDOF continues to watch the separation between Israeli and Syrian forces. The parties are called on to carry out resolution 338 of 1973 at once. The force's enforcement of the zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse is welcomed. A report is asked for at the end of the period.

Bosnia's EU force is renewed in Resolution 1948, adopted on 18 November 2010. Fifteen years after the Peace Agreement, implementation was still incomplete. A solution on state and defence property was outstanding. But the October 2010 elections had been orderly. The EU had just granted Bosnian citizens visa-free entry. EU foreign ministers confirmed EUFOR's executive mandate alongside training support.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes EUFOR, the EU's multinational stabilization force, and the NATO Headquarters in Sarajevo for a further twelve months. They act as legal successors to SFOR. They may use all necessary measures to enforce Annexes 1-A and 2 of the Peace Agreement and control Bosnia's airspace. It restates full support for the High Representative as final authority on civilian implementation, and reminds the parties that cooperation with the Yugoslavia tribunal, including surrendering indictees, remains obligatory. Reports are due at least every three months.

Jordan and Israel both put their cases to the Council in March 1968, in speeches and in letters. Observers on the ground supplied more information. The Council found that Israel had carried out a large military action on Jordan's territory. The action had been carefully planned in advance. Resolution 248 was adopted unanimously on 24 March 1968.

The Council deplored the loss of life and the heavy damage to property. It condemned the Israeli action as a clear violation of the United Nations Charter. The action also broke the cease-fire resolutions that followed the 1967 war. The text said that military reprisals of this kind could not be tolerated. If they continued, the Council warned, it might have to consider stronger steps. Israel was told to refrain from acts that broke the cease-fire terms.

Iran and Iraq step back from a border clash in Resolution 348. It passed on 28 May 1974, with fourteen votes in favor and none against. A UN envoy had worked between the two states. He won their word on a set of steps to cool the feud. The Council cheered their wish to calm things and mend ties.

The deal had four parts. Both sides would keep the truce of 7 March 1974 in full. Both would pull back troops massed along the whole border, at the same time. Both would halt all hostile acts, so talks could breathe. And both would meet soon, with no terms set in advance, to settle all their disputes. The UN chief was asked to help if asked.

Elections staged by the white minority regime in Southern Rhodesia are the target of Resolution 448, adopted on 30 April 1979. Ian Smith's government, which the UN treated as illegal, had held a vote that April under a constitution preserving white power. The Council heard statements from the African Group's chairman and from the Patriotic Front of Zimbabwe.

The Council strongly condemned the manoeuvres meant to keep racist minority rule in place. It declared the April 1979 elections and their results null and void, and told all states to give no recognition to any body created by that process. Mandatory sanctions against the regime were to be observed strictly. Within a year, real majority-rule elections brought Zimbabwe to independence.

War was days away in Palestine when the Council built a truce team. A truce call had gone out on 17 April 1948, in Resolution 46. It needed eyes and legs in Jerusalem. Resolution 48 passed on 23 April 1948 by eight votes to none. Three members held back.

The new Truce Commission drew on Council states with consuls in Jerusalem. Syria said it would not serve. The team would help watch the truce's terms. It had to report in four days, then keep the Council fed with news. Its staff could travel where the work led. The chief had to supply help fast, given the rush. The team's birth shows the UN grasping for tools as the British mandate ran out.

Lebanon asked for more time for the United Nations force in its south at the start of 1990, and the Council agreed. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 25 January, was before the Council. Lebanon's request had come in a letter that month. Resolution 648 was adopted unanimously on 31 January 1990. It concerns UNIFIL, the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon.

The Council extended UNIFIL's mandate for a further interim period of six months, until 31 July 1990. It restated its strong support for Lebanon's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence, within its recognized borders. The force's original terms of reference, set in 1978, were repeated. UNIFIL was expected to carry out its mandate in full. The Secretary-General was to keep consulting Lebanon and the other parties concerned, and to report back to the Council.

Resolution 848, adopted on 8 July 1993, records the Security Council's answer to a membership application. The Council examined the request from the Principality of Andorra. Andorra is a small country in the Pyrenees between France and Spain. The Council recommends to the General Assembly that Andorra be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The Charter requires that step first.
zoist-vol-06-1848:
March 1848 to January 1849 makes up the sixth volume of The Zoist. Europe's year of revolutions forms the backdrop to Elliotson's steady journal. Mesmeric cases arrive as usual: painless dentistry, cured fits, and sleeping subjects who seem to see afar. Cerebral physiology holds its share of the pages.

The journal's network of provincial doctors keeps the reports flowing. Elliotson, long expelled from polite medical society, edits with undimmed fight. Thirteen volumes from 1843 to 1856 form the movement's complete record. Volume six sits near the middle of that run. It shows mesmerism surviving scandal and fashion alike. The archive grows by accumulation.
